The Compass and the Looma complexity disputation

Principia Humanitatis · A Disputation in Complexity

The Compass
and the Loom

A complexity critique of two Cynefin instruments: SwarmCompass (Engage · Discover · Adapt · Enact) and the Weaving Risk and Strategy framework (WRAS, now WRASSE). It covers bees, gorillas, cleaner-fish and the substrate, and the old problem of a manager who wants to stand outside the system he steers.

Mark Downham
Based on Conversations with the Chaos Monkey Collective
London · November 2026

Argumentum

The Argument in Brief

This disputation examines two recent instruments from the Cynefin Company. They were released almost together and belong to the same programme: an "anthro-complexity" alternative to strategy. The first is SwarmCompass, a two-page brochure from 2025 powered by SenseMaker®. It sells "human-AI swarm intelligence" built on three images: bees choosing a hive, radiologists missing a gorilla on a CT scan, and Lincoln telling Congress to "think anew and act anew." The second is Weaving Risk and Strategy (WRAS, renamed WRASSE after the cleaner wrasse), introduced on the Cynefin Co blog on 23 September 2025. It is a two-by-two matrix that crosses natural versus stimulated emergence with fine versus coarse granularity. The resulting four domains are Directed, Opportunist, Hypothesis-based and Distributed, and each is placed on a "substrate" made of technological, cultural, procedural and network layers.

I take both instruments seriously. That rules out polemic, and it also rules out applause. Snowden has been one of the most consequential and combative voices in organisational complexity for a quarter-century. Many of his provocations are still correct: against best practice everywhere, against the tyranny of the average, against confusing a recipe with a context. The argument here is not that the instruments are worthless. The argument is that both instruments contradict, in their working assumptions, the complexity theory they claim as their warrant. Each one also falls back on a figure that complexity thinking has spent forty years trying to retire: the manager who stands outside the system, reads it, and then chooses whether to let emergence happen or to stimulate it.

The critique runs at three levels. The evidential level asks whether the natural-scientific stories the brochure tells are true. Two of them are not. The gorilla study contains no episode in which the people who saw it were talked out of it. The bee swarm does not "always" choose the best site, does not seek "true consensus", and does in fact stake everything on one option. The theoretical level brings the whole complexity corpus to bear: Stacey, Griffin and Shaw's five teleologies; Mead and Elias on gesture, figuration and power; Juarrero on constraint; Kauffman on the adjacent possible; Cilliers on incompressibility; Boisot on codification; Ashby on variety; Prigogine on bifurcation; Ingold on the meshwork; Hutchins on distributed cognition; Peirce on abduction; Boyd on orientation; Mowles on tools as ritual; Flinn on recognition. The political-economic level asks what it means that a theory of distributed sensemaking should come to market as a trademarked, patented, members-only instrument whose deepest promise is authentic alignment.

The critique ends with a reconstruction. If an instrument were faithful to the complexity it invokes, what would it have to give up, and what would it have to admit? Part V proposes a Tidal Loom. It is an alternative that keeps what is valuable in both instruments: distributed narrative sensing, the attention to what is difficult to change, and the preference for many small acts over one large bet. It removes the observer's privilege, the promise of mapped unknowns, and the fantasy of alignment.

A compass assumes a north. A loom assumes a frame. Complexity offers neither, only the next move made among others who are also moving.

Term
Anthro-complexity

What makes human complexity different?

Turn ↻
Anthro-complexity

Snowden's term for complexity in human systems, as distinct from ant colonies or weather. Humans have intentions, identities, stories and power, and they can change the rules of their own game. The disputation takes the term at its word and asks whether the instruments honour it. Do they treat people as agents inside the figuration, or as sensors and substrate to be read from outside? The recurring finding is the second: the term is human, the architecture is not.

Evidence, theory, political economy

Turn ↻
Three levels of critique

The critique runs three ways. The evidential level asks whether the natural-scientific stories are true. The theoretical level asks whether the instruments' assumptions match the complexity corpus. The political-economic level asks what follows when distributed sensemaking is sold as a trademarked product. A claim can survive one level and fail another. The bee fails on evidence, the substrate on theory, alignment on political economy.

Image
Compass and loom

Why these two emblems?

Turn ↻
Compass and loom

A compass assumes a fixed field and gives a bearing. A loom assumes a frame and produces a pattern. Each is a technology of order dressed as an image of navigation or weaving. Complexity grants neither a fixed north nor a fixed frame. The title names what each instrument assumes. The reconstruction keeps the loom as a warp offered by convenors and woven by everyone, and replaces the compass with the Pyxis Incerta, a dial that measures its own uncertainty.

Theses for Disputation

Twelve Theses

Twelve theses from the first edition, with three added in the second (XIII–XV), one amendment to Thesis VII, and eight more in the fourth (XVI–XXIII). Under the Additive Covenant nothing has been withdrawn.

  1. The gorilla is a fable. The brochure's founding anecdote adds a social-conformity episode that the 2013 radiology study does not contain. The study's real finding is that blindness comes from the task frame and not from the person, and that finding undercuts the instruction to "find the 17%" as individuals.
  2. The swarm is mis-sold. Seeley's honeybees decide by quorum, not consensus. They use cross-inhibiting stop signals to avoid premature alignment. They share a common genetic interest that no human organisation shares. And they commit the whole swarm to a single site. Each property contradicts a brochure claim.
  3. The wrasse bites back. The cleaner wrasse, the WRASSE emblem, is the best-studied case of an animal that cheats when unobserved, and it has a famous mimic that looks like a cleaner and eats its clients. The metaphor contains its own critique.
  4. Both instruments keep dual causality. In Stacey's terms, the system is given a formative teleology (it unfolds what is enfolded) while the leader or consultant keeps a rationalist one (choose, deploy, steer). Transformative teleology, in which the future is under perpetual construction and nobody stands outside it, is missing.
  5. "Natural versus stimulated emergence" is the observer in disguise. The WRAS vertical axis assumes someone who can decide to leave a social process alone. In Mead's account every withholding is already a gesture that calls out a response.
  6. The substrate is a stratigraphy and not a meshwork. Placing "culture" as a layer beneath strategy reifies what Elias, Griffin and Mowles show to be the patterning of interaction itself. People become a growth medium.
  7. Unknown unknowns cannot become mapped territory. Kauffman's adjacent possible cannot be stated in advance, and Cilliers's complex systems cannot be compressed. The brochure's central promise is a category error presented as a feature. Amended in the second edition, after the adversary's brief (Movement 11, Pro Parte Contraria): the form of the unknown (its rate, its missing mass, its shape of growth, its error distribution) can be stated in advance, and complex systems compress in their predictive structure. What cannot be stated is the identity, function and meaning of what comes. The category error lies in promising the inventory where only the form is available.
  8. SenseMaker codifies and abstracts, so it moves down the I-Space. In Boisot's terms, signifier triads turn tacit, situated meaning into codified, diffusible data. That data then becomes, explicitly, training data sets for further AI-based automation. The swarm is harvested.
  9. Risk is assigned to quadrants, though it lives in relations. Giving each WRAS domain "its" risk strategy treats risk as a property of a situation rather than an anxiety lived and negotiated among people, as in Shaw and Stacey's Experiencing Risk and Menzies Lyth's social defences.
  10. The novelty is genealogically thin. The four WRAS domains revisit Mintzberg and Waters (1985), March (1991), McGrath's discovery-driven planning and real-options theory without acknowledging them. "The last link in the chain" names a chain that others forged.
  11. Alignment is not leadership. By Flinn's recognition test, "authentic alignment (not just top-down compliance)" describes compliance more honestly than the brochure intends. Recognition, not alignment, separates followership from coercion.
  12. The Way is not a compass bearing. In 道理勢 terms, both instruments seize 勢 shì (propensity) and lose 道 dào, the way that is made only by walking it together. Cook Ding does not weave the ox. He finds the spaces it already has.
  13. The adversary wins half. (Editio secunda.) Tria, Loreto, Servedio and Strogatz predicted the statistics of novelty; Cortês, Kauffman, Liddle and Smolin predicted the timing of its explosion; Turing measured the mass of the unseen; Machta, Transtrum and Sethna showed why complex systems compress. Kauffman and Cilliers survive only for identity, function and meaning, which is where they always mattered.
  14. The watched needle never turns. (Editio secunda.) By the quantum Zeno effect, frequent measurement freezes evolution. An instrument of constant micro-pulses risks suppressing the emergence it claims to detect. Measure weakly.
  15. Harmony is recognised at the rendezvous, not broadcast. (Editio secunda.) By the no-communication theorem, entangled compasses share correlation without signal. Alignment cannot be transmitted to people. It can only be discovered when they meet and compare what each of them lived through.
  16. The answerer is rotated by the question. (Editio quarta.) Question-order effects obey the QQ equality that quantum probability predicts. An assessment that opens with "blind spots" changes the strategy answers that follow, and rotating question order hides the effect from the analyst without undoing it for the respondent.
  17. Every measure of people is a gesture to them. (Editio quarta.) Goodhart, Campbell, Lucas and Soros describe one loop: measure, target, respond, drift. Any instrument that publishes its findings enters that loop, and its period of good fit is the time for most vigilance.
  18. Acumen cannot be installed, only exercised. (Editio quarta.) Snowden's salience, sapience and sentience are a conjunction, which a barycentric triad cannot represent. Read through Boyd, acumen is orientation that can destroy and rebuild itself; read through Deleuze, collective acumen is a refrain. Naming its observables invites Goodhart, and "creating the substrate" risks striating the smooth space it means to nurture.
  19. The Mariner is the observer inside. (Editio quarta.) Kipling's Mariner works from inside the whale, with what is to hand, on a constraint rather than an outcome, and does not forget the suspenders. Design of constraints by insiders with stakes is legitimate; design of substrates by outsiders with products is what Movement 10 opposed.
  20. Leverage is a conjunction. (Editio quarta.) Agency, adjacency and tendency give leverage only together, and all three work by decomposition and recombination. A flash mob and a murmuration both reach scale with no algorithm in sight, by opposite routes.
  21. Leviathan is a pattern of motion. (Editio quarta.) Read as physics, Hobbes's commonwealth is a resultant of endeavours, a store of conferred power and a circulation that dies when it stops. A crowd becomes a Leviathan at the moment someone speaks for it; every convened crowd needs a dispersal rule.
  22. Three books, one confession. (Editio quarta.) Book I, Liber Secundus and Liber Tertius state at three scales that no one sees the form they stand in. Their answers converge: measure lightly, declare the form, offer rather than prescribe.
  23. A diagram is an instrument. (Editio quarta.) Every figure decides what stands out before the reader asks. An honest diagram marks the difference between the author's drawn assertions and the eye's inferred groupings, lets decoration be switched off, and sends the reader back into the argument rather than up to a centre of calculation.

Why theses?

The scholastic disputation

Why theses?

Medieval disputation began with numbered theses, stated sharply so they could be attacked. The form is used here for accountability: each thesis can be checked against the movement that argues it, and the Additive Covenant means a thesis is amended in place, never quietly deleted. Thesis VII shows the method. The adversary's brief forced a partial retreat, and the amendment stands beside the original so readers can see the argument move.

De Methodo

On Sources and Method

For SwarmCompass, the primary text is the two-page Interactive Brochure (Cognitive Edge Pte Ltd, ©2025; generated by InDesign on 5 August 2025). I read it in full and quote its own words where they carry weight. Its phrases are short and declarative, which makes them unusually easy to test.

WRAS has a looser documentary base, and that is partly what the critique is about. The framework was introduced in Snowden's blog post Weaving risk and strategy … (The Cynefin Co, 23 September 2025). It was followed by Wayshaping for substrate management (28 September 2025) and anticipated by The substrate of safety (3 September 2025). The Cynefin.io wiki page on risk management records the framework and carries the notice that it is still under development, do not use or share without permission. A conference abstract (devopsdays Atlanta, 2026) repeats the four substrates and the wrasse etymology. I worked from the published summary of the post, the wiki entry and these companion texts. Where the published material leaves the quadrant arrangement ambiguous, I say so and mark my reconstruction as a reconstruction.

The corpus is the body of complexity literature that has informed the Principia Humanitatis treatises. It includes the complex responsive processes school (Stacey, Griffin, Shaw, Mowles, Flinn) and its sources in Mead and Elias. It includes the complexity sciences (Prigogine, Kauffman, Holland, Bak, Cilliers, Juarrero, Boisot, Ashby), the processual turn (Chia and Holt, Ingold, Deleuze), the pragmatist and enactive traditions (Peirce, Schön, Weick, Hutchins), military theory (Boyd, Clausewitz, Sun Tzu) and the classical Chinese spine 道理勢. Attribution is kept exact. The 2003 IBM Systems Journal paper is Kurtz and Snowden's, but the Cynefin framework is Snowden's creation, and nothing here suggests otherwise.

Conventions. Tables carry a Commentarius tabulae. Figures can be expanded and each carries a Reading. Obligationes stage objection, counter and response in the scholastic manner. Verdict pills (fails partial holds) score claims against evidence. Interactive layer (third edition). Every diagram has an Explore this figure panel. Tap a dashed-outlined label inside the diagram or a numbered chip, or press Walk me through. Expand ↗ opens a zoomable, pannable view. Live models sit beneath key figures, and each movement ends with a deck of explainer cards: tap a card to turn it.

Pars Prima

The Instruments Laid Open

Before judging an instrument, take it apart. This part describes the anatomy only. Each claim is set out in its own words, sorted by kind, and placed in the lineage it comes from.

Movement 1

SwarmCompass: An Anatomy

The brochure has two pages, and its argument is a funnel. Three warrant-images (the bee swarm, the gorilla on the X-ray, Lincoln's annual message) set up a diagnosis: traditional leadership tools leave you adrift in a sea of data without direction. The cure is a fusion. AI sees the map. Humans feel the terrain. The cure is then sold through three movements, Chart the Territory, Plot Multiple Courses and Set Your Course, and closes with a sales sequence: take the SwarmCompass Assessment, discuss your result with a consultant, launch a pilot.

The four verbs on the masthead, Engage · Discover · Adapt · Enact, belong to the sequential improvement cycle. They read as a slower, more reflective cousin of plan-do-check-act or of Boyd's observe-orient-decide-act. A brochure promising human-AI swarm intelligence that doesn't just analyse uncertainty—it navigates through it opens, then, with a four-stage linear sequence. That is not yet a contradiction. Many complexity practitioners use sequences as scaffolding. It is the first sign of a tension that will recur: the instrument talks of distributed emergence and behaves like a staged programme.

The diagram shows that the argument is convergent, and that matters. Everything flows into one diagnosis and one cure. If any warrant on the left fails, the diagnosis loses some of its authority. Part II shows that two of the three fail and the third is misused. The funnel at the bottom does not belong to the science. It is the revenue model, and its first step is a survey designed to reveal what you cannot see, a paradox treated in Movement 4.

The claims, sorted by kind

The brochure makes roughly two dozen distinct claims. They are of four kinds. Empirical claims report facts about the world: radiologists, bees. Theoretical claims report how cognition or organisations work: AI is inductive, humans abductive. Metaphorical transfers carry a property from one domain to another, as in short-cycle feedback loops as a waggle dance. Commercial promises say what the buyer gets. A careful reader keeps these apart because each answers to a different tribunal. Empirical claims answer to the literature, theoretical claims to argument, metaphors to the fit of the analogy, and promises to delivery. The brochure blends all four in one register of confident assertion, and the blending is part of its persuasive method.

Turn for the full explainer ↻
Claim 1 · Empiricalholds
What the brochure says

The brochure opens under the banner “Find the 17%” and reports that 83% of radiologists looking for anomalies on X-rays did not see a gorilla forty-eight times the size of a cancer nodule.

What the tribunal finds

Drew, Võ and Wolfe, “The Invisible Gorilla Strikes Again” (Psychological Science, 2013). Twenty-four radiologists searched five chest CT cases for lung nodules while their eyes were tracked. In the last case a gorilla more than 48 times the size of the average nodule was inserted. Twenty of the twenty-four (83%) did not report it. Eye-tracking showed that most of those who missed it looked directly at it, scrolling past its layer several times. Shown the image afterwards, all of them could see it.

Why the verdict is “holds”

Three facts are right: the 83%, the 48×, and the expert setting. The images were CT slices rather than plain X-rays, a pardonable simplification. The verdict is green because the figure is accurate, not because the brochure’s reading of it is. The study locates blindness in the task: the instruction to look for nodules set a search template, and the gorilla lay outside it. Follow-up work by Williams, Drew and colleagues found that radiologists missed a large breast mass while hunting nodules but found it easily when asked to look, and that experience gave no protection.

What would make it hold

Already holds as a finding. To hold as a lesson it must be read as the study reads it: change the search template, not the searchers.

Claim 2 · Empiricalnot in study
What the brochure says

The brochure adds that the seventeen per cent who saw the gorilla came to believe they were wrong when they talked to the eighty-three per cent who did not.

What the tribunal finds

The study has no conversation phase. The radiologists worked alone and were questioned at the end. The four who saw the gorilla were never exposed to the twenty who did not, and nobody “came to believe they were wrong”.

Why the verdict is “not in study”

The added sentence reads like Solomon Asch’s line-judgment conformity experiments of the early 1950s grafted onto a study of attention. It is not decoration: it turns a perceptual finding into a social one, and the product’s central offer (find the few who see and protect them from the many who do not) rests on it. Both failure modes are real, but they are different. Perceptual framing is remedied by redesigning tasks and instructions; social conformity by changing the power relations that make reporting dangerous. The composite yields a remedy that cures neither.

What would make it hold

It could hold only if a study with a conversation phase were cited for it. The Asch tradition supports the general point about conformity; this study does not.

Turn for the full explainer ↻
Claim 3 · Empiricaloverstated
What the brochure says

Bee scouts seek out a new home, return to dance the site’s location and quality, and after a short period the whole swarm moves to the best of the sites investigated.

What the tribunal finds

In Thomas Seeley’s island experiments (with Visscher, Passino and others; summarised in Honeybee Democracy, 2010), swarms offered one superior and several mediocre nest boxes chose the superior site in most trials, even though it was never the first site found.

Why the verdict is “overstated”

Most trials is not every trial. The swarm’s accuracy is impressive because it is high and not perfect, and its cost is time: deliberation takes hours and often days. An instrument that cites the swarm’s accuracy while promising speed has taken the result and dropped the price.

What would make it hold

“Usually the best, at the cost of slow deliberation” would hold, and would carry the real lesson.

Turn for the full explainer ↻
Claim 4 · Empirical / metaphorinverted
What the brochure says

“Resilience-focused decision making”: the swarm never bets everything on one option, and neither should you.

What the tribunal finds

A swarm is the old queen and roughly half the colony. When it decides, it does not hedge across sites or move a little to each. It commits all of itself to one cavity.

Why the verdict is “inverted”

This is the most striking inversion in the brochure. The biology says: explore widely, commit wholly, and let a threshold, not unanimity, decide when. The brochure keeps the comfortable half of the analogy (many options) and reverses the radical half (total commitment).

What would make it hold

“Explore widely, then commit wholly” would hold, and is the lesson the bees actually offer.

Dynamic course correction through short-cycle feedback loops that act as the organisational “waggle dance”, rapidly aligning on optimal paths.

What the tribunal finds

Quorum biology: scouts revisit sites repeatedly and support builds slowly with site quality; Seeley’s own lesson for human groups is to discourage rapid consensus. Passino and Seeley model the choice as a speed–accuracy trade-off tuned by the quorum threshold, and stop signals (Seeley et al., Science 2012) implement cross-inhibition between rival advertisements.

Why the verdict is “misreads”

The brochure’s version is all positive feedback, dances aligning. The real swarm runs on advocacy and inhibition, a contest of signals rather than an alignment of perspectives, and “rapid” sits at the wrong end of the trade-off. From the complex responsive processes side, “optimal paths” assumes the optimum is latent in the option set (a formative teleology), where Stacey and Mowles see the future made in the present through conflictual interaction.

What would make it hold

“Slow the commitment so that quality, not first arrival, wins, and institutionalise the right to say ‘wait’.”

  • Movement 8 · Five teleologies

Turn for the full explainer ↻
Claim 6 · Theoreticalpartial
What the brochure says

Humans reason in abductive, analogical ways, whereas AI is digital, inductive and dependent on its training datasets.

What the tribunal finds

For Peirce, abduction is the only form of inference that introduces a new idea: the leap to a hypothesis that would make a surprising fact a matter of course. It is fallible, guided by il lume naturale, and it is the first stage of inquiry, followed by deduction and induction. Contemporary generative models produce candidate hypotheses and analogies that look like abductive leaps; whether they “really” abduce is a live question.

Why the verdict is “partial”

Partial, because the human capacity is real but the line between a human who guesses and a machine that only counts no longer holds without argument. The deeper Peircean point is that neither abduces well alone: abduction is disciplined by the community that tests it.

What would make it hold

Drop the possessive split and ask how guesses are generated, tested and corrected across people and tools together.

“Design how knowledge passes between people and tools” would hold.

Kauffman (Investigations, 2000; with Longo and Montévil, 2012): the adjacent possible cannot be prestated, because new functions and uses arise that were not in any prior list; there are no entailing laws, only enablement. A category error, not an overstatement: it treats an open space of possibility as if it were an unexplored but fixed territory. Movement 11′ gives the adversary its due. None of them names the unknown unknowns.

Promise “how much you have not yet seen” and reduce the latency of noticing: the time between something new becoming actual and someone able to respond recognising it.

Partial. “What it would cost to change” is defensible and the instrument’s best inheritance. “What is most likely to change” assumes stable likelihoods, which power-law systems (Bak) do not supply. Record every “cannot be changed” with a date and a condition, and revisit it when conditions move.

What the tribunal finds

Multi-horizon planning and scenario stress-testing are standard strategy practice, with a long scenario literature behind them (Wack’s work at Shell among it). Holling’s panarchy shows that horizons are coupled across scales: fast cycles can “revolt” upwards and slow ones “remember” downwards.

Why the verdict is “conventional”

Conventional: neither wrong nor new. The hidden assumption is that the horizons are separable. Cross-scale coupling means the interesting risk is often in the links between horizons. And Farmer and Lafond suggest that each horizon should carry an error distribution, not a point scenario.

What would make it hold

Watch the couplings between horizons, and give each horizon its error bars.

Boyd put Orientation at the centre of the OODA loop: shaped by heritage, tradition, experience, new information, analysis and synthesis, sending implicit guidance and control straight to observation and action. Why the verdict is “plausible”

Plausible, because faster feedback is achievable and valuable. But the speed Boyd prized depends on an orientation already rich enough to read the situation faster than it changes. That is grown through immersion and the destruction and recreation of one’s own models; no survey supplies it. An external compass that delivers orientation as a product locates the decisive faculty outside the organisation that needs it.

Pair tempo with cultivated orientation: a crew that has been at sea together.

The table is weighted towards red, and the reason should be clear. The red verdicts do not cluster round the peripheral claims. They cluster round the load-bearing ones: the gorilla anecdote that names the product's central metric (the 17%), the bee biology that names the product itself (Swarm), and the consensus and alignment promise that is its deepest value proposition. The green verdicts (the 83% figure, the tempo claim) are the ones where the brochure states something either well documented or modest.

The silent premise

Under the inventory sits one premise the brochure never states and could not do without. There is a vantage point from which the swarm can be read. Someone deploys the micro-pulses. Someone identifies the 17%. Someone sees which options hold under pressure and sets the course. The swarm scouts and dances, and the leader reads the dance. This is the oldest arrangement in managerial cybernetics: a system in the middle, a sensor array at its periphery, and a governor at the top who reads the instruments. Norbert Wiener named the governor kybernetes, the steersman. The brochure presents its steersman as a swarm member, but he is still the one holding the compass.

The swarm scouts. The swarm dances. The client reads the dance.

Altius The funnel as a dissipative structure

Read with Part VIII's kinetic ontology, the brochure's 'Next Steps' funnel is not a sales device bolted onto a theory; it is the field that keeps the theory's fold open. Assessment, conversation, pilot and training form a circulation through which attention and fees flow. Prigogine's dissipative structures persist only while energy passes through them, and the funnel is how the instrument stays far from equilibrium. The test this suggests is thermodynamic, not rhetorical: ask what happens to the instrument's claims if the circulation stops. A science survives without its funnel. A product does not. That is the cleanest way to tell which one SwarmCompass is.

Movement 2

Weaving Risk and Strategy: An Anatomy

WRAS has a different textual character. It is not a brochure. It is a working framework announced on a practitioner's blog, still openly under construction, still unsure of its own name. The September 2025 post offers several candidate expansions of the extra letters, all built on "Weaving Risk and Strategy…": through Sensemaking and Engagement, in Substrate Management, for Structural Evolution, from Emergent Substrates, through Substrate Entanglement. It invites readers' opinions. By then WRASSE was gaining traction, borrowed from the family of reef fishes.

The provisional status is an honest feature, and I count it in the framework's favour. A framework that admits it is unfinished is more complexity-congruent than one that arrives fully armoured. Even so, the provisional framework already makes strong claims. It is described as the last link in the chain towards a complexity-based alternative to strategy, and as taking a non-linear approach. Its core proposition, recorded on the Cynefin wiki, is that the basic principle of strategy is to respond to or manipulate the substrate before taking on the risk of a major intervention, which means starting from how things are rather than from an idealised vision.

The two axes

The framework crosses two dimensions. The vertical runs from natural emergence ("just let it happen") to stimulated emergence (acting in order to discover what is possible). The horizontal is granularity, from many fine-grained interventions to coarse-grained, massive allocations of resource. Four domains result:

Directed

Conventional research identifies what to do. It is combined with competitive analysis, and resources are then committed to the resulting strategy. The classic strategy approach.

Opportunist

An opportunity is spotted and significant resources are invested in it.

Hypothesis-based

Several hypotheses about what should happen compete and have to be resolved.

Distributed

Described as a key new area, with little further specification in the published material.

The published descriptions do not say with full clarity which quadrant sits where. The figure below is my reconstruction, built from the definitions. Directed and Opportunist are both coarse-grained (they commit "significant" or concentrated resources). Directed manufactures its object through research, which puts it towards stimulation. Opportunist waits for an opportunity to appear, which puts it towards natural emergence. Hypothesis-based and Distributed are fine-grained. Hypothesis-testing deliberately stimulates in order to discriminate, and distribution lets many small things happen. Readers should hold this placement lightly. The critique in later movements does not depend on it.

Read the matrix the way a strategist would and it looks like a menu: pick your quadrant. Read it the way a complexity theorist would and ask who is doing the picking. The axes are framed as modes of action available to an agent, and in that sense the framework is honest. It is a decision aid for someone deciding. Movements 8 and 9 argue that this same feature puts back, at the centre of the diagram, the sovereign chooser that the anthro-complexity programme set out to remove. The empty circle is the most important element in the figure.

The substrate

WRAS sits on a concept it takes from Estuarine Mapping: the substrate. The Cynefin wiki defines it as the properties of the underlying system and context, the space on, in and through which the organisation or individual grows. Within an organisation it is broken into four: the technological (software stack, data architecture, core technologies), the cultural (shared values, beliefs, behavioural norms), the procedural (core processes, governance, workflows) and the network (relationships with partners, suppliers, competitors). Strategy works on the substrate first, before any major intervention.

I stacked the layers deliberately to make the metaphor visible. The framework itself does not say that culture lies "under" process. The word substrate says it for the framework. Ask where the people are in the figure. They are dissolved into the "cultural" layer as values and norms and into the "network" layer as relationships, and they are absent as agents. Movement 10 treats this as the most consequential ontological decision WRAS makes.

Lineage

WRAS is the newest member of a family. Cynefin (Snowden, from 1999) sorts contexts by their causal ontology. The Flexuous Curves address time and the transition of narratives. Estuarine Mapping (first edition, October 2022) maps constraints by the energy and time needed to change them. It identifies what is in practice impossible to change and what cannot be controlled, and so locates the zone where strategic action can actually happen. Estuarine draws in turn on constructor theory through the Substrate-Independence Theory paper (Turner, Snowden and Thurlow, Systems, 2022). WRAS also links to AIMS and "the three As", which the wiki mentions without fully expanding. The wiki places WRAS largely in the top half of Cynefin, across the complex, complicated and aporetic/confused zones.

The timeline shows a drift from ontology (Cynefin asks what kind of system this is) through epistemology (SenseMaker asks how we can know it at scale) and energetics (Estuarine asks what it would cost to change) to decision (WRAS asks what we should do, at what grain) and finally product (SwarmCompass asks what you will buy). Each step moves closer to the client's question, and on the argument here, each step takes the instrument further from the complexity that justified the first.
Altius Granularity as a renormalisation choice

WRAS's horizontal axis, fine against coarse granularity, has a precise analogue in physics: the renormalisation group, in which one describes a system at a chosen scale by averaging out finer detail. Kenneth Wilson's insight was that the right description depends on the scale of observation, and that some properties survive coarse-graining while others vanish. Read this way, WRAS's granularity is not a property of a decision but a choice of observational scale, and different choices make different features of the same situation salient. The framework presents the axis as a fact about the world. Part VII would call it a measurement basis, chosen before the question is asked.

Movement 3

Family Resemblance

The two instruments have different registers and the same grammar. SwarmCompass is the shop window and WRAS is the workshop. Both promise to replace linear planning. Both make distributed small acts the virtuous default. Both rely on a natural-historical emblem, the bee and the wrasse. Both separate the system that emerges from the agent who reads, nudges or stimulates it.

Table 2 · The two instruments compared

Enemy"Traditional leadership tools"; data without insightLinearity in planning; idealised visionsPlanning as strawman

The right-hand column is the subject of this disputation. Each entry is an assumption the instruments share, so the critique of one carries over to the other. The fourth row, read, then act from above, is the root from which most of the others grow. Part III follows that root through the corpus.

Two instruments, one grammar. The system emerges, the client reads it, and the consultant sells the reading glasses.

Altius Family resemblance as a polythetic class

Wittgenstein's family resemblance has a formal counterpart in numerical taxonomy: a polythetic class, in which every member shares many features with others but no single feature is shared by all. Sokal and Sneath built classification on this idea in the 1960s. The Cynefin family of instruments is polythetic in exactly this sense, which is why critiques of 'the framework' keep missing: they attack a feature some members lack. The disputation therefore ranks claims by how many instruments carry them. A claim carried by all five, such as the substrate metaphor, is a structural commitment. A claim carried by one is a product feature.

The Natural Histories Examined

A framework that rests its authority on nature owes nature accuracy. This part checks each story the instruments tell against the literature it came from.

Movement 4

The Gorilla and the 17%

The brochure opens under the banner Find the 17%. Radiologists were asked to look for anomalies in a set of X-rays. Eighty-three per cent did not see a gorilla, forty-eight times the size of a cancer nodule, on the final image. The brochure then adds that the seventeen per cent who did see it came to believe they were wrong when they talked to the eighty-three per cent who did not. The second sentence carries most of the commercial weight. It turns a perceptual finding into a social one, and on that social finding the product's central offer rests: identify the few who see, and protect them from the many who do not.

What the study found

The study is Drew, Võ and Wolfe, The Invisible Gorilla Strikes Again: Sustained Inattentional Blindness in Expert Observers (Psychological Science, 2013). Twenty-four radiologists performed a familiar lung-nodule detection task on five chest CT cases, scrolling through the slices while their eyes were tracked. In the last case a gorilla, more than 48 times the size of the average nodule, was inserted. Twenty of the twenty-four did not report it. Eye-tracking showed that most of those who missed it looked directly at it. They scrolled past the gorilla's layer several times on average. Afterwards, shown the image again, they could all see it.

The brochure has three of these facts right: the 83%, the 48×, and the setting. (The images were CT slices rather than plain X-rays, a pardonable simplification.) The fourth claim is the problem. The study has no conversation phase. The radiologists were not brought together. The four who saw the gorilla were not exposed to the twenty who did not, and nobody "came to believe they were wrong". The radiologists worked alone and were questioned at the end. The added sentence reads like the plot of Asch's line-judgment conformity experiments of the early 1950s grafted onto a study of attention. However it got there, it is not in the source.

The left panel is a grid of independent cells, and the right panel is a crowd. The brochure's version needs the crowd, because the product sells a social remedy: find and protect the dissenters. The study's finding needs only the cell. What hid the gorilla was not peer pressure. It was the radiologists' own task, the instruction to look for nodules, which made them, in Wolfe's phrase, see what they were looking for. That remedy is institutional, not selective.

Why the error matters theoretically

The embellishment is more than a slip in footnoting, because it changes where blindness lives. In the study, blindness belongs to a situation: an expert, a task, an instruction, a search template. Change the instruction and the blindness changes. The Utah follow-up work by Williams, Drew and colleagues found that radiologists missed a large breast mass and enlarged lymph nodes at high rates while hunting for nodules, yet detected the same abnormalities easily when asked to look for them. The same work found that experience gave no protection: seasoned radiologists were as likely to miss the unexpected as trainees.

Now take the brochure's instruction: Identify your 17% – the individuals who sense shifts before they're measurable… find the mavericks you need to pay attention to. This moves blindness out of the situation and into the person. It suggests that some people see and others do not, and that the task is to find the seers. On the evidence, the four radiologists who saw the gorilla in 2013 are not a stable caste of noticers. Under a different instruction on a different day, the twenty might see and the four might not. Selecting mavericks does not remove inattentional blindness. It assigns the blindness to someone else's search template.

This is where the complex responsive processes school comes in. Stacey's long argument against the monadic individual (in the fifth edition of Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics, strategic choice theory treats the individual as prior to and primary over the group) applies directly. "The 17%" is a population of monads with a trait. In Mead's account, perception is a phase of the social act. What a radiologist sees is shaped by the generalised other of radiology, the "me" that knows what a scan is for. The gorilla was invisible because it was not a social object of the radiologists' practice. In Griffin and Stacey's sense, a social object is a generalised tendency to act that takes particular form in local interaction. Nodules were social objects; gorillas were not. The remedy is not to find the people who stand apart from the practice. It is to change the conversation in which the practice is constituted, so that the unexpected becomes something people are expected to report.

Objectio

The brochure is marketing, not scholarship. The point stands without the embellishment: minorities do perceive what majorities miss, and organisations do suppress dissent. Asch demonstrated as much. Why hold a sales page to the standard of a literature review?

Sed contra

The anecdote is not decoration. It is the headline (Find the 17%), it names the deliverable (identify your 17%), and it is offered as science. The final panel of the brochure says the company has a twenty-year history of science-based methods. A firm whose identity is the correction of pseudo-scientific management fads has to meet the standard it sets for others.

Respondeo

The suppression of dissent is real, and the Asch tradition documents it. It is not what this study shows, and running the two together hides the more useful lesson. Organisations should address both failure modes, perceptual framing and social conformity, and they need different remedies. Framing is addressed by redesigning tasks and instructions so the unexpected is something people are invited to report. Conformity is addressed by changing the power relations that make reporting dangerous. Neither is addressed by a survey that ranks individuals as noticers. The brochure's composite produces a remedy that answers neither problem.

The survey that maps what cannot be seen

One more irony sits in the "Next Steps" column. The first step is the SwarmCompass Assessment – a question survey to map your decision-making blind spots. The 2013 study is about precisely what cannot be self-reported. The radiologists did not know they had missed the gorilla. Asked directly afterwards, they said they had seen none. A questionnaire about blind spots meets the problem that blindness is invisible to the person who has it. At best it maps beliefs about one's blind spots, which is a different and more flattering object. At worst it becomes what Mowles and Stacey call a social defence: a procedure that relieves the anxiety of not-knowing by producing a document that looks like knowing.

You cannot ask someone where their blind spot is. That is what makes it a blind spot.

Altius Inattentional blindness and the attentional set

Since Mack and Rock (1998), inattentional blindness has been explained by attentional set: observers tune to the features a task makes relevant, and items outside that set fail to reach awareness even when fixated. Drew, Võ and Wolfe's radiologists searched for light, round nodules; the gorilla was dark and shaped otherwise. Most and colleagues (2005) showed that what is missed depends on how similar the unexpected object is to the attended features. The Part VII reading is exact: the task frame is a projection that sets the basis, and the gorilla lay orthogonal to it. Training 'mavericks' does not help; changing the search template does.

Movement 5

The Swarm That Always Chooses Best

The product is named after a swarm. The brochure describes bee scouts seeking out a new home and returning to perform a dance that shows the site's location and quality. After a short period the entire swarm moves to a new location, and the brochure says it is always the best of those to have been investigated. It then draws three lessons: adaptive scouting, dynamic course correction through short-cycle feedback loops that act as the organisational waggle dance, rapidly aligning on optimal paths, and resilience-focused decision making on the grounds that the swarm never bets everything on one option—neither should you.

The biology is among the most elegant in behavioural ecology, mostly through Thomas Seeley's decades of work at Cornell with Kirk Visscher, Kevin Passino and others, summarised in Honeybee Democracy (2010). It is worth getting right. Getting it right contradicts the brochure at nearly every point where the brochure draws a lesson.

Five corrections

First, "always" is "almost always". In Seeley's island experiments, swarms offered one superior and several mediocre nest boxes chose the superior site in most trials, even though it was never the first site found. Most trials is not every trial. The accuracy is impressive because it is high and not perfect, and the cost of that accuracy is time.

Second, the process is slow on purpose. The deliberation takes hours and often days. Seeley describes scouts debating for two days, revisiting sites, and slowly building up support. His own lesson for human groups is to discourage rapid consensus. The brochure's rapidly aligning on optimal paths reverses the biology. The swarm is accurate because it resists rapid alignment.

Third, the swarm decides by quorum, not consensus. Once about fifteen or more scouts are present at one site at once, they switch behaviour. They begin piping, which signals the swarm to warm its flight muscles, and the swarm leaves. In the paired-site experiments the swarm took off while scouts were still dancing strongly for the rival site. A decision without consensus is the mechanism. The brochure promises to surface true consensus through participatory intelligence, which is the opposite of what its emblem does.

Fourth, the decision depends on inhibition as well as advocacy. Seeley and colleagues showed in 2011–12 that scouts deliver stop signals, brief head-butts accompanied by a vibration, to dancers advertising rival sites. This cross-inhibition, formally similar to inhibitory circuits in primate brains, prevents deadlock and lets one option win. The brochure's version is all positive feedback, dances aligning. The real swarm runs on positive and negative feedback, advocacy and inhibition. It is a contest of signals, not an alignment of perspectives.

Fifth, the swarm bets everything on one option. This is the most striking inversion. A swarm is the old queen and roughly half the colony. When it decides, it does not hedge across sites or move a little to each. It commits all of itself to one cavity. The breadth is in the exploration phase. The commitment is total. The swarm never bets everything on one option—neither should you gets the biology backwards. If there is a lesson, it is explore widely, commit wholly, and let the threshold, not unanimity, decide when.

Compare the shapes. The left converges like a funnel. The right is a contest with inhibitory links, shown as red crosses, and a threshold. The left-hand shape is the one organisations already have: many inputs, one aligned output. The right-hand shape is the radical one, a decision that tolerates continuing dissent and does not wait for agreement. In borrowing the bee, the brochure has kept the conventional half of the analogy and left out the radical half.

The deepest disanalogy: interest

There is a sixth point, and it goes past a correction to a question of category. Visscher put it directly in commenting on the stop-signal research: all the bees have a common interest in choosing the best available site. A swarm is a superorganism of sisters with a single reproductive fate. No scout benefits from the swarm choosing a poor site. No faction of scouts profits from one site at the expense of another. No scout's bonus depends on her site winning. Information is honest because interest is shared.

Human organisations are made of exactly what the swarm lacks. Elias's figurations are webs of interdependent people bound by asymmetric and shifting power-ratios. In Complex Responsive Processes in Organizations Stacey makes power a property of every relationship and not a disturbance of some ideal neutral state. Mowles, in Rethinking Management and Complexity: A Key Idea for Business and Society, insists that any complexity-informed account of organising must take politics seriously, because people have interests, form coalitions and include and exclude one another. Scouts dance honestly because nothing is gained by dishonesty. Employees, customers and partners scanning the environment for SwarmCompass are in a different position. What they report bears on their careers, their budgets, their teams, their standing and their fears. In the anthro-complexity programme's own terms (the Multi-Ontology Sense Making paper distinguishes human from non-human complexity and coins contextual complexity for the difference), the bee is the wrong emblem precisely because it is not human.

The third column is not offered as advice to readers. It shows how much more interesting the true analogy is than the one sold. The real swarm offers organisations a genuine challenge: decide before agreement, institutionalise inhibition, commit wholly. That challenge is uncomfortable, and the brochure replaced it with something comfortable.

The bees teach that you can decide while others still disagree. The brochure sells the bees as a way to make everyone agree.

Altius Swarm decisions as a speed–accuracy trade-off

Passino and Seeley modelled nest-site choice as a trade-off that the swarm tunes through its quorum threshold. A high quorum gives accurate but slow choices; a low quorum, fast but error-prone ones. Seeley and colleagues (2012) showed that stop signals implement cross-inhibition, the same motif that prevents deadlock in models of neural decision-making, and Pais and colleagues showed it lets swarms break symmetry between equal sites. The brochure's 'rapid alignment' sits at the wrong end of this trade-off. A human group that wanted the bees' accuracy would deliberately slow its convergence and institutionalise stop signals: protected dissent with teeth.

Movement 6

The Wrasse and Its Mimic

WRAS became WRASSE partly for the fish. The devopsdays abstract gives the reasoning. Wrasse are known in ecology as cleaners of the ecosystem and masters of adaptation. Like the wrasse that changes colour to thrive in shifting environments, the framework helps organisations adapt. Like the wrasse that removes parasites and keeps the reef healthy, it helps identify and reduce risk. The name, the abstract says, evokes intelligent adaptation and symbiotic relationships within a complex system.

The emblem was well chosen, though not for the reasons given. The bluestreak cleaner wrasse, Labroides dimidiatus, is one of the most closely studied cases in the evolution of cooperation, and what has been learned about it is less comforting than the abstract suggests.

What the cleaner wrasse actually teaches

The cleaner prefers to cheat. Grutter and Bshary (2003) showed that cleaner wrasse prefer client mucus and tissue to the parasites they are supposed to remove. The relationship is mutualist only on the surface. Underneath it is a standing conflict of interest, held in check by the clients.

The cleaner behaves better when watched. In Image scoring and cooperation in a cleaner fish mutualism (Nature, 2006), Bshary and Grutter showed that clients eavesdrop on cleaning interactions and prefer cleaners they have seen behaving cooperatively. Cleaners, in turn, learned to feed more cooperatively when an image-scoring bystander was present. An earlier paper by Bshary had a franker title: Biting cleaner fish use altruism to deceive image scoring clients (2002).

Clients discipline cleaners through a market. Clients that can switch cleaners get better service. Clients punish cheating cleaners by chasing them or leaving. Cleaner mutualisms are a textbook biological market. The reef stays healthy not because the cleaner is virtuous but because the clients are vigilant and have alternatives.

The cleaner has a mimic. The sabre-toothed blenny, Aspidontus taeniatus, has evolved to look like the cleaner wrasse in colour, stripe and swimming display. Clients approach it expecting a cleaning and are bitten. It exists because the cleaner's reputation is valuable enough to fake.

"Changing colour" is usually sex change. Many wrasses are protogynous hermaphrodites. In Labroides harems the dominant female can become male when the male is lost. The colour changes the abstract celebrates are mostly changes of reproductive role inside a hierarchy, not adaptive camouflage.

The figure puts the framework's own emblem in its full ecology, and the ecology is a governance lesson. A cleaner does not stay honest because it means well. It stays honest because others can see it, compare it, and leave it. Applied to a consultancy-owned risk framework, the lesson is that the framework's value to clients depends on the transparency, comparability and contestability of its claims. That is exactly what the wiki's notice, do not use or share without permission, holds back. Critical disputation of this kind is the bystander that keeps the cleaner honest.
Table 4 · The wrasse: metaphor, biology, implication
Metaphor offeredBiology documentedImplication for a risk framework
Cleaner of the ecosystemPrefers client mucus. Cooperation is conditional.A risk service has its own interest, which can diverge from the client's. Name it.
Symbiotic relationshipKept up by partner choice and punishment, a market.Symbiosis needs exit options and comparison. Proprietary closure weakens both.
Master of adaptationBehaves better under observation, which is reputational adaptation.Adaptation can be adaptation to being watched. Audit when not watched.
Changes colour to thriveColour change mostly follows sex change within a harem hierarchy."Adaptation" may be a shift of position in a dominance order, not a fit to the environment.

This table is not meant as a gotcha. Snowden is a deliberate and literate chooser of metaphors, and the wrasse may have been picked partly for its ambiguity. Even so, a framework that chooses an emblem takes on the emblem's whole natural history. Read that way, the wrasse is a more honest emblem than the abstract allowed. It says that cleaning is a contested relationship, honest only under watching eyes.

The cleaner wrasse is honest when watched. So is every framework.

Altius Audience effects and reputation markets

Bshary and Grutter (2006) showed that cleaner wrasse cooperate more when observed by potential clients: an audience effect that turns each interaction into a reputation signal. Pinto and colleagues later showed cleaners adjust behaviour to the presence of bystanders. In game-theoretic terms, the cleaning station is a biological market in which partner choice disciplines cheating. The Part VII reading inverts the brochure's moral: cooperation here is produced by being watched, which is exactly the reflexive dynamic Goodhart warns about in human institutions. The wrasse does not teach trust; it teaches that observation is itself an intervention.

Movement 7

Lincoln, 1862: Borrowed Thunder

The brochure closes with Lincoln: the dogmas of the quiet past are inadequate to the stormy present; the occasion is piled high with difficulty, and we must rise with the occasion; as our case is new, we must think anew and act anew. The quotation is accurate and correctly dated, from the Annual Message to Congress of 1 December 1862.

Context matters for the reading, as it always does. The passage belongs to Lincoln's argument, in the second winter of the Civil War, for proposed constitutional amendments on compensated, gradual emancipation. It comes a month before the Emancipation Proclamation took effect. The sentences after the quoted lines are the famous ones: we must disenthrall ourselves, and then we shall save our country. Lincoln is not praising distributed sensemaking. He is a wartime executive using all his rhetorical sovereignty to persuade a legislature to make a deliberate, coarse-grained, irreversible intervention at the level of the Constitution, on the gravest moral question of the republic.

In WRAS terms the speech is Directed, not Distributed. The brochure borrows the thunder of a sovereign act of political will to sell an instrument whose stated philosophy is the opposite: many small probes, emergence over design, the swarm over the steersman. The quotation shows, more truthfully than the brochure intends, the desire running underneath it. The client wants to be Lincoln: to see the stormy present clearly, to rise with the occasion, and to act. The swarm is the method and the sovereign is the fantasy.

The 17% who saw the gorilla, the bees who found the best site, and the President who disenthralled the nation are three images of one hero: the one who sees rightly when others do not, and is vindicated.— the brochure's implicit myth

Shaw's warning in Changing Conversations in Organizations applies here. She says we are never on top of or ahead of the process we participate in, and that the wish to be so leads to delusions of omniscience and omnipotence. The closing Lincoln is not a flourish. It shows what the instrument is for. It promises the reader the place of the one who sees, which is the place complexity says nobody occupies.

The swarm is the method. The sovereign is the fantasy.

Altius Quotation as a speech act

Austin and Searle distinguished what an utterance says from what it does. Lincoln's 'think anew and act anew' in December 1862 did something specific: it prepared Congress for compensated emancipation and the reframing of a war. Lifted into a brochure, the same words perform a different act, conferring gravitas on a product. Skinner's Cambridge school would ask what Lincoln was doing in saying it, and the answer constrains legitimate reuse. The point is not pedantry. A borrowed illocution carries an unpaid debt: the authority of a moment that the borrower did not live through and cannot underwrite.

The Corpus Brought to Bear

With the natural histories corrected, the question turns from the instruments' stories to their theory. Ten movements bring the complexity corpus to bear, each on one load-bearing assumption.

Movement 8

Five Teleologies and a Split Causality

In Complexity and Management: Fad or Radical Challenge to Systems Thinking? (2000), Stacey, Griffin and Shaw gave organisational theory one of its sharpest diagnostic tools. They asked of any theory what kind of causality it assumes, meaning what it takes movement into the future to be for and towards. They identified five teleologies. The tool's force lies in a second finding: most management theories use two of them at once, one for the organisation and another for the manager, and never notice the split.

Table 5 · The five teleologies (after Stacey, Griffin & Shaw, 2000)
TeleologyMovement is towards…Reason for movementKind of future
Secular natural lawAn optimal, timeless stateUniversal laws; efficient causeRepetition of the past; predictable
RationalistGoals chosen by reasoning individualsHuman reason and choiceDesigned; the novelty is in the chooser
FormativeA mature form already enfoldedUnfolding of what is latent in the systemKnown in its essentials; development
Adaptionist (Darwinian)Survival / fit to environmentRandom variation, competitive selectionUnknown, but not chosen
TransformativeContinuity and transformation of identity at onceParadoxical movement of local interactionUnder perpetual construction; unknowable yet recognisable

The transformative teleology is the CRP school's own proposal. In it the future is created in the present through the interplay of intentions, and no one, not leader, consultant or theorist, stands outside the process as its author or observer. The guard-phrase is this: each moment is a repetition of the past with the potential for transformation.

Locating the instruments

Run the instruments through the table. The swarm, as the brochure presents it, is formative. It always arrives at the best site among those investigated, so the optimum is latent in the option set and the process unfolds it. The substrate in WRAS is also formative. Its energy gradients, propensities and dispositions are properties of the system that will express themselves along the paths of least resistance. Estuarine Mapping's aim, to manage dispositions so that what you want costs less energy than what you don't, is formative teleology stated as technique.

The client, though, is rationalist. The client deploys micro-pulses, identifies the 17%, sees which options hold, sets the course, chooses the quadrant, sets the granularity, decides whether to let emergence happen or to stimulate it. The consultant is doubly rationalist. The consultant designs the signifiers, the assessment and the pilot. The novelty of the future lives in the choosers. The system's job is to unfold.

Stacey's point is that this two-storey arrangement is the signature of systems thinking, not of complexity. The manager designs and the system unfolds the design. Complexity science, rightly understood, collapses the upper box into the lower one. The client is a dot. Their choosing is one more local interaction among others, with consequences they cannot foresee or control. The instruments speak the vocabulary of the lower box (emergence, swarm, substrate) and keep the architecture of the upper box.

Why the split survives

Why should a programme as deliberately anti-systems-thinking as Snowden's rebuild the split? The CRP answer is that the split is not an intellectual mistake waiting for a better argument. It is a response to anxiety. Clients do not buy instruments that tell them they are one dot among many, unable to stand outside the patterns they help produce. They buy instruments that give them back the upper box. In Complexity and Organization: Readings and Conversations and the later editions of Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics, Stacey and Mowles repeatedly observe how complexity concepts are taken up by management discourse and returned to the service of control. Emergence becomes a lever, self-organisation becomes a technique, the edge of chaos becomes a destination. The instruments are a fresh case of a familiar process.

To be fair, Snowden himself has argued against this capture for years. He objects to "complexity" sold as a fad, to the abuse of complex adaptive systems theory as metaphor, and to the claim that one can engineer outcomes in a complex system. His long insistence on managing the evolutionary potential of the present rather than designing for an idealised future is close in spirit to transformative teleology. The disagreement here is not about his values. It is about whether his instruments, once they are tools that someone deploys on someone else, can honour those values. Any tool sold to a client sets up an upper box by doing so. The real question is whether the tool acknowledges this and builds the acknowledgement into its practice.

Objectio

The criticism proves too much. Every intervention is made by someone. If any act of choosing reinstates the "upper box", complexity theory forbids action, and Stacey's school becomes a counsel of paralysis, as critics have often said.

Sed contra

Stacey, Shaw and Mowles have all said plainly that they do not counsel inaction. Managers continue to plan, decide and intervene. The question is how they understand what they are doing. In the transformative account, a plan is a gesture in an ongoing conversation. It calls out responses that will change it and its author, and its value lies in the conversation it provokes, not in its execution.

Respondeo

The distinction is between acting as if from outside and acting knowing one is inside. Both involve choosing, and they differ in what follows. The first expects the system to unfold what was chosen and treats deviation as noise or resistance. The second expects to be surprised, reads deviation as the conversation answering back, and is ready to be changed by the answer. An instrument faithful to complexity would build the second expectation into its structure, for example by requiring that every probe be reported back as a change in the prober. SwarmCompass and WRAS, as published, build in the first.

Every chooser is chosen too. An instrument that forgets this is systems thinking under a complexity name.

Altius Teleology and the problem of downward causation

Stacey's five teleologies can be read as positions on downward causation: whether and how a whole constrains its parts. Formative teleology makes the whole prior; rationalist teleology puts the cause in a chooser outside; transformative teleology puts it in the ongoing interaction itself. Juarrero's account of context-sensitive constraints offers a non-mystical mechanism for the third: wholes arise as constraint regimes that alter the probability distributions of their parts, without any extra force. The split causality the treatise criticises is a refusal to choose: the system obeys formative teleology while the consultant keeps rationalist teleology for itself.

Movement 9

There Is No Outside: Mead and Elias

The vertical axis of WRAS, natural emergence ("just let it happen") to stimulated emergence ("taking action to discover what is possible"), is the framework's most interesting move and its most vulnerable. It is interesting because it acknowledges that emergence goes on whether or not anyone intervenes. It is vulnerable because it treats letting it happen as a position available to an agent, a null option of non-intervention from which stimulation is a departure.

The gesture that cannot be withheld

For George Herbert Mead, social life is made of the gesture–response. A gesture is any act that calls out a response in another, and its meaning is not in the gesture but in the whole social act, gesture and response together. Meaning is always completed by the other. A raised eyebrow means something only in the response it gets. Mead adds that a gesture also calls out a response in the one who makes it, because humans can take the attitude of the other towards themselves. That is the origin of self-consciousness.

It follows that not acting is a gesture. A leader who "just lets it happen" is seen to let it happen. Their silence in the meeting, the project they do not cancel, the probe they decline to fund, the report they read and do not answer all call out responses. People infer approval, indifference, a hidden plan, a loss of nerve. Those responses then become the emergence the leader believed they were leaving alone. In a social figuration, natural emergence is not available to anyone whose position is visible. The only real distinction is between gestures one makes knowingly and gestures one makes without noticing.

The left picture shows a dashed line from L to the system: a channel that can be opened ("stimulate") or closed ("let it happen"). The right picture has no such channel, because L is connected, in every direction, all the time. The point is not that the left picture is never useful. In complicated, engineered domains a controller really can be decoupled. The point is that the WRAS axis is offered for exactly the domains (the top half of Cynefin, by the wiki's own account) where the left picture fails.

Elias and the asymmetry of power

Norbert Elias adds what Mead lacks: power. In What is Sociology? Elias builds game models of increasing complexity, from two players to many players at many levels, to show that power is not a thing one holds but a balance, or ratio, between interdependent people. As figurations lengthen and differentiate, no player, however strong, can control the game's course. Elias observes that the game then increasingly takes on a life of its own, beyond what any player intended.

Elias's model adds a crucial point. In long figurations the more powerful players experience themselves as standing outside or above the game, because their moves have larger effects. That experience is real, and it is still an illusion, because their larger moves call out larger responses that reshape their position. The WRAS chooser at the crossing of the axes is the powerful player. Being able to choose between "letting it happen" and "stimulating" is itself a measure of position in the power figuration, and the framework presents it as a neutral methodological choice. A junior nurse cannot choose to "let it happen" in the same sense as the chief executive. Her inaction is invisible, his is a signal. The axis hides the power that makes it meaningful.

In Complexity: A Key Idea for Business and Society Mowles describes the social game as one that influences us more than we are able to influence it. That observation is the counter-axis to WRAS. It runs from those who feel they influence to those who know they are influenced, and every organisation is distributed along it.

Table 6 · The WRAS axes re-read through Mead and Elias
WRAS termAssumesMead / Elias re-readingReformulation
Natural emergenceA neutral null optionWithholding is a gesture. Silence is read.Unnoticed gesture
Stimulated emergenceA deliberate departure from neutralA gesture whose meaning is completed by others' responsesNoticed gesture

Coarse-grainedLarge allocation → large commitmentLarge gestures call out large counter-gestures and coalitions.Mobilising gesture
(The chooser)Methodological neutralityThe power-ratio that makes choosing possiblePosition in the figuration

The reformulated axis runs from unnoticed to noticed gesture. It replaces a distinction between kinds of emergence with a distinction between degrees of reflexive awareness in the one who gestures. Emergence is not something one can choose to have or not have. What one can choose is how much attention to pay to one's own part in it. That is a discipline of the chooser, not a property of the situation.

On granularity specifically: Estuarine Mapping's preference for decomposing to the lowest coherent level of granularity is one of the most valuable practical ideas in the Cynefin family. It is a guard against grand programmes. But granularity is relational, not absolute. A "fine-grained" probe launched by the board, such as a small pilot in one ward, arrives in that ward as a coarse event: the board is watching us. The probe's grain depends on the distance and the power-gradient it travels across. The same intervention is fine at the top and coarse at the bottom. A complexity-faithful account of granularity has to include who is looking.

There is no "let it happen" for anyone whose silence is watched.

Elias returns in Liber Secundus twice: as the hidden figuration of the club (Question I) and as the established and the outsiders (Part Twenty-One).

Altius Gesture, response and the social act as a quantum of meaning

Mead's social act has a minimal unit: a gesture and the response that completes its meaning. This is structurally like a measurement in Part VII, where the outcome is fixed only in relation to the apparatus that registers it. Elias adds the scale dimension: figurations lengthen as interdependence chains grow, and longer chains make outcomes less controllable by any participant. Together they predict something testable: the more stakeholders between a leader's gesture and its eventual response, the larger the gap between intended and realised meaning. Long figurations are, in this sense, high-decoherence environments for intentions.

Movement 10

The Substrate as an Ontology

Every metaphor smuggles in an ontology, and the word substrate carries a heavy one. In biology a substrate is the surface on which an organism lives or grows, or the molecule an enzyme acts upon. In materials science it is the base layer on which other layers are deposited. In each sense the substrate is passive relative to what acts on it or grows on it, and prior to it. WRAS says strategy should respond to or manipulate the substrate before major intervention. The substrate is the thing worked upon.

Juarrero: constraint, not substrate

Much of the Cynefin family's recent sophistication comes from Alicia Juarrero, whose Dynamics in Action (1999) and Context Changes Everything (2023) rebuild causality around constraints: enabling and governing, context-independent and context-sensitive. Snowden has drawn on this work extensively, and the vocabulary of governing, enabling and dispositional constraints runs through Estuarine. On Juarrero's account constraints are not a substrate. They are relations: they alter the probability distribution of what can happen next, and the interactions they constrain produce and reshape them in turn. Context-sensitive constraints in particular are made by the dynamics they govern. A river's banks shape the flow, and the flow reshapes the banks. Tellingly, the estuary is the image Snowden himself chose.

A faithful reading of Juarrero cannot keep a substrate under strategy. Strategy and substrate are co-constituted. The "cultural substrate" is not a layer of values and norms waiting to be manipulated. It is the ongoing patterning of what people do together, and that includes what they do with strategy documents, consultants and SenseMaker surveys. An intervention on the cultural substrate is not an act on culture. It is more culture.

Gibson: affordance belongs to no one side

Estuarine work invokes James Gibson's affordances, the parts of the substrate one can get a handle on. In The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979) Gibson was emphatic that an affordance is neither objective nor subjective but both, a relation between an animal and its environment. A step affords climbing to a creature of a certain leg-length and not to another. Gibson's affordance cannot be mapped as a property of the substrate alone. It changes with the body, the skill, the history and the purpose of whoever encounters it. An affordance map of "the substrate" without the people whose bodies and histories complete it is a map of half a relation.

Griffin, Elias, Ingold: culture as the moving pattern

In Griffin and Stacey's account (especially in Experiencing Emergence in Organizations), what systems thinkers call culture is a set of social objects: generalised tendencies of large numbers of people to act in similar ways in similar situations. These exist only in being particularised in local interaction, here and now, by these people. They are not beneath interaction. They are its recurring shape. Elias's figuration makes the same point at larger scale: a society is not a layer under individuals, nor individuals a layer on top of society. "Individual" and "society" are two perspectives on one moving web.

Tim Ingold's distinction between the network and the meshwork (in Lines and Being Alive) gives the sharpest image. A network joins pre-existing points with connectors. A meshwork is made of lines of movement, entangled trails of beings who are themselves their paths. The WRAS "network substrate" (partners, suppliers, competitors) is a network in Ingold's derogatory sense: nodes and links. The organisation that lives is a meshwork, a tangle of lines still being drawn.

The irony is that WRAS calls itself weaving, and weaving is Ingold's preferred image for the meshwork. A woven fabric has no substrate. Warp and weft hold each other in tension and neither is ground to the other's figure. If WRAS took its own first word seriously, it would have to give up its second ontology. The framework is titled for the meshwork and built on the stratigraphy.

Constructor theory and the unchanged constructor

The deepest root of the substrate concept in the Cynefin family is constructor theory, proposed by David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto as a reformulation of physics in terms of which transformations are possible and which impossible. It was taken up in the Substrate-Independence Theory paper. In constructor theory a constructor is an entity that causes a transformation in a substrate and keeps its ability to cause it again. A catalyst is the paradigm case. The constructor is defined by being, in the relevant respect, unchanged by its work.

This is the precise point where the import fails for human affairs. On the CRP account, and on Mead's, no human participant remains unchanged by participation. The strategist who intervenes in the "cultural substrate" is changed by doing it: by the responses called out, by the reputational consequences, and by the shift in their own "me" as others now see them as the one who intervened. A catalyst that is transformed by the reaction is not a catalyst. It is a reagent. In organisations everyone is a reagent. Constructor theory may be a profound reformulation of physics. Carried into anthro-complexity, it brings with it the figure of the agent who acts without being acted upon, which is the upper box of Movement 8 restored at the level of fundamental ontology.
