The final row is the argument of the movement in a single line. The four substrates leave out the one group that a complexity-faithful account must not leave out: those doing the strategising. Put them back as a fifth, reflexive "substrate" and the stratigraphy falls apart, because a layer that reads the other layers and is changed by the reading is no longer a layer. It is the weave.

A catalyst changed by the reaction is a reagent. In organisations, everyone is a reagent.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Question IILiber II · Part Twenty-Two

Liber Secundus adds the third kind of constraint Book I's constraint grammar needs: constitutive constraints, which make a community what it is.

Altius Constraint closure

Montévil and Mossio (2015) define biological organisation as closure of constraints: a set of constraints each of which is maintained by others in the set. This is the precise opposite of a substrate. In a stratigraphy, lower layers support higher ones but are not maintained by them. In closure, every constraint is held in being by the whole circulation. An organisation's culture, procedures and networks behave far more like closure than like strata: procedures persist because culture enacts them, and culture persists because procedures reproduce it. Ingold's meshwork and closure of constraints are two vocabularies for one finding: there is no ground floor.

Movement 11

Against Prestatability

The brochure promises, twice, to turn "unknown unknowns" into mapped territory. It promises to map the energy gradients of the current state: what can't be changed and what is most likely to change. These are the most philosophically consequential sentences in either instrument, because they claim that the space of what may happen can be laid out in advance and populated with likelihoods.

Kauffman: the adjacent possible cannot be listed

Stuart Kauffman's Investigations (2000) and his later work with Giuseppe Longo and Maël Montévil (No entailing laws, but enablement in the evolution of the biosphere, 2012) make a precise claim. The phase space of an evolving biosphere, and of an economy or culture, cannot be prestated. The adjacent possible, the set of things one step from what exists, is not a fixed list waiting to be found. Its members come into being only as their precursors do, and they create new adjacencies in turn. Kauffman's emblem is the screwdriver: list in advance all its possible uses (open a paint tin, scrape a wall, defend oneself, prop a window, serve as a plumb-bob…) and you find the list has no algorithmic end. The uses depend on contexts that do not yet exist.

If the phase space cannot be prestated, then the unknown unknowns are not hidden regions of an existing map. They are regions that do not yet exist and that will be made by the moves, the brochure's included, taken in the present. You cannot map them, and not because the cartographer lacks skill. There is nothing there yet to map. The promise is not hard to keep. It is a category error.

The figure's rings are temporal, not spatial. The inner dashed ring is what is one step away now. The outer dotted ring is what will be one step away once something in the inner ring has happened, and it cannot be drawn in advance because its contents depend on which inner possibility comes about. The map's grid is a fine tool for the actual, and for the near adjacent possible in slowly changing domains. Over the outer ring it is not inaccurate. It has no referent.

Cilliers: no compression

Paul Cilliers, in Complexity and Postmodernism (1998) and the papers collected as Critical Complexity, argued that complex systems are incompressible. No model of a complex system can be simpler than the system without leaving something out, and we cannot know in advance whether what we left out matters. Cilliers drew an ethics of modesty from this. Every frame is a choice, every choice excludes, and the responsible modeller acknowledges the exclusion as theirs. A complexity practitioner faithful to Cilliers can promise a useful partial view and must say what it leaves out. They cannot promise to turn the unknown into the mapped.

Snowden against the brochure

The sharpest refutation comes from inside the Cynefin family. The Cynefin.io page on risk management argues that conventional risk assessment wrongly assumes a Gaussian distribution, whereas complex systems show power-law distributions with fat tails, so that extreme events are more likely than they first appear. It concludes that risk calls for continuous sensing, early detection and rapid response rather than detailed prediction and avoidance. That is good complexity science, in line with Bak's self-organised criticality and Taleb's critique of the bell curve. It is also incompatible with mapping what is most likely to change. Under a power law the "most likely" changes are the small, frequent ones, and the changes that matter, the tail events, are by construction not the most likely. A map of likelihoods is the Gaussian instinct coming back.

Table 8 · The brochure's mapping claims against the complexity sciences
ClaimAssumesContradicted byDefensible versionVerdict
Unknown unknowns → mapped territoryA prestated phase spaceKauffman; Longo & Montévil; CilliersIncrease the rate of noticing of the newly actualcategory error
What is most likely to changeStable likelihoods over outcomesBak; power laws; the Cynefin wiki itselfWhat changes cheaply and what changes at great costrescuable

The right-hand column matters. Each claim has a defensible complexity version, and the Estuarine heritage is often near it. The brochure takes the defensible version (constraint mapping, the energy cost of change) and inflates it into the indefensible one (mapping the unknown, predicting likelihood). The inflation is commercial and not scientific, and it is the commercial inflation that Movement 17 examines.

Prigogine's contribution should be kept separate. In Order Out of Chaos (with Stengers, 1984) and The End of Certainty (1997), far-from-equilibrium systems reach bifurcation points where tiny fluctuations decide which branch the system takes, and the branch taken cannot be deduced from the state before it. "What can't be changed" is therefore always indexed to a distance from equilibrium. Near equilibrium a constraint is rigid. Far from it, the same constraint can become the fluctuation that tips the system. Estuarine's "what cannot be changed" is sound practical wisdom only if dated: it cannot be changed under present conditions, and conditions are what bifurcations change.

You cannot map what does not yet exist. You can only become quicker at noticing that it now does.

Altius Non-ergodicity

Ole Peters's ergodicity economics names a deep reason why prestatement fails in complex systems. A process is ergodic when the average over many possible worlds equals the average over time in one world. Most organisational processes are not: an agent lives one path, and ruin on that path is not averaged away by success elsewhere. Kauffman's adjacent possible makes the same point from biology: the state space itself changes as the system moves, so there is no fixed ensemble to average over. Risk matrices assume ergodicity silently. The quantum uncertainty compass exists because the walker has only one path.

Movement 11 · Pro Parte Contraria

The Adversary's Brief: The Adjacent Possible Stated, the Complex Compressed

A disputation that only argues one side is a sermon. The scholastic method requires the master to put the opposing case in its strongest form before replying, and to put it better than its own advocates did. Movement 11 argued that the adjacent possible cannot be stated in advance (Kauffman) and that complex systems cannot be compressed (Cilliers). This movement argues the contrary as forcefully as the literature allows. It then shows exactly how much of Thesis VII survives and how much has to be given up.

Videtur quod sic: it seems that the adjacent possible can be stated, and the complex compressed.

I. Six ways the adjacent possible is stated in advance

1 · It was born stateable

The first argument is genealogical, and it is the most embarrassing for the strong thesis. Kauffman first developed the adjacent possible in his work on molecular and biological evolution. There the adjacent possible of a chemical soup is the set of molecules one elementary reaction step away from those that exist. Tria, Loreto, Servedio and Strogatz restate the concept in exactly these terms: the things one step from what actually exists, reachable by incremental modification and recombination of existing material. Give a reaction grammar and a set of species, and the one-step neighbourhood is enumerable. It may be astronomically large, but it is listable in principle. In its founding sense the adjacent possible is a combinatorial neighbourhood, and combinatorial neighbourhoods can be stated in advance.

The strong thesis of unprestatability is a later and narrower claim, made by Longo, Montévil and Kauffman in 2012. What cannot be prestated is the phase space of biological evolution: the ever-new relevant observables and functions that selection reveals, such as the swim bladder that becomes a niche for a worm. The adversary's first point is therefore that the strong thesis concerns functions, not configurations. Movement 11 slid from one to the other.

2 · Intension, not extension

To state a set in advance you do not have to list it. A grammar of a few dozen rules states the infinite set of a language's sentences. A recursive definition states the integers. The objection from the screwdriver (list all its uses and the list never ends) shows that the uses cannot be listed. It does not show that they cannot be generated. Treat the screwdriver as a vector of properties (rigid, pointed, elongated, conductive, a lever-arm of known length, a mass of so many grams) and the space of physical operations those properties afford is the image of that vector under a finite vocabulary of actions: prise, pierce, wedge, conduct, weigh, prop, scrape, strike. "Prop a window" is not mysterious. It is rigidity × length × wedge. The adversary says that the uses of the screwdriver have an intension even where they lack a finite extension.

3 · The statistics of novelty can be predicted

The empirical counter-blow came in 2014. Tria, Loreto, Servedio and Strogatz built a model of the adjacent possible, a generalisation of Pólya's urn in which each novelty adds new possibilities to the urn ("triggering"). The model predicts statistical laws for the rate at which novelties occur (Heaps' law), for the distribution over what is explored (Zipf's law), and for signatures of one novelty enabling another. They tested these predictions against Wikipedia edits, annotation tags, the words of texts and online music listening, and all four datasets showed the predicted patterns. One sentence of their paper amounts to a direct rebuke: it had not been clear how to extract testable predictions from Kauffman's idea. They extracted them.

4 · The shape of the explosion can be predicted

The adversary's most ironic witness is Kauffman himself. The TAP equation, the Theory of the Adjacent Possible, worked out by Cortês, Kauffman, Liddle and Smolin, counts the ways new objects can be generated from combinations of existing ones, minus an extinction rate. Its generic behaviour is a long plateau followed by a sharp, explosive divergence, and the authors derive accurate analytic approximations for the blow-up time, validated against simulation. Which objects will appear is not stated. When the space of objects will explode is.

Neither panel says what the next novelty will be. Both say, before the fact, how novelty will behave: how fast it accrues, how it is distributed, and when its combinatorics will explode. That is a prestatement, of the space's dynamics rather than its inventory. Movement 11 argued against inventories, and this figure shows that dynamics are a different matter.
Live model
An urn that grows when it surprises

A Pólya urn with triggering, after Tria, Loreto, Servedio and Strogatz. Each draw adds ρ copies of the drawn colour. A never-seen colour also adds ν+1 brand-new colours, so novelty enlarges the space of the possible. The points trace Heaps' law on log–log axes. Change ρ and ν and run again.

5 · The mass of the unseen can be measured

The adversary's most elegant witness was English and worked in Buckinghamshire. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and his assistant I. J. Good developed what Good published in 1953 as the Good–Turing estimator. Given a sample, the probability that the next observation belongs to a species never yet seen is estimated as N₁/N: the number of species seen exactly once, divided by the sample size. The estimator is largely independent of the distribution of species frequencies. It has since been shown to coincide, under Pitman–Yor priors, with the modern Bayesian nonparametric estimator of discovery probability.

Here, read carefully, is a formula for the missing mass: the total probability carried by what you have not seen and cannot name. Turing used it against Enigma's keys. Ecologists use it for unseen species, and language models use it for unseen words. It does not tell you what the unknown unknowns are. It tells you, with known error, how much of the world they occupy. The adversary presses the point. "Unknown unknowns" was always a loose phrase. Turing turned half of it into a number.

6 · Even technological surprise has a distribution

The sixth witness is economic. Farmer and Lafond (Research Policy, 2016) treated generalised Moore's laws as correlated geometric random walks with drift. Across 53 technologies they derived a closed-form approximation for the distribution of forecast errors as a function of time horizon. In hindcasting, forecast errors across many technologies and horizons collapse onto the same universal distribution. Technological futures, archetypal sources of novelty, are not stated in advance in their content. They are forecastable in their error bars, and you can estimate the probability that one technology overtakes another at a given date.

Read the staircase from top to bottom. Each step moves from the formal towards the semantic, and the colour moves from teal (stateable) to rose (unstateable). The gold dashed line is where the argument actually lives. Kauffman's insight survives in rungs ⑦ to ⑨: which novelty, for what use, meaning what. The adversary wins rungs ① to ⑥ outright. A complexity practitioner who claims "nothing about the unknown can be said in advance" is as wrong as the brochure that claims "the unknown can be mapped".
Live model
Turing's Glass: measure what you have not seen

A hidden world of 400 kinds with a long-tailed (Zipf-like) distribution. Each click samples 25 observations. Gold is Turing's estimate of the unseen mass, the share of kinds seen exactly once. Rose is the true unseen mass, which in real life you never get to see. Watch the estimate track a quantity no one can name.

II. Six ways complex systems are compressed

1 · Why science is possible at all

Cilliers held that a complex system cannot be given an account less complex than itself without losing some of its aspects. The adversary answers from statistical physics and systems biology. In a 2013 paper in Science, Machta, Chachra, Transtrum and Sethna showed that parameter space compression underlies the emergence of effective theories. Using the eigenvalues of the Fisher Information Matrix, they found that a few "stiff" parameter combinations govern macroscopic behaviour while most directions are "sloppy" and barely matter. The pattern holds in the diffusion equation, at the Ising critical point, and in multiparameter models across the sciences. Sethna puts it plainly: if one needed to extract every detail of the true underlying theory to make a useful theory, science would be impossible. In a cell with thousands of interacting parameters, only a few combinations predict how the system behaves.

This figure gives an unexpected rescue to Estuarine Mapping. Its central move, separating what is too costly to change from what is cheap to change, is a qualitative sloppy-model analysis. Stiff directions are where an intervention changes behaviour. Sloppy directions are where effort disappears into detail. The adversary can say, with justice, that Snowden's best instrument is a compression technique and works because complex systems compress.

2 · The minimal optimal predictor exists

Crutchfield's computational mechanics gives the most rigorous answer to "how much can a process be compressed without losing predictive power?" The rule is simple: do not distinguish histories that lead to the same predictions of the future. The resulting causal states and their transitions form the ε-machine, the process's unique optimal predictor of minimal size, which is in effect its equations of motion. Shalizi and Crutchfield proved the causal-state representation is the minimal one consistent with accurate prediction. This is compression with a guarantee: nothing predictive is lost, and nothing redundant is kept.

Honesty requires the qualification the adversary would sooner omit. For most processes the statistical complexity, the information the causal states store, is infinite, so storing them exceeds any learner's capacity. That is why Marzen and Crutchfield developed lossy causal states and predictive rate-distortion theory. Compression is real, and it is graded. One can compute exactly how much prediction is bought with each bit of model.

3 · Macro can beat micro

Cilliers's incompressibility assumes that compression always loses. Hoel, Albantakis and Tononi showed in 2013 that this is false in a precise sense. Using effective information as a measure of causal power, they found that a coarse-grained macro model can carry more causal information than the micro model it is built from, even when the macro is completely specified by the micro. This happens when macro mechanisms are more deterministic or less degenerate, enough to outweigh the smaller state space. They call this causal emergence. A map can be more informative than the territory. Some compressions are gains.

4 · A city compresses to an exponent

The social sciences have their own striking compression. Bettencourt, Lobo, Helbing, Kühnert and West (PNAS, 2007) found that socioeconomic quantities in cities, such as wealth and new ideas, scale with population as a power law with an exponent β ≈ 1.15. The same family of exponents covers wealth, innovation and crime, and infrastructure scales sub-linearly. A city of millions, with all its uncountable interactions, compresses in these respects to a number, and the number recurs across urban systems. The 2010 follow-up found that each city's deviation from the line is itself stable over decades, a second-order compression of the city's character.

5 · Cilliers against Cilliers

The adversary's fifth point is internal. Cilliers never counselled refusing to model. His tribute literature records his insistence that reduction is necessary in order to deal with complex problems at all. What he called for was modesty: an attitude open to the provisional and ethical character of partial models. Critics have also noted that Cilliers preferred connectionist neural networks as the best way to model complex systems, a commitment that sits uneasily with his post-structural claim that no model is privileged. A neural network is, among other things, a compression of its training data. Cilliers's own favoured model of complexity was a compressor.

6 · Learning is compression

The sixth point is general. Every successful predictor of a complex system, whether a weather model, a language model or an experienced receiver's feel for a distressed asset, is a compression that discards the incompressible residue and keeps the predictive structure. It is now a commonplace of machine learning that predicting and compressing are two sides of one operation. If complex systems were incompressible in the strong sense, no organism could learn anything about its environment. Organisms do learn, so complex environments compress far enough to be lived in.

The rose box at the lower right carries the reply the next section develops. In physical systems the compression stays put. A critical exponent does not change because a physicist has published it. In human systems the compression is itself an intervention. Once a city learns its scaling exponent, or a firm learns which of its parameters are stiff, people act on what they have learned, and the stiff directions can move.

Respondeo: what survives and what is surrendered

The adversary has won a great deal, and Thesis VII has to be amended openly in his favour. The Additive Covenant governs this treatise, so the original text stands above, and the amendment is added here and in the Twelve Theses.

First concession. The adjacent possible can be stated in advance in its configurations (given rules), its generator (as intension), its rates (Heaps and Zipf), its shape (TAP), its missing mass (Good–Turing) and its error distribution (Farmer and Lafond). Movement 11's sentence, "there is nothing there yet to map", was too strong. There is something to map, namely the form of the not-yet.

Second concession. Complex systems are compressible in their predictive structure (ε-machines), their parameter geometry (sloppiness), their causal grain (causal emergence) and their aggregate scaling (urban exponents). Cilliers's incompressibility holds exactly for the complete micro-description and loosely for what is left over. It does not hold for the knowledge that action needs.

What is retained. Three things survive. First, the identity, function and meaning of particular novelties remain unstateable (rungs ⑦ to ⑨). Longo, Montévil and Kauffman's thesis concerns precisely these: new observables, new functions, new niches. Second, every compression of a human system is reflexive. Its publication is a gesture in Mead's sense and calls out responses that move what was compressed. MacKenzie's study of options pricing (An Engine, Not a Camera, 2006) showed a model reshaping the market it described. Third, Cilliers's ethical point survives untouched and is sharpened. Because compression is possible, choosing what to keep and what to discard is a real choice made by someone. Modesty is not the claim that nothing can be compressed. It is the acknowledgement that every compression has an author and an exclusion.

The table turns the earlier critique of the brochure (Movement 11, Table 8) into something more precise and more useful. The brochure's sin was not that it claimed too much knowledge of the unknown. It claimed the wrong kind. It promised inventory ("mapped territory") where the science supports only mass, rate and form. A SwarmCompass rebuilt on Good–Turing, Heaps' law and sloppy-model analysis would be a defensible instrument, more so than the one on sale.

On Turing's compass. The Good–Turing estimator is the most honest compass in this treatise. It points at nothing and names nothing, yet it tells the traveller how much of the sea is still uncharted, and the estimate tightens with every new sighting. If the twenty radiologists of Movement 4 had kept a Good–Turing log of their "seen once" anomalies, the gorilla would still have been missed, but the mass of the missable would have been on the record. That is the epistemic virtue the instruments lack: not seeing everything, but knowing how much one has not seen.

The form of the not-yet can be stated. Its name cannot. Wisdom is knowing which is which.

Altius Stating the form of the unforeseeable

Movement 11′ argued that while the identity of the next novelty cannot be stated, its rate, mass and shape can be. A further result supports this: Loreto, Tria and colleagues showed that the urn model with triggering reproduces Heaps' and Zipf's laws together, so one generative mechanism constrains several statistics at once. The prestatable part of the future is therefore not a list of events but a set of scaling relations. An instrument honest about complexity would forecast exponents, not scenarios, and would be judged by whether those exponents hold.

Movement 12

Codification: Boisot, Ashby and the Triad

SenseMaker® is the engine of SwarmCompass. The brochure says it uses a patented approach to capture human attitudes, going beyond text analysis to tap into intuition at scale and in quantitative form. Any serious critique has to begin by granting what is genuinely original in it.

What SenseMaker gets right

In conventional survey and qualitative research the analyst interprets what respondents say. SenseMaker's central innovation is self-signification. Respondents tell a short narrative of their experience, a "micro-narrative", and then interpret it themselves by placing it on a set of prepared signifiers. The best known are triads, triangles in which the respondent places a point according to how far each of three labelled qualities is present. There are also dyads (sliders between two poles), canvases and multiple-choice items. The narrative stays attached to its signification, so analysts can move from a pattern in the aggregate (a cluster of points in one corner of a triad) back to the stories that make it up. This is an elegant answer to the expert-interpretation problem, and it is fairly credited as one of the most intelligent attempts to make narrative usable at scale without simply counting words.

Boisot's I-Space

Max Boisot's Information Space (Knowledge Assets, 1998) gives the tool for seeing what self-signification does, both its achievement and its cost. Knowledge can be placed on three dimensions. Codification runs from uncodified (tacit, embodied, hard to articulate) to codified (formalised and compressed into a few symbols). Abstraction runs from concrete (tied to a particular situation) to abstract (general categories that hold across many situations). Diffusion runs from undiffused (held by a few) to diffused (available to many). Boisot's Social Learning Cycle follows knowledge as it moves: scanning, codifying (problem-solving), abstracting, diffusing, absorbing, impacting, and back into the tacit.

A lived experience in an organisation (the nurse's near-miss, the trader's unease, the tenant's complaint the receiver heard on site) starts at the origin of the I-Space: uncodified, concrete, undiffused. Telling a micro-narrative moves it some way along codification: it becomes words. Signifying it on a triad moves it far along codification and abstraction at once. A situated, ambiguous, many-sided experience becomes a point with three coordinates against categories designed in advance. Aggregation then moves it along diffusion, though only towards those who hold the dashboard.

The path climbs steeply. Steps ② to ③ are where SenseMaker does its work and where most of the loss happens: a narrative with many possible meanings is fixed to one position against three words someone else chose. Step ⑤ is the brochure's explicit addition (create epistemically balanced & multi-perceptive training data sets for further AI-based automation). Boisot's Social Learning Cycle closes only when codified, abstract knowledge is absorbed back into practice by those who generated it. Here the return arc runs through someone else.

The triad as search template

This brings us back to the gorilla. The radiologists missed it because their search template, nodules, set what counted as a finding. A signifier set is a search template. The three words at the corners of a triad set the dimensions along which an experience can register. Whatever the narrator felt that has no vertex is not lost exactly: it stays in the story. But it is invisible to the aggregate, which is what the client sees. The person who designs the signifiers stands exactly where the brochure's own anecdote puts the radiologist: an expert looking for a known kind of thing. The 17% the instrument wants to find are, almost by definition, those whose experience does not fit the template, and the template is the instrument's own.

Ashby: requisite variety

W. Ross Ashby's law of requisite variety (An Introduction to Cybernetics, 1956) says that only variety can absorb variety. A regulator must be able to take at least as many distinct states as the disturbances it means to counter. Measured this way, a triad is a severe variety reducer. It maps experience onto a two-dimensional simplex with three named axes. The point is not that this is wrong. All sensemaking reduces variety, and that is what makes it sensemaking. The point is that the claim to "tap into intuition at scale" overstates what survives the reduction. What survives is intuition as categorised by the designer. The brochure presents a reduction as an amplification.

Two of the losses are worth pulling out. The conversation is absent because SenseMaker collects narratives addressed to an instrument, not to another person. On the CRP account meaning is made in the conversational back-and-forth, so a story told to a form is a different social act from a story told to a colleague. The later reinterpretation is lost because a signification is a snapshot. Weick's sensemaking, as distinct from the trademarked "sense-making", is retrospective, plausible rather than accurate, and endlessly revisable. The narrator may understand the experience quite differently next week. The aggregate will not.

The triad is a search template. The gorilla is whatever has no vertex.

Altius Requisite variety and the good regulator

Conant and Ashby's good regulator theorem (1970) states that every good regulator of a system must be a model of that system. Combined with requisite variety, it sets a hard limit on codified instruments: a framework with three corners and two axes has fixed variety, and can regulate only what is no more varied than itself. Boisot's I-Space explains why the limit is tempting to ignore: codification makes knowledge diffusible and saleable precisely by stripping the variety that regulation would need. The triad is not a neutral recording device; it is a variety attenuator, and its attenuation is the product.

Movement 13

Risk Without Quadrants

WRAS's most original claim is in its name: risk and strategy should be woven, not handled by separate departments with separate registers. On this the framework is right, and right in a way that conventional enterprise risk management badly needs. Its wiki entry adds a second correct claim: complex systems are fat-tailed, so risk needs continuous sensing and fast response more than prediction and avoidance. The difficulty is the third claim, that each domain has its own risk strategy, matched to the domain's characteristics and to the risk profile of a portfolio.

Risk as a property, risk as an experience

Assigning a risk strategy to each quadrant treats risk as a property of the situation. A Directed situation has Directed risks, an Opportunist situation Opportunist risks, and you read off the right posture once you know the quadrant. This is how risk registers have always worked, with the quadrant taking the place of the old likelihood-impact grid.

The corpus offers a different ontology. In Experiencing Risk, Spontaneity and Improvisation in Organizational Change (2006), Patricia Shaw and Ralph Stacey's collection, risk is not something situations possess. It is something people live. It is felt as anxiety, negotiated in conversation, displaced onto others, defended against. The collection's argument about improvisation applies directly: improvisation is not a skill located in an autonomous individual, it is a quality of interaction, and it holds together only when driven by a theme the participants recognise. Risk in this sense lives in the relations, and so does the capacity to meet it.

Mary Douglas and Aaron Wildavsky (Risk and Culture, 1982) made the anthropological version of the same point. Societies select the risks they attend to according to their forms of social organisation. Which dangers count as risks is a social choice reflecting who holds power and what order they are protecting. A quadrant that assigns risks cannot ask whose risks they are, or who chose to see them.

Risk management as a social defence

Isabel Menzies Lyth's study of a London teaching hospital (The Functioning of Social Systems as a Defence against Anxiety, 1960) is foundational for the CRP school's view of procedure. Nursing routines (task lists, rotation, depersonalised categorisation of patients) existed largely to defend nurses against the anxiety of intimate contact with suffering and death. They worked as defences and failed as care. Stacey's The Tools and Techniques of Leadership and Management (2012) and his earlier "wiggly world" writing extend the diagnosis to strategic planning and risk registers. These instruments are performed alongside the real work as rituals that relieve the anxiety of not knowing. Stacey's line that muddling through is what managers do anyway, and is no second-best process, is the deflationary counterpart.

The question for WRAS is whether a four-quadrant risk posture is a better way of attending to risk or a more sophisticated defence against the anxiety of being unable to. The answer depends on use. A framework that prompts the conversation "whose anxiety are we managing, and what are we not looking at because of it?" attends to risk. A framework that tells a board which risk posture belongs to which quadrant is a defence.

From the receiver's chair. In fixed-charge receivership and secured lending, risk never presents itself as a property of an asset. A distressed property's "risk" is a negotiation among lender, borrower, tenants, valuer, agent, insolvency practitioner and court. Each holds a different picture and a different exposure, and each picture changes as the others act. A covenant breach is not a fact that triggers a response. It is a gesture that calls out responses, standstill, enforcement or renegotiation, which change the asset's value, which changes the breach. Anyone who has stood in a vacant building with a nervous lender on the phone and an anxious tenant at the door knows that risk lives in the relations. It is woven, though not on a grid.
Table 11 · Per-domain risk strategy: plausible content, objection, relational reformulation
WRAS domainRisk posture it impliesComplexity objectionRelational reformulation
DirectedDue diligence before commitment; competitive analysis; plan riskAnalysis is a social defence when the future is fat-tailed. It produces confidence, not foresight.Ask whose confidence the analysis is producing, and what it lets them stop looking at
OpportunistSpeed with a large stake; risk of overcommitmentAn opportunity is a social object: it exists because a coalition sees it. Its risk is the coalition's fragility.Map who must keep believing in the opportunity, and what would make them stop

The second column is a reconstruction. The published WRAS material says each domain has a risk strategy and does not spell them out. The reconstruction follows the logic of the definitions. The fourth row carries the most important point: "distributed" strategy does not just spread risk evenly. It moves risk down the power gradient. A hundred small probes run by front-line teams put a hundred small exposures on the people least able to say no.

Risk does not live in quadrants. It lives in whoever is left holding it.

Altius Risk as social defence

Isabel Menzies Lyth's study of nursing (1960) showed that organisational routines often function to protect staff from anxiety rather than to perform the task. Michael Power's 'risk management of everything' (2004) extended the insight: risk frameworks frequently manage reputational and personal exposure, not hazard. A quadrant is an ideal social defence: it converts dread into placement. The Part VIII reading adds a kinetic twist. A defence that works stores anxiety rather than discharging it, and stored anxiety, like Hobbes's stored power, eventually needs an outlet. Risk without quadrants means letting anxiety circulate where it can be worked on.

Movement 14

The Human/AI Hybrid and the Harvest

The brochure's second page is headed Human-AI Hybrid: The Only Way to Navigate Foggy Futures. It separates two kinds of "superpower". Humans offer intuition for weak signals, ethical judgment, analogical thinking ("this feels like the 2008 crisis…"), and the capacity to think in stories and weave patterns in narrative over time to scaffold meaning. AI offers processing speed, pattern detection at scale ("if properly trained") and data aggregation. Earlier it claims humans reason in abductive, analogical ways, whereas AI is digital, inductive and dependent on its training datasets.

Peirce on abduction

The appeal to abduction is welcome, and Peirce deserves a better hearing than the brochure gives him. For Peirce, abduction is the only form of inference that introduces a new idea. It is the leap to a hypothesis that would, if true, make a surprising fact a matter of course. It is fallible, instinctive, guided by what he called il lume naturale, and it is the first stage of inquiry, followed by deduction (working out consequences) and induction (testing them). Abduction is not a human "superpower" set against machine induction. It is one phase of a cycle, and the cycle is social. For Peirce the community of inquirers, not the individual mind, converges on truth over the long run.

The clean split is also now empirically doubtful. Contemporary generative models produce candidate hypotheses, analogies and explanations that look like abductive leaps. Whether they "really" abduce is a live philosophical question, but the line between a human who guesses and a machine that only counts no longer holds without argument. The more interesting point is Peircean: neither humans nor machines abduce well alone. Abduction is disciplined by the community that tests it.

Hutchins: cognition in the wild

Edwin Hutchins's Cognition in the Wild (1995) studied navigation on a US Navy ship and showed that the cognition needed to fix the ship's position was not located in any one head. It was distributed across people, charts, alidades, plotting tools, speech and the division of labour. The system navigated. The brochure's image (AI sees the map. Humans feel the terrain.) divides cognition into two possessors with two kinds of property. Hutchins shows that the interesting cognition is in the arrangement, in who passes what to whom, in what form, at what moment. The question is not which superpowers to fuse. It is how to arrange the passing.

The harvest

The most revealing line in the brochure is a deliverable listed under Chart the Territory: Create epistemically balanced & multi-perceptive training data sets for further AI-based automation.

Read it closely. The human superpowers the brochure praises (weak-signal intuition, ethical judgment, narrative pattern-weaving) are to be captured through SenseMaker and turned into training data so that further activity can be automated. The 17% are found, and their seeing is recorded, so that it can be reproduced without them. If the human contribution really were irreplaceable, there would be nothing to automate. If it can be automated, the human/AI hybrid is a transitional stage: humans are the scaffolding the machine is built on and then dismantles.

Every label on the loop is quoted from the brochure. The figure adds nothing except the closing arc and its question mark. The brochure presents the human and the machine as permanent partners with complementary powers, but its deliverables describe a conversion of one into the other. In Boisot's terms (Movement 12), knowledge moved to the top of the I-Space can be diffused without its originators. That is the point of codifying it.
Objectio

Automation of routine scanning frees human attention for the frontier. Training data drawn from diverse perspectives is better than training data drawn from a narrow elite or scraped text, and that is what "epistemically balanced" means. This is responsible AI, not extraction.

Sed contra

"Epistemically balanced" assumes there is a balance point: a mix of perspectives that is correct, set by whoever designs the sample. Every balance is struck by someone. And the frontier that automation frees humans for is where the 17% already were. Once their noticing is codified, the frontier moves and the automation follows it.

Respondeo

The objection is partly right. Training on diverse, self-signified narratives is better than training on scraped text, and in some settings it may be the most ethical way to build such systems. The concern is not automation as such. It is the silence about the relation of exchange: who consented to their noticing becoming a training set, who owns the resulting model, who benefits when it replaces them. A complexity-faithful instrument would make these questions part of the deployment. They are questions about power in the figuration, and the brochure's vocabulary of "superpowers" hides them.

They praise the human superpower, and then they train on it.

Altius Model collapse

Shumailov and colleagues (Nature, 2024) showed that generative models trained recursively on their own outputs lose the tails of the original distribution: rare events vanish first. This is the technical form of the treatise's worry about harvesting sense-making into training sets. The outliers SenseMaker is designed to catch are exactly what recursive training erases. An instrument that feeds human narratives into AI, then feeds AI pattern alerts back to humans, risks a loop in which weak signals are progressively smoothed away. Snowden's grating, a human who must sense before the machine decides, is the architectural defence.

Movement 15

Compass, Star-Path and Orientation

The product is a compass. The metaphor is apt in ways its authors may not have meant. A magnetic compass gives a direction relative to a field that is invisible, global and independent of the traveller. It does not tell you where you are or where to go. It tells you which way is north.

Declination

A magnetic compass does not point to true north. It points to magnetic north, and the angle between the two, declination, varies with place and drifts over time as the Earth's field changes. A navigator who trusts the needle without correcting for local declination goes systematically wrong, and the error grows with distance. So a compass is honest only when used with local knowledge of its own error. A swarm compass would need a declination table: a running account of how its signifiers, its sample, its designers' assumptions and its clients' wishes bend the needle away from the situation. The brochure offers no such table. Its needle points to authentic alignment, which is the magnetic north of every management instrument ever sold.

The star compass

The Pacific wayfinding traditions studied by Ben Finney, David Lewis and others, and in other treatises of this imprint, used a very different instrument: the star compass, a mental division of the horizon into rising and setting points of stars, together with etak. In etak the canoe is held still and the islands move past it along the star bearings. The navigator does not stand outside the voyage reading a fixed field. The navigator reads swell, cloud, birds, the colour of the water and the feel of the hull, and continuously re-imagines the canoe's place in a world that is moving with it. Ingold's distinction in Lines between wayfaring (knowing as you go, along a path) and navigation by map (knowing from above, between points) is the philosophical form of the same contrast.

The difference is epistemological, not technical. The magnetic compass is a delegation of orientation to a field. The star compass is a cultivation of orientation in a person and a crew. One can be bought and the other has to be learned. The brochure's very name places orientation in the instrument.

Boyd: orientation is the Schwerpunkt

John Boyd, whose OODA loop is probably the most misdrawn diagram in strategy, put Orientation at the centre. In his final sketch of the loop, Orientation is shaped by genetic heritage, cultural traditions, previous experiences, new information, and the analysis and synthesis that bring these together. It sends implicit guidance and control directly to observation and to action, bypassing explicit decision. Boyd's point was that the decisive advantage lies in the quality of one's orientation, and that orientation is built through immersion, varied experience and the destruction and recreation of one's own mental models (Destruction and Creation, 1976). It is not consulted.

Against this, an external "compass" that delivers orientation as a product is a regression. It locates the decisive faculty outside the organisation that needs it. The brochure's one undeniably Boydian promise, Course-correct in days, not quarters, is about tempo, and tempo without orientation is just agitation. Boyd's advantage came from getting inside the opponent's loop, operating at a tempo that disoriented them. That requires an orientation already rich enough to read the situation faster than it changes, and no survey supplies one.

Orientation cannot be bought. It is grown in a crew that has been at sea together.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part Thirteen

Boyd's Orient box is read in Liber Secundus as the jacket in diagrammatic form.

Altius Dead reckoning and integrated error

Inertial navigation integrates acceleration twice to obtain position, so a constant bias produces an error that grows with the square of time. This is why every unaided navigator drifts, and why declination must be declared and corrected. Polynesian etak manages drift differently: it reframes position as the moving relation between reference islands and the canoe, updating continuously from swells, birds and stars. The organisational lesson is that orientation errors accumulate silently and quadratically unless something external, a star, a swell, an outsider, interrupts the integration. A framework without outside reference drifts exactly as an uncorrected gyroscope does.

Movement 16

A Genealogy the Framework Omits

WRAS is introduced as the final link in a decade-long chain towards a complexity-based alternative to strategy, the step that completes the anthro-complexity approach. It deserves a genealogy, because its four domains have strong ancestors in mainstream strategy scholarship, and the absence of those ancestors from the framing gives an inflated sense of rupture.

Mintzberg and Waters, 1985

Forty years ago, in Of Strategies, Deliberate and Emergent (Strategic Management Journal, 1985), Henry Mintzberg and James Waters set out a continuum from deliberate to emergent strategy, with eight types along it: planned, entrepreneurial, ideological, umbrella, process, unconnected, consensus and imposed. Mintzberg's Crafting Strategy (1987) added the image of strategies that grow like weeds in a garden and called on managers to recognise emergent patterns rather than impose designs. WRAS's vertical axis, natural to stimulated emergence, is a reworking of the deliberate–emergent continuum with emergence on both ends. Its quadrants have clear Mintzbergian counterparts.

Table 12 · WRAS domains and their unacknowledged ancestors
WRAS domainClosest ancestor(s)What WRAS addsWhat the ancestor already had
DirectedMintzberg & Waters' planned strategy; Ansoff; the design schoolPlacement within an emergence frame; substrate-first prefaceThe full critique of planning (Mintzberg, The Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning, 1994)
OpportunistEntrepreneurial strategy; Kirzner's entrepreneurial alertnessThe coarse-grained commitment named as suchAlertness to unnoticed opportunity as the core of entrepreneurship
Hypothesis-basedMcGrath & MacMillan, Discovery-Driven Planning (1995); real options; the lean start-upSafe-to-fail probes; coherence testsAssumption-testing, milestone gating, options value of small bets
DistributedMintzberg's umbrella, process, unconnected; Quinn's logical incrementalism (1980); Burgelman's internal ecology (1983, 1991)SenseMaker-enabled sensing; "a key new area"Autonomous strategic behaviour from below, selected by internal ecology
(The axes)March, Exploration and Exploitation (1991); Brown & Eisenhardt, Competing on the Edge (1998)Granularity as an explicit dimensionThe balance of variation and commitment; time-pacing; patching

None of this makes WRAS derivative in a damaging sense. Good frameworks recombine. The objection is to the claim of rupture. A framework presented as the last link in a chain towards an alternative to strategy suggests that mainstream strategy never conceived of emergence, hypothesis-testing or distributed initiative. It conceived of all three, debated them for decades, and, in Burgelman and Quinn, documented them empirically in large firms. Acknowledging this would strengthen WRAS. It could then say exactly what its complexity lens adds: granularity, substrate and narrative sensing, which are real contributions.

The fad cycle

There is a further irony. Snowden has long and rightly mocked the management fad cycle, the repackaging of old ideas under new acronyms for a new round of consulting revenue. The WRAS naming history (several candidate expansions published, readers invited to vote, a reef fish adopted for its marketable metaphor) shows a framework that knows it will be branded and is shopping for a brand. In MacIntosh and colleagues' SAGE classification of complexity work, this is the drift from the critical-pluralist register towards the metaphorician one: complexity concepts used for their evocative power and not their explanatory force. The bee and the wrasse are metaphorician moves. The fat tail and the constraint are scientific ones. The instruments switch between the two registers, and the switching is the problem.

The chain was forged before its last link was announced.

Altius Strategy as practice

The strategy-as-practice movement (Whittington, Jarzabkowski) studies strategy as something people do in meetings, documents and talk, not as something an organisation has. Its central finding complements the genealogy the framework omits: strategic tools such as SWOT and matrices function as boundary objects and occasions for conversation more than as analytic engines. Jarzabkowski and Kaplan (2015) showed that a tool's affordances shape what participants can say. Read through Liber Tertius, a framework is an offer, and its value is the conversation it opens. Read through Part VII, that conversation is also a measurement, and the tool sets its basis.

Movement 17

The Political Economy of the Framework

The brochure ends with two lines of small print: copyright ©2025 Cognitive Edge Pte Ltd, and the SenseMaker® logos and name as trademarks of Cognitive Edge Pte Ltd (misprinted Pte td.). The final panel describes a patented approach. The WRAS wiki page says the framework is still under development and not to be used or shared without permission, and invites premium members to take part in its development. These are not incidental. They are the institutional form complexity takes when it comes to market.

Enclosure

Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons (1990) showed that common-pool resources can be governed sustainably by the communities that use them, without either privatisation or central control, given certain design principles: clear boundaries, rules matched to local conditions, participation in rule-making, monitoring by users, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution. The intellectual commons of complexity thinking (concepts like emergence, constraint, attractor, safe-to-fail, distributed cognition) was built by a vast, mostly unpaid community of scientists and practitioners. A framework built on that commons and then fenced with trademarks, patents and permission requirements is an enclosure in the precise historical sense: the conversion of a commons into property.

The conversion is legal and, commercially, perhaps necessary. Firms must earn revenue and research costs money. But it sits uneasily with the epistemology the instruments claim. A theory that knowledge emerges from distributed interaction, that the edge is where novelty lives, and that the 17% at the periphery see what the centre misses is a theory that argues against enclosure. Enclosure stops exactly the distributed recombination and peripheral challenge that complexity says produces new knowledge.

Alignment and recognition

The brochure's deepest promise is to navigate uncertainty as One Swarm: achieve authentic alignment (not just top-down compliance). Kevin Flinn's work on leadership development offers a test that cuts through this. Working within the complex responsive processes tradition, Flinn argues that leadership exists only where it is recognised by others, granted from below in the ongoing interaction and not imposed from above. Without recognition what remains is authoritarianism or coercion, which produce compliance and not followership. Leadership, in Flinn's account, is not about people adopting your story.

Measured by this, "authentic alignment" is a confusion. Alignment describes the outcome in which many vectors point the same way. It says nothing about how they came to point that way. Under Flinn's test, alignment produced by an instrument that surveys, ranks, identifies mavericks and sets a course is compliance with a more sophisticated mechanism. What separates followership from compliance is whether the people involved recognise the direction as theirs. They can recognise it only if they were part of the conversation that made it, not merely data for the instrument that found it.

Tools that control bodies

The darkest and most precise sentence in the corpus on this subject is Stacey's, from The Tools and Techniques of Leadership and Management: no one can control outcomes, but the powerful can control human bodies to a considerable degree. He names the mechanisms as power constraints, ideology, socialisation and disciplinary power. Put next to SwarmCompass, the sentence clarifies. The instrument cannot control the swarm's outcome, and it admits as much. It can arrange what people attend to (the signifiers), what they are asked to report (the micro-pulses), who is singled out (the 17%) and what their reports become (training data). That is not control of outcomes. It is the shaping of attention and conduct, which is what Foucault meant by disciplinary power. The phrase continuous scanning via human agents on the brochure's last panel names it.

Read left to right, the figure is a supply chain. Read along the dashed arc, it is the question of reciprocity. Ostrom's commons survive where users monitor and make the rules. Flinn's leadership survives where direction is recognised and not imposed. Both point to the same design requirement: the instrument's outputs must belong in some real sense to those whose attention it shapes.

A theory of the periphery, sold from the centre.

Altius Commons, enclosure and the knowledge economy

Hess and Ostrom (2007) extended commons theory to knowledge, showing that knowledge commons face not overuse but enclosure and under-provision. The political economy the treatise describes, practitioner insight harvested and trademarked, is enclosure in exactly this sense. Benkler's commons-based peer production names the alternative. The Part VIII reading supplies the dynamic: enclosure is the apparatus of capture applied to a knowledge flow. Flinn's recognition test then becomes measurable: a framework passes it if practitioners can modify, redistribute and contest it without permission, which is what Ostrom's design principles would require of any lasting commons.

Pars Quarta
道 · 理 · 勢

Way, Grain, Propensity

The spine of this imprint's work, read against the two instruments. Classical Chinese thought supplies what the Western corpus states only in parts: an account of efficacy that does not depend on an outside.

Movement 18

Way, Grain, Propensity

Credit comes first, and generously. Of all the Western complexity frameworks, the Cynefin family's recent work is the closest to classical Chinese strategic thought. Estuarine Mapping asks practitioners to start journeys with a sense of direction rather than abstract goals, to work with propensities and dispositions so that the desired costs less energy than the undesired, and to begin from how things are rather than an idealised vision. This is very close to what François Jullien, in The Propensity of Things (1992) and A Treatise on Efficacy (1996), identified as the core of Chinese strategy. One does not project an ideal model and impose it on reality by force of will, which is the Western means–end schema Jullien traced from Aristotle to Clausewitz. One reads the potential of the situation and lets effect come from it.

Because the convergence is real, the divergence is instructive. Read through 道理勢, the instruments seize one term of the triad and lose the other two.

勢 Shì: propensity seized

勢 shì is the configuration's potential: the slope that gives the boulder its force, the bow drawn and ready, the position that makes victory follow. Sunzi's fifth chapter, 勢篇, says the skilled commander seeks victory in 勢 and does not demand it of his men. He chooses people and lets the configuration work. The Estuarine "energy gradient" and the brochure's map the energy gradients of the current state are 勢 rendered in thermodynamics. The instruments grasp 勢 well. They locate it in the substrate, read it, and propose to act along it.

Jullien insists on something the instruments leave out: 勢 includes the strategist. The commander does not stand outside the configuration reading its potential. Their own disposition, timing and restraint are part of the configuration, and the opponent reads it too. 勢 is not a property of the terrain. It belongs to the whole situation, both armies, ground, season and morale, and it changes with every move. To map 勢 is to turn it into a landscape, a substrate, and to lose its essential mobility. Jullien's term for the mobility is transformation: 化 huà, silent and continuous, which no one sees happen and everyone sees has happened.

理 Lǐ: grain lost

理 lǐ first meant the veins in jade, the grain along which the carver must work. The great image is Zhuangzi's Cook Ding (庖丁解牛, chapter three). After nineteen years his blade is as sharp as the day it was ground. He does not hack at the ox. He relies on the heavenly pattern, 依乎天理, and slips the edge, which has no thickness, into the spaces that are already there. 以無厚入有閒: insert what has no thickness into what has room. When he comes to a difficult knot he slows, his gaze settles, and the blade barely moves.

Ding's skill is a perception that comes through the hands, over years, in contact with this ox. He says he no longer sees with his eyes but meets the ox with his spirit. That is 理. It cannot be surveyed, and it cannot be found with a triad. It is the grain as known by someone who has cut along it a thousand times, the radiologist's real expertise without its search template, the navigator's feel for the swell. The instruments' substitute for 理 is pattern detection at scale, the aggregation of many points. Aggregated pattern and grain are opposites. The first is seen from above across many oxen. The second is felt from inside one.

道 Dào: the way that is walked

Zhuangzi's second chapter contains one of the most compressed statements of process philosophy in any language: 道行之而成, the Way is made by walking it. The Dào is not a road laid down in advance and then travelled, still less a bearing given by a compass. It comes into being in the going, and it is made by those who go together. This is transformative teleology in six characters: a future under perpetual construction, made in the present by participants who cannot stand outside it.

A compass offers a bearing, and a bearing is a Dào laid down in advance. This is where the instruments come closest to Western means–end thinking, despite their Jullienesque vocabulary. "Set Your Course" is not 道行之而成. It is the course set before the walking, with the walking reduced to correction.

Position in the triangle is a matter of emphasis, not exclusion. The instruments are not ignorant of grain or way. Snowden's work on expertise and his scepticism of "best practice" respect 理, and his evolutionary potential of the present is close to 道. But what the instruments make operational, sell and deploy is overwhelmingly 勢 as reading of the terrain. The centre of the triangle cannot be sold, because it is a practice and not a product.

無爲 Wúwéi: neither natural nor stimulated

The WRAS vertical axis, natural versus stimulated emergence, meets its most elegant dissolution in 無爲 wúwéi, usually translated "non-action" and better understood as action that does not force. Wúwéi is not "just let it happen". The sage is not idle. Nor is it "stimulated emergence", the deliberate perturbation of a system to see what it does. It is a third thing the axis has no room for: action so closely fitted to the propensity of the situation that it does not register as intervention. Cook Ding's blade does not let the ox fall apart by itself, and it does not stimulate the ox. It moves where the ox already opens. The Laozi says the best rulers are those the people barely know exist, and that when the work is done the people say 我自然: we did it ourselves.

We did it ourselves is Flinn's recognition test stated two and a half millennia early. Direction is followed when it is experienced as one's own. The brochure's "authentic alignment" wants that result while keeping the steersman visible. The Laozi suggests the steersman has to become nearly invisible, and not through technique. It happens through a disposition of restraint that cannot be faked, because the people, like the wrasse's clients, are watching.

經 Jīng: the warp that is also management

One more character, given to us by WRAS's own first word. 經 jīng is the warp, the long threads fixed on the loom through which the weft passes. It also means a classic or canonical text (the threads that hold a tradition), and as a verb it means to pass through, to regulate, to lay out. Paired with 營 it gives 經營 jīngyíng, the ordinary modern word for management. Management in Chinese is literally warping and encamping, laying out the long threads and setting up the camp.

The compound has a classical source that could be a parable for this disputation. The Book of Odes describes King Wen laying out the Spirit Tower: 經始靈臺，經之營之, he began the Spirit Tower, he measured it and laid it out. The common people worked on it and it was finished within days. The king had said not to hurry, and the people came as children come to a parent: 經始勿亟，庶民子來. Mencius cites the ode (Mencius 1A2) to make one point. The people came because the king shared his joy with them. Warp was laid, and the weft wove itself, because those who carried it recognised the work as theirs.

Table 13 · The instruments through the Chinese spine

The table ends where the instruments began, with weaving. The classical image of 經營 is a warp laid by a king and a weft woven by people who came because they wanted to, not because a survey had found them, aligned them or harvested them. If WRAS is to deserve its first word, it has to accept that the weft cannot be woven by the one who lays the warp.

The warp can be laid. The weft comes, or it does not.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part Seven

Part Seven of Liber Secundus extends the 道理勢 spine through Confucius's carpenter's square, Mencius against Xunzi, and the farmer of Song.

Altius Shì and configurational causality

François Jullien's reading of shì as the propensity inherent in a configuration anticipates a modern idea: configurational causality, as in Ragin's qualitative comparative analysis, where outcomes arise from combinations of conditions rather than single causes. Sunzi's general wins by arranging conditions so that the situation itself does the work; Ragin's analyst asks which combinations are sufficient. Both refuse the additive model in which each factor contributes separately. Part VIII's leverage conjunction is the same refusal: agency, adjacency and tendency produce leverage only as a configuration, which is why changing one alone so often does nothing.

Pars Quinta

Reconstruction

A disputation that only takes apart is not finished. This part asks what an instrument faithful to the complexity both frameworks invoke would have to give up, and what it would have to admit.

Movement 19

The Tidal Loom

Much is worth keeping. From SenseMaker: self-signification, narrative at scale, and the link between pattern and story. From Estuarine: the energy cost of change, the honest identification of what is, for now, too costly to move, and the discipline of fine granularity. From WRAS: the weaving of risk with strategy, against the departmental split, and the recognition that complex domains are fat-tailed. From SwarmCompass: the insistence on tempo, days not quarters, and on looking to the periphery. These are real contributions and the reconstruction keeps them all.

What goes is the observer's privilege, the promise of mapped unknowns, the fantasy of alignment, and the assignment of risk to quadrants. I call the result the Tidal Loom. Tidal because, as in Snowden's estuary, the flow runs both ways: what goes in from the centre comes back changed, and the centre is changed by its return. Loom because, as 經營 suggests, a warp can be laid but the weft is the participants' own act.

Note what is not in the figure: no compass, no quadrant, no dashboard at the top, no substrate at the bottom. Sponsors and consultants are wefts like everyone else. Their lines pass over and under the same warp as the narrators' and the front line's. The seventh warp, return, is the structural guarantee that what is learned goes back to those who produced it. The cloth is what Ingold would call a meshwork and Elias a figuration. The pattern is emergent, and the weaving can be done well or badly.

Ten principles

  1. No reader without a reading of the reader. Every deployment begins and ends with the convenors signifying their own experience on the same instrument. The sponsor's anxieties, hopes and blind spots are data, and they are published alongside everyone else's.
  2. Declination before direction. Every signifier set comes with a declination table: what its designers expected to find, what they hoped to find, what the sponsor would prefer not to find, and which dimensions have no vertex. The table is revised after every round.
  3. Frames, not seers. Do not identify "the 17%". Rotate the search template: change what people are asked to notice, so that different people see different gorillas. Blindness lives in the task, so change the task.
  4. Quorum with inhibition. Take the bee's real lesson. Decide by threshold and not consensus, institutionalise stop signals (the formal right to say "wait, consider this"), then commit wholly. Do not seek alignment. Seek a decision people can live with while they still disagree.
  5. Dated limits. Record every "cannot be changed" with a date and a condition, as in Prigogine. Revisit it whenever conditions move far from where they were when it was written.
  6. Noticing, not mapping. Do not promise to map unknown unknowns. Measure and improve the latency of noticing: the time between something new becoming actual and someone in a position to respond recognising it.
  7. Risk follows anxiety. For every probe, ask whose anxiety it creates, whose it relieves, and where the exposure lands on the power gradient. Make failure socially safe and not just financially small.
  8. Return as a design requirement. What narrators give comes back to them as patterns, as decisions and as changed conditions, and it comes back before it goes anywhere else. Ostrom's users monitor. Boisot's cycle closes.
  9. Consent to the harvest. No narrative becomes training data without the narrator's informed consent and a share in what is built from it. If the instrument automates, it says so, says what, and says who benefits.
  10. Recognition, not alignment. The success test is Flinn's and the Laozi's, 我自然: do the people say we did this ourselves? If they say it was done to us, however well, the loom has become a compass.

Each row could be put into practice tomorrow, and none needs a new framework, a new patent or a new acronym. That is deliberate. On the account given here, the problem with the instruments is not a missing method. It is a stance that keeps rebuilding the outside. Changing the stance makes the existing methods, SenseMaker included, more faithful to the science they draw on.

Objectio

The Tidal Loom is unsellable. No board will buy an instrument whose first act is to signify the board's own anxieties and publish them, whose success test is that the people forget the board was involved, and whose outputs go first to the front line. The reconstruction is a counsel of perfection, and the market will choose the compass.

Sed contra

Mencius told King Hui of Liang that the king who shares his pleasures with the people will find them arriving like children to build his tower. The objection assumes that boards buy control. Many buy the appearance of control because they have not been offered anything else. Some, the ones that have been burned by the compass, are ready for the loom.

Respondeo

The objection is right about the market and wrong about necessity. The market will mostly choose the compass, as it mostly chose the five-year plan, the balanced scorecard and the transformation programme. That is a fact about anxiety, not about efficacy. The task of a complexity disputation is not to win the market. It is to keep open the space where a different practice can be recognised by those ready for it. The cleaner wrasse stays honest because some clients are watching, and a disputation is one of those clients.

You cannot sell the weft. You can only lay a warp worth weaving on.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part NineLiber II · the audit of jackets

The dated limit has a twin in Liber Secundus: the discipline of declared form, with its six questions for any gathering.

Altius Sunset clauses and adaptive governance

Dated limits have a legal pedigree: sunset clauses, which make rules expire unless renewed, and the adaptive management of natural resources, which treats policies as experiments with built-in review. Studies of sunset legislation find their value lies less in expiry than in the forced deliberation at renewal: the rule must be seen again. That is the Tidal Loom's purpose. Part VIII adds the kinetic argument: a constraint without a date tends to become part of the field that holds the fold, invisible to those inside it. Dating it keeps it a declared object rather than a jacket.

Pars Sexta
測不準

The Quantum Uncertainty Compass

A counter-instrument. Its needle does not point to north, and its direction is not settled until the user stops and looks. Here it is examined three ways: as physics that already flies, as a drift-instrument for walking a city, and as a relic for those who tell stories.

Movement 20 · Propositio

The Instrument Proposed

Here is the proposal. A quantum uncertainty compass is a conceptual wayfinding instrument that replaces the fixed needle with a system governed by quantum mechanics and probability. It does not point to a single, rigid destination such as magnetic north. It moves through superposition, uncertainty and observer interaction to guide a traveller through physical or metaphorical space. It can be read three ways: as a real device in physics, as a design philosophy, and as a speculative or fictional artefact.

The proposal deserves to be taken seriously because it is the exact inverse of the SwarmCompass. The brochure's compass promises collapse: alignment, a set course, unknowns turned into mapped territory. The quantum compass promises to delay collapse, and to give up the pretence of knowing the destination in exchange for knowledge of the field. Where the first sells certainty about direction, the second offers disciplined uncertainty about it. Part VI asks how much of this is physics, how much is good metaphor, how much is bad metaphor, and how much is worth turning into a playable relic.

The face gives up the single needle but not orientation. The lobes are bearings with weights. The ghost needles are low-probability directions that the dial still shows, the visual form of the brochure's "17%" handled honestly, as small weights and not as special people. The bottom strip carries what a magnetic compass hides: how disturbed the reading is (decoherence), how often it has been checked (Zeno-lock), how much of the terrain has never been sampled (missing mass, after Turing), and the compass's own bias (declination). Each gauge answers one of the earlier critiques.
Table 15 · Traditional compass, quantum uncertainty compass, and the correction physics requires
FeatureTraditional compassQuantum uncertainty compass (as proposed)What physics actually licenses
Reference pointMagnetic northThe user's intent, desire, or an entangled targetReal quantum navigators refer to a map (magnetic or gravity anomaly) or to inertia, not to intent
DisplaySolid needleShifting interference patterns, glowing mistAtom interferometers do read out fringes; the mist is an honest image of a probability distribution
Accuracy vs speedConstantHeisenberg trade-off: fast motion blurs the destination; stillness reveals location but erases the pathToday's sensors are limited mainly by projection noise and vibration, not Heisenberg position–momentum limits; the trade-off works as complementarity metaphor
LockingAlways readableLocks only when the user stops and looksBetter modelled as the quantum Zeno effect: frequent looking freezes change
Entangled pairNonePartner's compass shifts instantly when one turnsforbidden by the no-communication theorem; correlation appears only when the two compare notes
Failure stateMagnetic interferenceDecoherence: noise or rigid expectations make the needle spin or vanishDecoherence is real; "expectation as environment" is a strong metaphor (einselection)

The fourth column is this movement's contribution. Where the proposal is right, it is kept. Where it is wrong, it is replaced with the true physics, which in each case is a stranger and richer image than the error. The no-signalling correction in particular, discussed in Movement 23, turns a telepathic gimmick into a parable of meaning made at the meeting.

Altius An instrument for second-order uncertainty

Decision theory distinguishes risk (known probabilities) from ambiguity (unknown probabilities), and Ellsberg (1961) showed people treat them differently. The quantum uncertainty compass is an instrument for ambiguity: its lobes display not a probability but the shape of one's ignorance about probabilities. Imprecise probability theory, as developed by Walley, represents beliefs as sets of distributions rather than single ones. A needle with weighted lobes is a visual imprecise probability. Its honesty consists in never collapsing that set into one number before the walker must commit.
