Movement 21 · Physica

How Quantum Navigation Works Without GPS

This part is not speculative. Satellite navigation is now routinely attacked, and quantum navigation has left the laboratory. A joint submission to the International Civil Aviation Organization by Sweden and five neighbouring states reported that nearly 123,000 flights by 365 airlines suffered GNSS interference over the Baltic region between January and April 2025, more than 27% of flights in April alone. In the June 2025 Iran–Israel war an estimated 970 ships a day experienced GPS jamming in the Strait of Hormuz region. When the sky's signal can be jammed or spoofed, navigation has to turn to things the adversary cannot fake: inertia, the Earth's magnetic fingerprint, and its gravity.

Family one: the cold-atom inertial sensor

A classical inertial navigator integrates acceleration twice to get position. Every small bias in its accelerometers grows into a large position error over time, which is why inertial systems drift. A quantum accelerometer replaces the mechanical proof-mass with a cloud of atoms laser-cooled to near absolute zero. The atoms are in free fall, so they are perfect test masses. The laser pulses that probe them are a ruler marked off in wavelengths of light.

The working core is a light-pulse Mach–Zehnder atom interferometer. A first laser pulse (a "π/2 pulse") puts each atom into a superposition of two momentum states, so that each atom's wave-function travels two paths at once. After time T a "π pulse" swaps the paths like a mirror. After another T a final π/2 pulse recombines them. The two paths interfere, and how many atoms end in each output state depends on a phase φ ≈ keff·a·T², where a is the acceleration of the apparatus relative to the falling atoms. Rotation enters through the Sagnac effect on the enclosed area. The sensitivity grows with T², which is why laboratory fountains are tall and field devices are a compromise.

This is the deepest irony of the proposal and its strongest vindication. In a real quantum accelerometer the needle does travel in superposition, and the measurement only becomes a reading when the paths recombine. The proposal's poetic image, a compass that points everywhere until it is read, is what happens to each atom. What the physics adds is that the superposition is useful only because it is closed again, by a deliberately designed recombination. Uncertainty that is never recombined yields no reading.

The UK has been unusually active here. Imperial College London's team demonstrated their first "quantum compass" prototype in 2018 and tested it aboard the Royal Navy research ship XV Patrick Blackett in May 2023. In February 2024 the system went to sea again in a container aboard MV Hurst Point, and in December 2025 a revised Quantum Inertial Navigation Sensing unit was trialled in the Arctic aboard MV Anvil Point, measuring accelerations and rotations from the wave-like behaviour of cold atoms. The practical advantage is not some magical knowledge of position. It is long-term stability: the atoms do not drift the way a phone's accelerometer does.

Family two: the Earth's magnetic fingerprint

The second family navigates by map-matching. Beneath the Earth's main magnetic field lies a crustal anomaly field of the order of hundreds of nanotesla, produced by the rocks below. It is unique from place to place, like a fingerprint. A sensitive magnetometer measures the total field, software subtracts the vehicle's own magnetic noise, and a filter fuses the result with inertial data, comparing the measured profile with a pre-surveyed anomaly map. The vehicle finds where it is by finding where the world looks like this.

The leading field results come from Q-CTRL's Ironstone Opal. In February 2025 the company flew more than 6,700 km in a Cessna 208B Grand Caravan near Griffith, Australia, with magnetometers mounted inside the aircraft, where avionics interference is more than ten times larger than at typical external mounts. The system outperformed a strategic-grade inertial navigation system by at least 11× in the air and up to 50× on the ground. Later reports cite accuracy up to 111× better than the best conventional alternative and positioning down to 4 metres over flights of up to 700 km. A companion gravimetric system ran for more than 144 hours aboard an Australian Navy vessel. The system is passive and emits nothing, so there is nothing to jam or spoof.

The magnetometers can themselves be quantum. In a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre, a nitrogen atom sits next to a missing carbon in a diamond lattice. Lit by a laser, the defect fluoresces more or less brightly depending on the surrounding magnetic field. Because the NV axis can lie along four crystallographic orientations in the tetrahedral lattice, one diamond yields vector magnetometry. A Warwick and Element Six team operated such a magnetometer in a moving van in 2024.

Look at the fourth box. The quantum magnetometer does not abolish the map. It depends on one. The researchers formulate localisation as a map-matching problem, show that map quality bounds achievable accuracy, and find that in magnetically smooth regions the match is ambiguous. One group therefore builds an entropy map and a path-planner that steers the vehicle towards regions with the most informative magnetic signatures. That is the most beautiful wayfinding lesson in the literature: go where the world is most itself. Featureless terrain cannot locate you, so the wise navigator seeks out the distinctive.

Corrections the physics requires

A quantum accelerometer does not "calculate exact position". It measures acceleration and rotation. Position is still integrated, and still drifts, only far more slowly. Map-matching systems infer position relative to a map. Neither family gives absolute position by quantum fiat.

The operative limit is not Heisenberg's in the popular sense. In atom interferometers the fundamental noise floor is quantum projection noise, the binomial noise of counting N uncorrelated atoms, which gives the standard quantum limit Δφ ≈ 1/√N. The Heisenberg limit, Δφ ≈ 1/N, is an ideal that can be approached only by entangling the atoms, for example in spin-squeezed states. The record of about 20 dB of squeezing in an ensemble of 10⁶ atoms produced the most precise relative phase measurement ever made with cold matter-waves. In fielded sensors the daily enemies are more mundane: vibration, dead time between measurements, and aliasing. Heisenberg is a horizon, not today's wall.

The "observer effect" is not the uncertainty principle. Popular accounts merge two ideas: that measurement disturbs, and that conjugate quantities cannot both be sharp. Barad devotes an appendix of Meeting the Universe Halfway to showing that the uncertainty principle is not the basis of Bohr's complementarity. For Bohr the point is not that looking disturbs a pre-existing state. It is that a property is defined only within a specific experimental arrangement. The difference is decisive for the metaphor in Movement 23.

A metaphor hides in the slopes. Uncorrelated agents average their noise down only as the square root of their number, so a crowd of independent opinions improves slowly. Correlated agents, entangled in the technical sense, can do better: they accumulate information about the quantity collectively. In social terms the advantage comes from relationship, not headcount. This is a disciplined image for why a swarm of disconnected survey respondents is a weak sensor compared with a group of people who have learned to sense together, the CRP point of Movement 12 restated in metrology.
Live model
Headcount against correlation

Choose the number of atoms and the degree of spin squeezing. Teal is the standard quantum limit 1/√N, gold the Heisenberg limit 1/N, violet a squeezed ensemble ξ/√N. The read-out gives the headroom that correlation could buy.

The robin's eye: the first quantum compass

Long before the Royal Navy, the night-migratory songbird had a quantum compass. The leading hypothesis for avian magnetoreception is the radical-pair mechanism. Blue light striking a cryptochrome protein in the retina creates pairs of radicals, molecules with an unpaired electron, in a coherent spin state whose chemistry is sensitive to the direction of the Earth's field. In 2021 Xu, Mouritsen, Hore and colleagues showed in Nature that cryptochrome 4 from the European robin is magnetically sensitive in vitro, more so than the same protein from non-migratory chicken and pigeon, through four successive flavin–tryptophan radical pairs. The authors were careful: this was isolated protein in a laboratory, not proof that CRY4 is the sensor in the living bird.

Three features of the robin's compass bear on our instrument. It needs light: it is a compass that works only when it can see. It works by keeping a fragile quantum coherence alive in a warm, wet, noisy cell, so it resists decoherence well enough to be useful. And it gives the bird an orientation, not a destination. The robin does not know where Africa is. It knows how the field lines are inclined, and it migrates by staying faithful to that inclination night after night.

The oldest quantum compass is a bird's eye. It points nowhere, and it carries the robin to Africa.

Altius Quantum sensing and the standard quantum limit

The precision of quantum sensors is bounded by counting statistics: with N independent atoms, phase uncertainty scales as one over the square root of N, the standard quantum limit. Entanglement can in principle reach the Heisenberg limit, one over N, and spin-squeezing experiments have beaten the standard limit in the laboratory. Fielded navigation sensors are still dominated by technical noise: vibration, dead time, aliasing. The organisational parallel is precise and humbling: the bottleneck in sensing a complex situation is rarely the theoretical limit of one's method, and usually the noise of the setting in which the method is used.

Movement 22 · Deriva

The Drift Instrument: Psychogeography and the Probability Cloud

The second register of the proposal is speculative design and psychogeography, which Debord in 1955 called the study of the precise laws and specific effects of the geographical environment, consciously organised or not, on the emotions and behaviour of individuals. Here the compass is not meant to bring you home. It is meant to make you lost well.

Debord's dérive

Guy Debord's Theory of the Dérive (1956) defines the drift as a technique of rapid passage through varied ambiances. Two of its sentences could serve as a specification for the quantum compass. First: chance is a less important factor in this activity than one might think, because from a dérive point of view cities have psychogeographical contours, with constant currents, fixed points and vortexes that strongly discourage entry into or exit from certain zones. Second, the dérive includes both a letting-go and its necessary contradiction: the domination of psychogeographical variations by the knowledge and calculation of their possibilities. Debord also gives the drift's sociometry. One can drift alone, but the most fruitful arrangement is several small groups of two or three, and with more than four or five participants the specifically drifting character quickly fades. The average dérive lasts a day.

The proposed compass is an instrument for exactly this double movement. Its probability cloud is the letting-go: no bearing is imposed. Its lobes are the calculation: the currents and vortexes of the city given weights. Read through Debord, the "glowing haze indicating where meaningful paths are likely to be" is not mysticism. It is a psychogeographical contour map rendered as probability.

A real quantum drift-device, and its aura

The speculative instrument already has a crude real ancestor. Randonautica, launched in February 2020, claimed inspiration from chaos theory and Debord's dérive. It generated coordinates near the user from a quantum random-number source at the Australian National University and offered "attractors" (dense clusters of quantum points), "voids" (sparse regions) and "anomalies". The app invited users to "set an intention" before generating a point. Its own developers' material describes Attractor generation as resting on the claimed ability of the user's intention to influence random quantum processes.

The critique is straightforward. One sceptical review notes that only one of the app's entropy sources is quantum at all, and that a quantum random-number server simply produces a number like any other. No evidence supports intention bending vacuum fluctuations. The "quantum" in Randonautica is aura in Walter Benjamin's sense: a halo of authenticity attached to a mechanism that a die could reproduce. And yet the design works as Debord meant it to. It breaks habitual routes, sends people to places their routines avoid, and produces encounters. The lesson for the quantum compass is to keep the drift and discard the aura. Its value lies in disrupting habit, not in claiming that randomness is sacred.

Barad: the walker, the compass and the city as one phenomenon

The most serious philosophical ally for the drift-instrument is Karen Barad's agential realism. Barad is a theoretical physicist and develops it from Bohr's philosophy-physics in Meeting the Universe Halfway (2007). For Barad the basic units of reality are phenomena, the "ontological inseparability of intra-acting agencies". Her neologism intra-action, as opposed to interaction, means that the agencies do not exist as separate things before they meet. Their distinctness is made in the meeting, through what she calls an agential cut. Applied to the drift, the walker, the compass and the city are not three things, one of which reads the others. They are one phenomenon, and "direction" is something made within it.

This is the philosophical opposite of the SwarmCompass. There the client stands outside and reads the swarm. Barad places the reader inside the reading and makes the reading part of what is read. It is a quantum-flavoured statement of Mead's gesture–response and Elias's figuration from Movement 9.

Objectio

All this is metaphor dressed as physics. Quantum effects decohere far below the scale of walkers and cities. Using quantum language for social life is precisely the "metaphorician" failure this treatise condemned in the bee and the wrasse. Critics of Wendt's Quantum Mind and Social Science have found misconceptions in its physics and its philosophy, and Prozorov warns that a quantum social ontology risks reducing the plurality of social worlds to the physical world's laws.

Sed contra

Barad and Wendt make different arguments. A 2023 analysis in the European Journal for Philosophy of Science separates Wendt's claim, that quantum physical effects are present in the social world, from Barad's, that quantum metaphysics matters even where quantum effects are negligible. It finds that some criticism of Wendt properly applies to Barad, and that both arguments face severe challenges. The analogy is not innocent. Nor is it uniform.

Respondeo

The answer is analogical discipline, applied with the same rule the treatise used against the bee. An analogy is admissible when the structure it borrows is real in the source domain and the inference drawn from it does not depend on the source's physics. "Correlated agents beat the square-root law" is admissible: the structural claim, collective accumulation beats independent averaging, is true in metrology and can be tested in social life on its own terms. "Intention bends random numbers" is not: the inference depends on physics that does not exist. Table 16 applies the test.

One, Wendt's identity thesis, is set aside as a question of ontology that this disputation does not need to settle.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part Twenty-ThreeLiber II · Part Four

Liber Secundus reads the dérive as a drift with rules, and notes that 'going nowhere' is a privilege, a charge the dérive shares.

Altius Agential cuts

Karen Barad's agential realism holds that the boundary between object and apparatus is not given but enacted by each measurement: an 'agential cut'. The dérive is a sequence of agential cuts made by walking: each turn decides what counts as the city and what as the walker. This explains a feature of psychogeography that maps cannot capture: the same street is a different phenomenon on different drifts. The drift instrument is honest when it records the cut along with the reading. A dérive log that notes only places, and not the turns that made them, is a map pretending to be a measurement.

Movement 23 · Quattuor Leges

Four Laws of the Uncertain Needle

The proposal names four mechanics: observer collapse, the Heisenberg trade-off, entangled wayfinding and decoherence. Each is examined here against the physics. Each is either kept, corrected or replaced, and each is translated into a law of practice that bears on the instruments this treatise has criticised.

First law: the watched needle never turns (Zeno)

The proposal says the needle locks only when the walker stops and looks, and otherwise stays in superposition. The physics offers something stronger. In 1977 Misra and Sudarshan showed that a quantum system measured frequently enough will, in the limit, stay in its initial state. They named this after Zeno's arrow, which cannot move because at every instant it is where it is. Itano, Heinzen, Bollinger and Wineland demonstrated the effect experimentally in 1990 with trapped beryllium ions, and it is the experiment most often cited as the demonstration. Frequent observation does not just collapse the needle. It freezes the evolution of what is observed. Physicists sometimes summarise it as "a system cannot change while you are watching it".

This is the treatise's sharpest structural analogy and passes the test of Table 16: the claim that over-frequent monitoring suppresses change can be examined in organisations on its own terms. An organisation that pulses its people constantly, asking them to signify, report and re-signify, may be freezing the very emergence it claims to detect. Each micro-pulse asks the system to declare its state. Declaring the state again and again keeps it in that state. The Zeno law of practice: monitor less often than the change you hope to see.
Live model
Watch the watched needle

A two-level system needs one full period to change state completely. Drag the slider to measure it more often within that period. Each measurement resets the evolution. This is the quantum Zeno effect, computed exactly as survival = [cos²(π/2n)]ⁿ.

Second law: path or place (complementarity)

The proposal's "Heisenberg trade-off" says that moving fast blurs the destination, while standing still reveals the exact location and erases the path. As literal physics this is loose, because position–momentum uncertainty concerns conjugate variables of a quantum object, not a hiker's speed. As Bohrian complementarity it is admissible and beautiful. Some descriptions require mutually exclusive experimental arrangements, so one cannot have both in a single reading. Ingold gives the human version: the wayfarer knows along a path and the navigator knows from above between points. The law of practice: every reading chooses between knowing where and knowing how. A strategy instrument that claims both in one dashboard has confused two arrangements.

Third law: harmony appears only at the rendezvous (no-signalling)

The proposal's most attractive mechanic, two entangled compasses that let travellers move "in subtle, non-verbal harmony" because one's turn instantly shifts the other's weighting, is the one physics forbids. The no-communication theorem states that during measurement of an entangled state, one observer cannot transmit information to another by measuring their subsystem, regardless of distance. Each party's local results look random. Bob cannot tell whether Alice did anything at all. The correlation becomes visible only when the two compare their records over an ordinary, light-limited channel.

The correction is better than the original. The proposal wanted telepathy. The physics gives retrospective recognition: a correlation that existed throughout and becomes meaningful only in the conversation at the rendezvous. This is Weick's retrospective sensemaking, Mead's meaning completed in the response, and Flinn's recognition test in one image. Alignment cannot be broadcast to a distant partner. It can only be discovered when people meet and compare what each of them lived through.

Fourth law: expectation is an environment (decoherence)

The proposal's failure state, in which external noise or rigid expectations make the needle spin wildly or vanish, is the most defensible of its metaphors. In decoherence theory, associated especially with Wojciech Zurek, a quantum system that becomes entangled with its environment loses the phase relations that make interference possible. The environment in effect continuously "monitors" the system. Zurek's further concept of einselection (environment-induced superselection) explains why only certain robust "pointer states" survive this monitoring and appear classical.

The social translation passes Table 16 with care. An environment saturated with expectation (targets, KPIs, the publicly declared strategy) continuously monitors an organisation and einselects its robust pointer states: the clichés, safe answers and reportable outcomes that survive scrutiny. Interference, the recombination of divergent possibilities into something new, is lost. The law of practice: protect pockets of low monitoring where possibilities can still interfere. These are not ungoverned spaces. They are spaces governed by a lighter touch, which leads to the last image of this movement.

Coda to the laws: weak measurement as wúwéi

Quantum theory has a concept the proposal did not name and the treatise needs. In 1988 Aharonov, Albert and Vaidman introduced weak measurement: a coupling between a system and a probe gentle enough to extract a little information while barely disturbing the system, with the information recovered statistically over many trials. It is the physicist's form of 無爲 wúwéi, action that does not force (Movement 18). A leader who measures weakly learns without freezing, and observes without einselecting. The quantum uncertainty compass, rightly built, is a weak instrument: often read lightly and rarely read hard, and it never pulses its people into Zeno stillness.

Strong measurement freezes. Weak measurement learns. The sage's eye is weak.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part Twenty-TwoLiber II · Part Twenty-Five

The two strokes of facilitation and Stalker's nuts are weak-measurement disciplines in human form.

Altius Quantum Darwinism

Zurek's quantum Darwinism explains why some facts become objective: information about pointer states is copied redundantly into the environment, so many observers can read it without disturbing the system. This gives the four laws a fifth implication. In an organisation, a fact becomes 'objective' when it is recorded redundantly, in documents, routines and memories, so that many people can consult it independently. Facts recorded once, in a single dashboard, are fragile in exactly the quantum sense: reading them changes them. Redundancy of record, not authority of source, is what makes organisational facts robust.

Movement 24 · Codex Artefacti

Pyxis Incerta: Rules and Lore for a Relic

The third register is fiction and play. What follows is a complete, system-agnostic artefact for tabletop role-playing or interactive fiction. It uses six-sided dice, converts easily to d20 systems, and translates every law of Movement 23 into a mechanic. The physics is the rulebook, so the relic teaches what it is while it is played.

PYXIS INCERTA
The Compass of Unsettled North · Wondrous Instrument · Very Rare · Requires Attunement by one who has been lost

It was not forged. It was cooled. The makers, remembered only as the Order of the Unmapped, took a diamond with one nitrogen wound in its heart and a mote of atoms chilled to within a breath of absolute stillness, and sealed them under a crystal that does not reflect. There is no needle. There is a weather inside the glass: a slow aurora of possibilities that thickens towards what may matter and thins over what the world is hiding.

The Order kept three sayings. The watched needle never turns. You may know where, or know how — never both at one glance. What you share with your twin you will learn only at the meeting. A fourth was scratched into the bezel of the one surviving pair, in a later and more desperate hand: Count what you have seen once. That is how much you have not seen at all.

Properties

Bearing Pool. The keeper (GM) secretly sets 3–5 candidate lobes for the current region: places of meaning, danger or need. Each has a weight from 1–6. The dial shows them as mist of matching density.

Attunement Dice. The bearer has an Attunement rank (I–V) equal to their number of dice (d6).

Gauges. Decoherence 0–6 · Zeno-Lock 0–3 · Log of Kinds · Declination (hidden).

Curse

Declination. Every Pyxis leans towards its maker's desire. Each compass has a hidden Declination (roll d6: 1 safety, 2 wealth, 3 the past, 4 a person, 5 a grudge, 6 the sea). In ties, the dial favours the lobe aligned with it. Learning one's Declination is a quest, and doing so lets the bearer correct for it, as a navigator corrects for magnetic declination.

The Seven Rules

  1. Collapse (Stop and Look). To draw a bearing, the bearer must halt and gaze. This takes a scene beat or a combat round. Roll Attunement dice. Each 5–6 is a clarity. With 0 clarities the dial shows only weather. With 1, reveal the heaviest lobe's direction. With 2 or more, reveal one additional lobe per extra clarity, heaviest first.
  2. Path or Place (Complementarity). On each collapse, declare Path or Place. Path reveals the safest next leg towards the chosen lobe but not its distance or nature. Place reveals what and how far it is but no route. A single reading never gives both.
  3. The Watched Needle (Zeno-Lock). Each further collapse in the same scene adds +1 Zeno-Lock. At Lock 3 the dial freezes and the keeper may not add new lobes to the Bearing Pool. The world stops offering novelty. Lock falls by 1 for each scene travelled without looking.
  4. Decoherence. +1 Decoherence for each source of Noise (crowds, machines, open conflict, a deadline spoken aloud) and +1 each time the bearer declares aloud what they expect to find. Subtract Decoherence from clarities. At 6, roll on the Decoherence Table. Decoherence resets after a night's rest in a quiet place or after a Rendezvous (Rule 5).
  5. The Twin (No-Signalling). A paired Pyxis exists. Apart, each twin's dial shows only noise to the other's movements, and nothing passes between them. When the two bearers meet and each reads their Log aloud, the keeper reveals the hidden Correspondence: one Shared Site that neither could find alone, and +2 dice to both on their next collapse.
  6. Turing's Glass (Missing Mass). Keep a Log of Kinds: each distinct kind of place or encounter met while following the Pyxis, with a tally. Once per session the bearer may ask "How much remains unseen?" The keeper answers honestly with the fraction (kinds seen exactly once) ÷ (total tallies). Below 0.10 the region is well known, and the keeper may retire it. Above 0.40, the world here is still mostly unmet.
  7. Weak Reading (Wúwéi). Instead of collapsing, the bearer may glance while moving. Roll one die only. On a 6, the keeper whispers which lobe is heavier than the bearer currently believes. A glance never adds Zeno-Lock or Decoherence. Three glances in three scenes count as one collapse for Rule 1, without its costs.

A scene, played

The rain has driven the market indoors. Mara, a Drifter, stops beneath the arcade and lifts the Pyxis. Two dice: a 6 and a 2, one clarity. The keeper reveals the heaviest lobe as a thickening of gold to the north-east. Mara declares Place. "It is a bookbinder's shop that should not exist, three streets away, and it is closing." She looks again, wanting the route: Zeno-Lock 1, a 5 and a 5, two clarities, but she must now choose Path, and the second lobe appears, faint and rose-coloured, to the south. She says aloud, "The bookbinder will have the map." Decoherence +1. The glass dims a little. She goes north-east. In the shop, in Turing's Glass, she counts eleven kinds seen once among twenty-six tallies. Nearly half of this quarter is still unmet. Across the city her twin, Ilse, has been walking south all afternoon for no reason she can name. They will learn why only when they meet.

Designer's note. Every rule is a physical law in costume. Rule 1 is the closed interferometer: superposition yields a reading only when recombined. Rule 2 is Bohrian complementarity. Rule 3 is the quantum Zeno effect. Rule 4 is decoherence and einselection, with expectation as environment. Rule 5 is the no-communication theorem: correlation without signal, recognised at the meeting. Rule 6 is the Good–Turing estimator played literally. Rule 7 is weak measurement. The Drift Table encodes Debord, and smooth versus distinctive terrain encodes magnetic-anomaly navigation. Playing the relic is a seminar in disguise.
Playable
Hold the Pyxis Incerta

The relic, running under its seven rules. Look for Path or Place (Rule 1–2), glance weakly (Rule 7), walk on to a new scene and grow your Log of Kinds, declare an expectation or court noise (Rule 4), consult Turing's Glass (Rule 6), or meet your Twin (Rule 5). Look too often and the needle freezes (Rule 3).

Altius Games as epistemic instruments

The Pyxis Incerta is a game, and games have a respectable epistemic history: war games at Kriegsakademie, Shubik's gaming in economics, and the RAND tradition of scenario play. Their value is that they let players experience non-ergodic consequences safely: a lost game is one path, lived. Caillois's distinction between alea and agôn applies to the Pyxis directly: its dice give chance, its skill tracks give contest, and its log gives memory. A good epistemic game makes the player feel the difference between bad luck and bad judgement, which no framework diagram can do.

Movement 25 · Comparatio

The Uncertain Compass Against the Swarm

Now the counter-instrument is set beside the instrument it answers. SwarmCompass and the Pyxis Incerta are both called compasses. Both reach for nature for their authority, the bee and the atom. Both promise to guide through uncertainty. Their logics are opposite at every joint.

Read across, not down. Each pair is one question answered two ways. How often should we look? Constantly, or weakly. Where does alignment come from? Broadcast from a centre, or recognised at the meeting. What do we know about the unknown? Its map, or its mass. Who sees? Selected seers, or everyone, weighted. Where is the reader? Outside, or inside. What is the instrument's bias? Unstated, or declared. The right column contains no new method. It is the same science read without the wish for certainty.

Look weakly. Meet often. Count the once-seen. Correct your declination. Commit wholly when you must.

Altius Exploration–exploitation under non-stationarity

Bandit problems formalise the choice between exploring new options and exploiting known ones. When the environment changes, the restless or non-stationary bandit, optimal policies keep exploring indefinitely and discount old evidence. The swarm instrument is tuned for convergence, which is exploitation; the uncertain compass is tuned for continued exploration under drift. Neither is wrong in general. The decisive question is how fast the world changes relative to the cost of being wrong, and that question is exactly what both Cynefin instruments assume rather than measure.

Pars Septima

The Observer Inside

Six movements on what happens once the measurer is placed inside the measured: in surveys, in physics, in markets, in Boyd's dialectic, in a distressed building on a wet Tuesday, and in the drift of a wayfinder who has given up the map for the middle.

Movement 26 · Quaestio Ordinis

The Survey That Does Not Commute

The SwarmCompass funnel begins with an assessment, a "question survey to map your decision-making blind spots", and SenseMaker works by asking people to place their stories on a sequence of signifiers. Both assume something classical social science also assumes: that asking a question reads an attitude already there, so the order of questions is noise to be averaged away. A striking result from 2014 says this is false in a precise and mathematically predictable way.

Seventy surveys and one equality

Survey researchers have long known about question-order effects: the order of two questions changes the answers, which is why survey organisations usually rotate question order between respondents. Zheng Wang, Tyler Solloway, Richard Shiffrin and Jerome Busemeyer (PNAS, 2014) asked whether these effects were mere carry-over noise or had structure. They modelled each question as a measurement that changes the state of the respondent, using the mathematics quantum theory uses for measurements that do not commute. Before looking at any data, they derived a prediction: the quantum question (QQ) equality. When two questions are asked back to back in reversed orders to different groups, the shifts in agreeing and disagreeing combinations must exactly offset.

They tested it on 70 national representative surveys (Gallup and Pew polls from 2001 to 2011, each with 651 to 3,006 participants) and on two laboratory experiments. The equality held strongly across all of them. In one Gallup poll, when respondents were asked about Clinton first, 49% said both Clinton and Gore were honest and trustworthy; when Gore was asked about first, 56% did. Meanwhile the share saying neither was trustworthy fell from 28% to 21%. The seven-point rise in "yes-yes" was cancelled by the seven-point fall in "no-no", as the theory requires. The equality fails exactly where the theory says it should: in a survey on admitting Pete Rose and "Shoeless" Joe Jackson to the Baseball Hall of Fame, new information was given between the questions. Wang is careful to say the result does not show the brain is a quantum computer. Quantum probability describes the judgement; it makes no claim about neurones.

The right panel is the important one. Classical probability treats an attitude as a fixed point that questions merely read. Quantum probability treats a question as an operation that moves the state it measures. The second question is therefore asked of a different person from the one who answered the first. The QQ equality is the fingerprint this geometry leaves in the data, and it appeared in every one of the 70 surveys. The live model below lets you rotate the question axes and watch order effects appear while the equality holds.
Live model
Rotate the questions

A two-dimensional quantum-probability model of two yes/no questions. Move the attitude state ψ and the two question axes. Gold bars are answer patterns when A is asked first, teal bars when B is asked first. Order effects appear and vanish while the QQ difference stays at zero, as Wang et al. predicted and 70 surveys confirmed.

What this does to a sensing instrument

The implication for SenseMaker and the SwarmCompass Assessment is direct. A signifier set is a sequence of measurements that change their respondent. The triad answered third is answered by someone the first two triads have already moved. Counterbalancing order across respondents, which careful survey designers do, averages the effect away statistically. It does not remove it from any individual, and it hides a structured phenomenon as if it were noise. The deeper point is the one Movement 12 made through Boisot and Ashby, now with stronger evidence. The instrument is not a window onto attitudes. It is one of the forces that forms them.

The complex responsive processes school reached the same view without the mathematics. For Mead, meaning is completed in the response, and for Shaw, conversation is where selves and organisations are continuously re-formed. A question is a gesture. Wang's group has shown that the gesture leaves a measurable, lawful mark.

Table 18 · Order effects and the design of sensing instruments
Design choiceClassical assumptionQQ-informed realityBetter practice
Fixed signifier orderOrder is irrelevant noiseEach item moves the respondent's stateRotate order and report the order effects as findings
Long instrumentsMore items, more informationLater items measure a respondent reshaped by earlier onesShorter, purposeful sequences; ask the crucial item first in some arms
Explanatory text between itemsHelpful contextNew information breaks the QQ structure (Rose–Jackson case)Treat inserted information as an intervention and record it

Comparing groupsDifferences reflect groupsMay reflect sequence and framingHold instrument order constant across groups being compared

The fourth row closes a loop opened in Movement 4. A questionnaire about blind spots meets two obstacles: blindness cannot be self-reported, and asking about it in a particular order changes the stance from which respondents answer. Both point the same way. Sensing in human systems cannot be done from outside, because the sensing changes what is sensed.

Every question is asked of someone the previous question has already changed.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · the Overture

Liber Secundus's central idea, to the strait-jacketed the other always seems baggy, is an order effect on the scale of whole traditions.

Altius Quantum cognition beyond order effects

The QQ equality is one of several regularities quantum cognition explains: conjunction fallacies, disjunction effects and violations of the sure-thing principle also follow naturally from non-commuting projections (Busemeyer and Bruza, 2012). The models do not claim the brain is quantum; they claim that judgement under uncertainty has the algebra of projections onto subspaces. For instruments the implication is sharp: any multi-question assessment is a sequence of projections, and its order is part of its design. An instrument that does not publish and justify its question order has not specified what it measures.

Movement 27 · De Perspectivis

Facts Relative to Observers: Rovelli, QBism and Wigner's Friend

If questions change the questioned, a harder question follows: is there any view from which the facts are simply the facts, the same for everyone? Classical management assumes so; the dashboard is its icon, and the "single source of truth" its creed. Three developments at the foundations of physics have made that assumption newly contestable. They do not settle it, but they force anyone who invokes quantum language, as SwarmCompass and this treatise both do, to say which observer they mean.

Relational quantum mechanics

In 1996 Carlo Rovelli proposed that the source of quantum puzzlement is the notion of an observer-independent state of a system, in the same way that relativity removed observer-independent time. In relational quantum mechanics, a system has a state only relative to another system, and physical quantities take values only in interactions. All systems are treated as equivalent, with no special class called "observers"; the theory describes the information systems have about one another and is claimed to be complete. Rovelli's guiding analogy is velocity, which classically makes sense only relative to a frame. The view has serious critics: Muciño, Okon and Sudarsky conclude that it fails to give a satisfactory understanding of the quantum world.

QBism

Christopher Fuchs, Rüdiger Schack and David Mermin go further towards the agent. In QBism a quantum state is not an element of reality but an agent's personal degrees of belief about her future experience. A measurement does not reveal a pre-existing state of affairs; it is an action by an agent that creates an outcome, a new experience for that agent. The "collapse" is the agent updating her beliefs. On this reading the old Wigner's friend paradox dissolves: the friend in the sealed laboratory and Wigner outside assign different states, and both are right, each relative to their own experience.

The Wigner's friend experiments

In 2020 Bong, Utreras-Alarcón, Ghafari, Liang, Tischler, Cavalcanti, Pryde and Wiseman turned the paradox into a theorem with an experiment (Nature Physics 16, 1199). They defined Local Friendliness as the conjunction of three assumptions: that observed events are absolute (the same for everyone), that there is no superdeterminism, and locality. They showed quantum theory predicts violations of inequalities that follow from these assumptions, and observed such violations in a proof-of-principle experiment in which the path of a photon played the role of the "friend". The authors argue this constrains reality more strictly than Bell's theorem. The limits matter: the "friend" was a degree of freedom of a photon, not a person, and a 2022 assessment argues such theorems fail to impose significant constraints on the nature of physical reality. What can be said is that the assumption of observer-independent facts is no longer innocent in physics.

Analogical discipline (Table 16) applies. Nothing here proves that a nurse and a board inhabit different physical realities. What crosses legitimately is a structure. The assumption that every observer's facts can be stitched into one observer-independent record is an assumption. It is now contested even in physics, and in organisations it has always been an act of power. Mead said as much in 1927: perspectives are objectively real, and the "objective" is the whole set of them, not a view from nowhere above them.

Mead's objective relativism

The complexity corpus anticipated this long before Rovelli. In "The Objective Reality of Perspectives" (1927) Mead argued that a perspective is not a subjective distortion of a world seen properly from nowhere. Perspectives are features of nature, the ways the world is organised relative to organisms acting in it. Elias's figurations are networks of such perspectives bound by power-ratios, and a companion treatise of this imprint, on the Stacey Matrix and Hockney's photo-joiners, took as its thesis that there is no view from nowhere. Relational quantum mechanics gives this thesis a physicist's vocabulary. Its relevance to the instruments is plain. The SwarmCompass dashboard and the WRAS chooser at the crossing of the axes both presuppose a view from which everyone's facts compose into one. The physics now treats that as a hypothesis, not a premise.

Objectio

This is precisely the "quantum social science" the treatise criticised in Movement 22. The Local Friendliness experiment used a photon's path as an observer. Nothing about board dashboards follows.

Sed contra

The claim is not that dashboards are quantum. It is that a premise organisations treat as obvious, the absoluteness of observed events, is treated as optional in the most rigorous science of measurement we have, and that the social theory of the corpus (Mead, Elias, Barad) had independently rejected it for social life.

Respondeo

The physics is used as a solvent, not a foundation. It dissolves the confidence with which the premise is held, and leaves its rejection to be argued on social grounds, where Mead and Elias argue it well. The practical consequence is modest and testable: instruments should record whose observation each datum is, and treat disagreement between nested observers as information rather than error to be reconciled away.

There is no dashboard outside the lab. There are only friends, and friends of friends.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part FourteenLiber II · Question V

Ryōan-ji, Hockney's joiners and the 'god trick' are Liber Secundus's versions of the Wigner's-friend lesson.

Altius Contextuality

The Kochen–Specker theorem shows that quantum outcomes cannot be assigned values independently of the measurement context. Experiments on contextuality in human judgement (Dzhafarov and colleagues) have found that apparent contextuality in surveys usually reduces to direct influences between questions, an important caution against over-reading. The deeper lesson survives the caution: whether an answer is 'the same' across contexts is itself an empirical question. Relational and QBist readings agree that the context is part of the fact. A manager's answer in an appraisal and in a corridor may both be true, as facts relative to different apparatus.

Movement 28 · Reflexio

The Real Observer Effect: Goodhart, Lucas, Soros and the Performative Model

Quantum measurement disturbs at the scale of atoms. In human affairs there is an observer effect far larger, older and better documented, which the instruments' quantum vocabulary tends to obscure. People read the measurements made of them and change their behaviour in response. This is reflexivity, and it is the most serious obstacle to every compression conceded in Movement 11′.

Four laws of the same family

Goodhart (1975). Writing on British monetary policy, Charles Goodhart observed that any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes. The popular form, "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure", is Marilyn Strathern's 1997 generalisation.

Campbell (1976). Donald Campbell's version: the more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures, and the more apt it will be to distort the social processes it is meant to monitor.

Lucas (1976). Robert Lucas argued it is naive to predict the effects of a policy change from historical relationships alone, because any change in policy will systematically alter the structure of econometric models. People's expectations respond to the policy.

Soros. George Soros's theory of reflexivity holds that participants' views and theories condition the situations they participate in, which in turn condition their views. All views are fallible, so markets are driven by feedback between belief and reality rather than tending to equilibrium. Robert Merton's self-fulfilling prophecy (1948), a false definition of a situation that evokes behaviour making it true, is the sociological ancestor.

The model that made its market

The most precise case study is Donald MacKenzie and Yuval Millo's history of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (American Journal of Sociology, 2003). The Black–Scholes–Merton option-pricing model was published in 1973, the year the CBOE opened. Over the following years option prices came to fit the model's predictions more closely, in part because traders used the model to set prices and arbitrage. The model, MacKenzie argues, was not a camera recording the market but an engine shaping it: performativity. After the crash of October 1987 implied volatilities no longer lay flat and the "volatility skew" appeared. MacKenzie calls this counterperformativity: use of the model helped produce conditions that falsified it. The case is contested. Nicolas Brisset argues the model never became fully self-fulfilling and that the skew reflects traders' awareness of the model's falsity. Either way, the market and the model co-evolved.

The right panel is schematic, not plotted data. Its shape is the claim: a model can make its world fit it for a while, and then produce conditions that break the fit. This is the strongest qualification of the concessions in Movement 11′. Sloppy-model analysis, scaling exponents and Good–Turing estimates are real compressions. In human systems, publishing any of them starts the loop on the left. The live model below shows the Goodhart curve forming as targeting pressure rises.
Live model
Watch a measure stop measuring

Three hundred units each have a true quality and a private cost of gaming. Raise the targeting pressure: units with cheap gaming inflate their indicator. Left, indicator against true quality. Right, how the correlation collapses as pressure rises. This is Goodhart's law as a dynamic, not a slogan.

Reflexivity and the instruments

Apply the loop to the instruments under examination. "Identify your 17%" invites people to perform maverick-ness once it is known to be rewarded. A novelty-rate indicator borrowed from Heaps' law, made into a KPI, will be gamed by relabelling the familiar as new. A Good–Turing log kept for a bonus will fill with invented "once-seen" kinds. WRAS quadrant assignments, once tied to budgets, will be argued for strategically. None of this means measurement is futile. It means a complexity-faithful instrument must be designed with its own reflexivity in view: measures rotated before they harden into targets, kept advisory rather than evaluative, and their gaming studied as data about the organisation's anxieties.

Both say the period of apparent order is the time to pay closest attention, and an instrument that celebrates its fit during the plateau is the one most likely to be caught by the break.

The atom does not read its measurement. The manager does.

Altius Reflexivity as a fixed-point problem

A performative model is a self-fulfilling prophecy only if a fixed point exists: a forecast which, when published and acted on, produces itself. Grunberg and Modigliani (1954) proved such points exist for many economic forecasts; Simon made a related argument about bandwagon effects in polls. Counter-performativity arises when the fixed point is unstable: small departures grow, as Black–Scholes discovered in 1987. For instruments the question becomes mathematical: does publishing this assessment drive the organisation towards it, away from it, or into oscillation? Most instruments never ask, and so cannot know which kind they are.

Woven · Liber Tertius The Map That Eats the Territory

Baudrillard's precession of simulacra, in Liber Tertius Part One, is performativity at its limit.

Movement 29 · Destructio et Creatio

Boyd's Quantum Compass: Destruction and Creation

On 3 September 1976, a year after retiring from the US Air Force, John Boyd finished a short essay that he regarded as the foundation of everything he later wrote. Destruction and Creation opens with a claim about survival: to comprehend and cope with our environment we develop mental patterns or concepts of meaning, and we must continually destroy and create them so we can shape and be shaped by a changing environment. To support the claim Boyd brought in three results from mathematics and physics: Gödel's incompleteness theorems, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, and the second law of thermodynamics.

Three results, one conclusion

Boyd's reading of each is compressed. From Gödel, any logical system rich enough to be interesting cannot establish its own consistency from within, so any model of reality is incomplete and must be continually refined. From Heisenberg, there is a limit to how precisely we can observe reality. From the second law, the entropy of a closed system tends to increase, so a system cut off from its environment runs down even as effort is spent maintaining it. Taken together, Boyd concludes, they show we cannot determine the character or nature of a system within itself. An inward-oriented attempt to improve the match between concept and reality generates uncertainty and disorder. The remedy is to go outside the system and create a new one.

Whether Boyd uses the physics as analogy or as something more is disputed. Chet Richards, who worked with Boyd on the essay, argues he did not intend loose analogies but drew a structural conclusion about all closed conceptual systems. By the standard of Table 16 the Heisenberg leg is the weakest, for the reason Movement 21 gave: observational limits in practice are mostly not Heisenberg's. The Gödel and entropy legs carry the argument. The structure Boyd extracts is admissible: no system can fully audit itself; openness to the outside is the price of staying matched to reality.

Destructive deduction, creative induction

Boyd's mechanism has two moves. Destructive deduction breaks existing concepts apart, separating their particulars from the domains that held them. Creative induction then synthesises particulars from many shattered domains into a new concept. His example is the snowmobile. Take skis from the ski slope, an outboard motor from a boat, tank treads from a tank, and handlebars from a bicycle. Destroy each object's identity as part of its original whole, then recombine the parts into something none of their domains contained. The cycle repeats indefinitely, because each new concept is itself a closed system that will eventually fail to match a changing world.

The snowmobile is Kauffman's adjacent possible drawn by a fighter pilot: a new object one recombination away from what exists, invisible from inside any single parent domain. The dashed return arc is Boyd's warning against his own success. Every synthesis becomes a closed system and must be broken again. The figure also corrects a common misreading of Boyd. His advantage was not speed of decision. It was the continual destruction and recreation of orientation.

The loom in Boyd

Richards notes that two of the "aha" moments in the creation of lean production came from outside the car industry: from the weaving industry and from American supermarkets. Toyota began as a maker of automatic looms. The loom of this treatise's title turns up at the root of the most celebrated "going outside" in modern operations. A loom that stopped itself when a thread broke taught a car-maker to stop the line when a fault appeared. The weft, again, came from elsewhere.

Go outside, or entropy will do your thinking for you.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part Six

Heidegger's breakdown, in Liber Secundus Part Six, is destructive deduction felt from inside.

Altius Gödel, Heisenberg and the second law, read cautiously

Boyd's essay leans on three famous results, and commentators rightly warn against reading them as physics of organisations. Gödel limits formal systems that prove their own consistency; Heisenberg limits joint precision of conjugate quantities; the second law describes closed thermodynamic systems. Boyd used them as analogies for one claim: no closed conceptual system can stay matched to an open world without periodic destruction and recreation. That claim stands without the physics. The strongest version is cybernetic: a model that cannot import variety from outside loses requisite variety as the world changes, and must be broken to be rebuilt.

Movement 30 · Nomadologia

OODA as a Quantum Uncertainty Compass: Wayfinding, the Dérive, the Rhizome and the Assemblage

This movement brings the threads together. Boyd's OODA loop, usually drawn as a four-step cycle and sold as a decision speed-up, is better understood as the Pyxis Incerta in its native military dress: an instrument that holds orientation open and collapses only to act. Read through Pacific wayfinding, through Debord's drift and through Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome and assemblage, it becomes a theory of moving well in a world without a map.

The loop Boyd actually drew

Boyd's final sketch of the loop, from his 1995 briefing The Essence of Winning and Losing, is not a circle of four equal boxes. Observe takes in outside information, unfolding circumstances and the unfolding interaction with the environment. Orient is a large central structure in which genetic heritage, cultural traditions, previous experiences, new information, and analysis and synthesis interact. Decide is labelled a hypothesis; Act is labelled a test. Most important, Orientation sends implicit guidance and control directly to Observation and to Action, bypassing explicit decision, and feedback runs from Decide and Act back to Observe. The fastest loops are the ones that hardly pass through Decide at all.

Read as a compass, the loop's centre of gravity is not Decide but Orient. Orientation is the dial on which lobes are held in weighted superposition, the field where Boyd's destruction and creation happen. The implicit guidance arcs are the quantum compass's real secret. A well-oriented crew acts without collapsing into explicit decision, the way Cook Ding's blade moves without deliberating each cut. The advantage Boyd prized, operating inside an opponent's loop, comes from orientation rich enough to act from superposition, while the opponent is still forcing every reading through a decision gate.

The loop as wayfinding

The Pacific navigator of Movement 15 runs an OODA loop that looks nothing like a staff process. Observation is continuous and bodily: swell against the hull, birds at dusk, cloud colour, star rising-points. Orientation is etak, the canoe held still with the islands moving past, kept up across days and nights as a living mental model, constantly corrected and never written down. Decisions are rare and small, such as a change of heading at a star's rising. Action is the voyage itself, and its feedback is the next swell. This is the loop at its purest: almost all orientation, very little decision, and feedback built into motion. Boyd's "implicit guidance and control" is what Ingold calls wayfaring, knowing as you go, along a line.

The loop as dérive

Debord's dérive is a deliberately disoriented OODA loop. The Situationist lets go of the habitual orientation (work, routine, the city's functional meaning) so that observation can register what the habitual template filters out: currents, vortexes, the zones that push you away. But the dérive also contains, in Debord's own words, its necessary contradiction, the domination of psychogeographical variations by knowledge and calculation of their possibilities. In Boyd's terms, the dérive is destructive deduction applied to one's orientation towards a city: shatter the familiar map so the particulars come loose. The psychogeographic report that follows is creative induction, a new orientation synthesised from fragments. The quantum compass formalises the drift: the dial thick over attractors and thin over voids is the drifter's orientation made visible, and Zeno-lock is the drifter's sense that checking the phone too often ends the drift.

Rhizome: a map, not a tracing

Deleuze and Guattari's A Thousand Plateaus (1980) opens with the rhizome, set against the tree. A tree, or "arborescent" system, has a root, a trunk and a hierarchy of branches; it reproduces a pre-given structure. A rhizome, like couch-grass or a burrow, can be connected at any point to any other, is made of heterogeneous elements, is a multiplicity not reducible to one or many, can be broken anywhere and will start up again along old or new lines, and is a map, not a tracing. The distinction matters here. A tracing copies a structure assumed to exist already, which is what a dashboard does with "mapped territory". A map in Deleuze and Guattari's sense is open, connectable, reversible and modifiable, and made in the experimenting. It is closer to an orientation than to a chart. A rhizome, they write, has no beginning or end; it is always in the middle, between things. A companion treatise of this imprint took that phrase, always in the middle, as its title and its method.

The OODA loop as Boyd drew it is rhizomatic in the ways that matter. Its parts connect in several directions at once (implicit guidance skips Decide; feedback skips Orient). Orientation is a heterogeneous multiplicity: genes, culture, experience, information. Destruction and creation are its asignifying ruptures, breaks from which new lines grow. The loop drawn as four boxes in a circle is the tracing of this rhizome: a tree with its roots cut off, sold as a process.

Assemblage and the agential cut

Deleuze and Guattari's assemblage (agencement) names a working arrangement of heterogeneous parts (bodies, tools, signs, territories) that hold together without a unifying essence. It varies along two axes: from the material ("content") to the expressive, and from territorialisation, settling into a stable arrangement, to deterritorialisation, coming apart along a line of flight. The navigator, canoe, swell, stars and chants form an assemblage. So do the drifter, city, rain and companions, and so do pilot, aircraft, adversary and doctrine. None of these is a subject using a tool on a world. Each is a single working arrangement whose capacities belong to the whole, which is close to Barad's phenomenon of intra-acting agencies and Hutchins's distributed cognition.

Seen this way, a quantum uncertainty compass is not an instrument an orienter holds. It is a component that changes the assemblage. Added to a drifter, it territorialises some lines (lobes thicken) and opens others (ghost needles, voids), and its gauges register the assemblage's own state (decoherence as over-coding by expectation, Zeno-lock as over-territorialisation by monitoring). SwarmCompass, by contrast, is an apparatus of capture, Deleuze and Guattari's term for the State form's way of striating smooth space and taking in what flows. It turns a rhizome of noticing into a tree with a dashboard at its root.

Smooth and striated space

The last concept is the most directly navigational. In the plateau on the smooth and the striated, Deleuze and Guattari distinguish striated space, gridded, measured, crossed point to point, from smooth space, occupied by moving through it and sensed through local, tactile, "close-range" signs. Their privileged example is the sea, the archetypal smooth space that state navies and cartography progressively striated with longitude, charts and sea-lanes. A magnetic compass and a chart striate. Etak and the swell are smooth navigation. The OODA loop, read as Boyd meant it, belongs to nomad science: it follows the material's own lines, as the woodworker follows the grain, the 理 of Movement 18. The dérive is an attempt to re-smooth the striated city.

The left panel is not wrong. It is what an organisation needs for many complicated tasks, and Deleuze and Guattari insist the two kinds of space keep passing into each other: the smooth is striated, the striated re-smoothed. The error the treatise attacks is dressing a striating instrument in rhizomatic language: calling a dashboard a swarm, a tracing a map, a capture a weave. The quantum uncertainty compass is offered as a tool that knows which side it is on. It smooths the space it moves through and says so in its gauges.

Read the table across, not down. Each row is one function of orientation expressed in four vocabularies. The last row shows the failure is the same each time: orientation hardening into a structure that no longer moves with the world. Debord warned that drifters fixate on newly discovered axes. Boyd warned that every synthesis closes. Deleuze and Guattari warned that rhizomes have their own knots of arborescence. The quantum compass names the same failure Zeno-lock.

The loop is not a circle of four boxes. It is a weather of orientation, collapsed for a moment to act.

Make a map, not a tracing. Stay in the middle. Go outside.

Altius OODA as active inference

Karl Friston's active inference treats organisms as minimising prediction error either by updating their model (perception) or by changing the world to fit it (action). Boyd's Orient box, with implicit guidance and control running directly to Act, maps onto this closely: orientation is the generative model, and action is a way of testing and fulfilling it. The Part VII reading adds that every action is also a measurement, and the Deleuzian reading that the model is never a closed tree but a rhizome of priors. Getting inside an opponent's loop means changing the world faster than their model can update.

Movement 31 · Casus

A Worked Case: The Distressed Asset

Theory owes practice a test. What follows is a composite and fictional case drawn from the ordinary texture of secured lending in England and Wales. It describes no real property, borrower, lender or firm, and it is an illustration, not legal or professional advice. It runs the same situation through WRAS, through SwarmCompass, and through the treatise's own apparatus of Tidal Loom, Pyxis laws and OODA.

The situation

A part-completed mixed-use scheme, retail at ground floor and residential above, sits on the edge of a regional town centre. The development loan is in default and the borrower is in negative equity. The main contractor has left site, a planning condition is unresolved, two ground-floor units are let to tenants who are anxious about access, and the last valuation is nine months old. The lender appoints fixed charge (LPA) receivers. This is a busy market. The trade association nara's figures showed fixed charge appointments rising sharply through 2025, and commentators on the first half of 2026 describe lenders taking a more considered approach: monitoring assets before enforcement and treating distress as a question of protecting value rather than simply of default. At a 2025 industry panel, practitioners noted the recent Fairmont Property Developers v Venus Bridging decision reconfirming the wide discretion given to fixed charge receivers, particularly in negative-equity cases.

There is no position on this diagram from which the asset has one value. The lender sees recovery and timing. The borrower sees lost equity and guarantee exposure. The tenants see trading days. The valuer sees comparables that predate the default. Every move (a marketing launch, a standstill, a tenant letter) is a gesture that calls out responses and changes the value the next observer will report. That is Movement 27 and Movement 28 in a hard hat.

Three runs of the same case

The third column introduces no exotic technique. Every move in it is something experienced receivers already do on good days: walk the site often but lightly, keep the valuation question separate from the exit question, take tenants seriously as observers, recognise that the marketing story makes the market, and break a stalled scheme into parts to see what recombinations the market will bear. The treatise's claim is that these good habits are complexity practice. Instruments that dress them up as quadrants or swarms add vocabulary, not capability, and can make them harder to see.

The law as a constraint, not a quadrant

Receivers act within a legal frame that a strategy matrix cannot treat as optional. As generally understood in English law, a receiver selling charged property owes a duty to take reasonable care to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable at the time of sale, while keeping considerable discretion over when to sell and generally being under no obligation to improve the property first. The Fairmont decision, as practitioners reported it, reconfirmed how wide that discretion is. In Juarrero's terms this frame is a governing constraint: it does not dictate the path, but it shapes the probability of every path. A complexity-faithful instrument starts from it as a dated limit (Movement 19, principle 5). It is not a substrate to manipulate.

The building has as many values as it has observers. The receiver's craft is to weave them into one sale.

Walk the site lightly. Count the once-seen. Keep Path apart from Place. Publish the price as a gesture. Meet in the room.

Altius Optionality in distress

Real options theory values the right, without obligation, to act later: to wait, expand or abandon. In receiverships, optionality is often the most valuable asset and the least visible: the option to let a planning appeal run, to stage a sale, to hold vacant possession. A receiver's acumen consists largely in not exercising options prematurely, the financial form of measuring lightly. The legal duty to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable at the time of sale fixes when the option must be exercised, not how long it may be kept alive beforehand. Path and Place, kept apart, preserve the option.
