Movement 32 · De Acumine

Acumen Under Observation: Salience, Sapience, Sentience

Snowden's recent writing returns, again and again, to one old word. Acumen comes from the Latin for a sharp point, and behind that from acus, a needle. The OED gives it as sharpness of wit, quickness or penetration of perception, keenness of discrimination, and now especially the ability to make good judgements and decisions. Around this word Snowden has built two things: a triad of deep conditions (salience, sapience, sentience) and a framework of observable qualities, ACUMEN, worked through the figure of a stranger at a collapsed border crossing. This movement reads both through the six lenses of Part VII. The question is not whether acumen matters. It plainly does. The question is what happens to acumen once an instrument is placed inside the situation that acumen is meant to navigate.

The corpus: five posts and a definition

The material spans about three years and has a clear order.

Acumen Incited (two posts, January and February 2024) opens with empathy and plays on the letters A and I in the title: the "AI" in the word incited is the point. The first post uses Masahiro Mori's uncanny valley (1970). Empathy for a robot rises as it becomes more humanlike, then collapses into revulsion as it nears but does not reach full likeness. Snowden takes from this that we cannot be empathetic with perfection, and that empathy depends on proximity: it happens in a moment, in time and space, and probably uses more senses than sight and sound. The second post widens the claim. Acumen in human systems is not only an individual quality. It is linked to empathy, it can be executed collectively, often without conscious direction, and it cannot be captured by an algorithm. It adds that network intelligence has to be engendered, which means creating the substrate and enabling connection.

Acumen revisited (24 February 2026, the fourth anniversary of the Russian invasion of Ukraine) sets out the ACUMEN framework. Its worked example is Natalia, a stranger met on the train who took charge of Snowden through a collapsed crossing at Rava-Ruska on the Polish–Ukrainian border. The post says the triad and the framework are not in competition. Salience, sapience and sentience are the deep conditions that make acumen possible. ACUMEN names the observable qualities: what you can actually see in a person navigating a complex situation well. Among the conditions is embodied and enacted existence: acumen is not a cognitive process running on neutral hardware.

The full text gives six conditions for acumen and six letters. The conditions are: embodied and enacted existence (a being that is hungry, tired and cold, with proprioception, smell and the physical memory of having done things before); growth through dependency and learning from failure, where getting it wrong has real consequences and is not a recoverable token; social embedding in communities with shared meanings and informal protocols; biological imperatives, epigenetic consequences included, so that the body is part of the cognitive system and not its vehicle; phenomenal consciousness, what it is like to be; and existential consequences, living with the results of one's own judgements. The letters are Adaptability (reconfiguring in real time, which Snowden distinguishes from resilience as bouncing back), Contextual Wisdom (knowing which rules are still operative in a changed situation and which have become nominal), Understanding (a semantic grasp of the situation as a socio-technical system with its own informal rules), Moral Judgement (the experienced perception of what matters and the will to act on it, made quickly and without announcement: virtue ethics), Empathic Resonance (empathic precision, which tracks what another person needs as the situation changes, and is more demanding than empathic warmth), and Nuanced Perception (fine-grained reading of signals against a background of long prior exposure). Snowden is explicit that the acronym is an ostensive definition, a description of what acumen looks like when it is functioning, and not a formal one.

The worked example is told in detail. The train from Poland did not come south. A Polish bus replaced it, then waited in the cold for a slot to leave Ukraine and again for a slot to enter Poland. The plan to reach Lublin for the last Warsaw train failed, and the bus stopped for another hour while a replacement driver was found. Natalia, whom Snowden had helped with a bag on the train, had already decided that Lublin, not Warsaw, was the realistic end of the line. She had worked out a shared taxi and the best route for dropping eight passengers at their homes and hotels. She translated context as well as language: why one queue moved and another did not, and what the rhythm of the crossing that night meant for timing. She brought Snowden to his Warsaw hotel at three in the morning. Snowden maps each letter onto her conduct, and closes on a sentence that matters for Part VII: the system is stressed, not broken, which is the condition ACUMEN is built for.

Don't Forget the Suspenders (9 November 2026) returns to the definition. Its opening says the February post emphasised the back half of the OED entry, penetration of perception and keenness of discrimination, and passed quickly over the first clause, sharpness of wit. The title comes from Kipling, not from the idiom "belt and braces" as this edition first guessed. In How the Whale Got His Throat a shipwrecked Mariner "of infinite-resource-and-sagacity" is swallowed by a Whale, cuts his raft into a grating, ties it with his suspenders, and wedges it in the Whale's throat; and the suspenders, Kipling insists, you must not forget. Snowden reads the suspenders as the unglamorous things that hold the clever part together: the small courtesy on the luggage rack, the informal networks, the trust, the people who notice. Movement 33 takes up this post in full.

Correction (editio quarta, second impression). The first impression of this movement guessed that the title alluded to "belt and braces" and described the anthro-complexity post as "1/3". Both were wrong. With the full texts now in hand, the account above follows Snowden's own wording. The covenant permits this correction because it fixes an error and removes no argument.

Anthro-complexity 1/5 (12 March 2026) offers what Chris Corrigan welcomed as the long-missing definition. Anthro-complexity holds that human complex adaptive systems are part of the natural world and embedded within it, while being irreducibly different from other natural systems in ways that matter. Their agents have intelligence, identity and intention: a reflexive capacity enacted in language, relationship and cultural practice rather than located in any bounded interior. This continues the older "3Is" (intelligence, identity, intent) and the claim that human beings, as homo faber, homo ludens and homo narrans, "are not ants, or birds".

The same post places the 3S triad as a second layer. The 3Is describe what human agents have; the 3Ss describe what they do with it. And it pairs them: intelligence shapes sapience (and sapience corrects intelligence), identity shapes salience, and intention shapes what sentience registers as significant. Two further claims in it bear directly on Part VII. Because humans theorise about their own situation and act on the theory, any framework applied to a human system becomes an actor within it. Human systems are therefore reflexively complex: the act of description changes the thing described. And the practitioner's question shifts from "what should this system become?" to "what is it doing, and what is becoming possible or impossible within it?", because, as Snowden's daughter put it in review, the system cannot be a noun or something outside of us.

Method note. The thecynefin.co pages could not be fetched from this workspace. The first impression relied on search excerpts. This second impression works from the full texts of Acumen revisited, Don't Forget the Suspenders and Anthro-complexity 1/5, supplied by the author, and from search excerpts and summaries for the two Acumen Incited posts. Quotations are kept short; the argument is paraphrased.

The triad as a figure

Each term of the triad is old, and each names a different kind of contact with a situation.

Salience is what stands out: the figure against the ground, the signal that pulls attention. In the vocabulary of Movement 2 it is affordance-detection. Gibson would say the environment offers; salience is the offer being taken up as an offer. Sapience is judgement: knowing what a thing means, what follows from it, and what to do. It is the faculty Aristotle calls phronēsis, practical wisdom about particulars. Sentience is felt stake: the situation matters to someone, in the body. It is what makes salience more than detection and sapience more than calculation.

Snowden's own definitions in Anthro-complexity 1/5 sharpen each term. Sentience is felt experience, the having of qualia, and its affective colouring is constitutive of how a signal is processed, not noise around it: a weak signal that carries fear is handled differently from one that carries curiosity, even with identical content. Sapience is phronēsis, judging well where rules are unclear and values compete, which is why experienced practitioners outperform formal models and why sapience cannot simply be transferred by training. Salience, which he calls the most under-theorised and perhaps the most important for practice, is the process by which some signals come to the foreground and others recede. It is never neutral. Two practitioners in one room see different things because they bring different salience landscapes, and so distributed attention across diverse landscapes is a positive method, not a concession.

The treatise's addition is to read the triad by its edges. Snowden insists the three must come together. If that is so, the interesting cases are the pairs, where one condition is missing. Figure 36 names those failures. They are our extrapolation from his claim, not his own list.

Read the edges as diagnoses. A trading desk, a risk model or a well-tuned dashboard often sits on the left edge: it notices and judges, but nothing is at stake for it, so it optimises the wrong thing elegantly. A crowd at a failing border sits on the right edge: everyone sees the danger and feels it, and the judgement collapses into a surge. A seasoned committee can sit on the bottom edge: wise, humane, and looking at last quarter's problem. Natalia is described as having all three at once, in full and operational form.
Live model
The triad that cannot say "all three"

Set the strength of salience, sapience and sentience. Left: where a barycentric SenseMaker-style triad would plot them, with the three weights normalised to sum to one. Right: acumen read as a conjunction (the geometric mean), which falls to zero if any condition is absent. Try 90-90-90 and then 10-10-10: the triad point does not move, the conjunction does.

The triad that cannot say "all three"

There is a formal problem here, and it cuts close to Snowden's own instruments. SenseMaker asks respondents to place a story inside a triangle whose corners are three signifiers. The position is barycentric: the three weights always sum to one. More of one means less of the others. The centre of a SenseMaker triad therefore means balanced. It does not mean maximal.

Acumen, as Snowden describes it, is a conjunction. It needs salience and sapience and sentience together, each in strength. On a barycentric triad, a person strong in all three and a person weak in all three land on exactly the same point: the centre. The geometry that the Cynefin school uses most for sense-making cannot represent the property it most wants to cultivate. The widget below makes the point concrete. Set the three intensities. The left panel shows where a triad would plot them; the right panel shows the conjunction, here the geometric mean, which falls to zero if any one condition is absent.

First lens: salience is a measurement (Movement 26)

Movement 26 showed that questions do not read attitudes; they rotate them. The QQ equality of Wang and colleagues holds because each question is a projection that changes the state the next question meets. Salience is the same operation performed by attention. What stands out first sets the basis in which everything later is judged.

The Natalia episode, as Snowden tells it, starts there. At a crossing where the usual order has collapsed, the first act of acumen is to make some things salient and let others fall back: this queue, that document, this official. Each act of salience is a projection on the crowd's shared state. Done in one order, the crossing holds; in another, it can surge. Salience is not passive perception. It is the first non-commuting operator in the sequence, and acumen includes knowing which question to put first.

That has a hard consequence for the instruments. A SwarmCompass assessment that asks about "blind spots" first and strategy second makes blind spots salient and so shapes the strategy answers. Rotating the order between respondents averages the effect away for the analyst. It does not undo it for the respondent, who leaves the survey rotated.

Second lens: sapience and sentience are agent-relative (Movement 27)

Relational quantum mechanics says facts are relative to systems; QBism says a quantum state is an agent's degrees of belief about her own future experiences. Both put the agent inside the account. Snowden's definition of anthro-complexity does the same for people. Intelligence, identity and intention form a reflexive capacity enacted in language, relationship and cultural practice, not located in any bounded interior.

The fit is close. QBist probability is personal because the agent has a stake: the bet is hers, and so is the experience that will settle it. That is sentience in a precise sense. Sapience is then the disciplined updating of those personal bets in contact with the world. Acumen is the QBist agent done well. It does not need to be a view from nowhere. It needs to be a view from somewhere, with skin in the game, and open to correction.

The lens also sharpens the uncanny-valley argument. An AI system can produce probabilities. On the QBist reading it cannot produce its own probabilities in the strong sense, because no experience of its own will settle the bet. That is a more exact way to say what Snowden says about empathy: what cannot be had is not the output but the stake. A simulated sentience that nearly matches the real thing produces the valley, because people sense the missing stake.

Third lens: acumen named is acumen gamed (Movement 28)

Snowden separates the conditions (triad) from the observables (ACUMEN). This is a careful move, and it creates a risk Movement 28 predicts. Observables are what institutions measure. Once the qualities of acumen are listed as observable, they can be assessed, then rewarded, then performed. Goodhart's law needs no bad faith. It needs only that the indicator be cheaper to move than the thing it indicates.

The tension is internal to the Cynefin offer. Acumen Incited argues that acumen emerges from habit, experience and talent that cannot be flattened into a training data set. The SwarmCompass guide, examined in Part I, presents collected sense-making material as something to feed machine learning. A list of observable acumen-qualities, harvested at scale and used as training targets, is the very flattening the essays warn against. Snowden's own position is more careful than the brochure's. As Acumen revisited summarises the second Acumen Incited post, AI should do what it does well (clustering, outlier detection, pattern alerts) while human judgement reads context, weighs consequences and decides what matters. The defence is that SenseMaker harvests narrative, not ratings of acumen. The rejoinder is that once the framework exists, the signifiers will drift towards it, as they drift towards any vocabulary that buyers recognise.

Fourth lens: orientation is where acumen lives (Movement 29)

Boyd puts the heaviest box of the OODA loop at Orient, fed by genetic heritage, cultural traditions, previous experiences, new information, and analysis and synthesis. That box is the closest thing in the strategy literature to Snowden's triad. Genetic heritage and cultural tradition are the embodied ground of sentience. Previous experience is the stock of sapience. New information, filtered, is salience.

Destruction and Creation adds the dynamic. Acumen is not a fixed orientation but the capacity to break one's own orientation and rebuild it: destructive deduction, then creative induction. At Rava-Ruska the usual crossing script had already been destroyed by events. Natalia's acumen, as described, was the creative half: recombining particulars (people, papers, routes, officials) into a working order no one had designed. The snowmobile was built from skis, a motor, treads and handlebars. The crossing was built from strangers.

The diagram makes one claim precise. Boyd thought the fast, implicit path from Orient to Act was where skilled organisations win, and the explicit Decide box was a fallback. Snowden's collective acumen sits on that same path. Both men are describing competence that bypasses deliberation without being thoughtless. Neither can be installed by a briefing, because a briefing travels by the slow, explicit route.

Fifth lens: acumen as refrain and assemblage (Movement 30)

Movement 30 read the OODA loop as a quantum uncertainty compass for drift and wayfinding, and linked it to Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome, assemblage, and smooth and striated space. The acumen essays fit that reading closely, and one Deleuzian concept fits better than any other: the refrain (ritornello). The plateau on the refrain in A Thousand Plateaus opens with a child in the dark, frightened, who comforts herself by singing. The song makes a small, stable centre in chaos. Then it marks out a territory around that centre. Then it opens a way out.

That is the shape of the Natalia story. A collapsed crossing is smooth space in the worst sense: the striations of queues, desks and timetables have gone. Natalia's acumen produces a small, temporary territory: a group, an order of tasks, a set of who-does-what. It then opens onto the way through. The refrain is not a plan imposed from above. It is a rhythm taken up by bodies in place. In assemblage terms, her acumen is not a property of Natalia alone. It is a property of the assemblage she catalyses: people, papers, a phone, a train timetable, a border post. The arrangement holds for a few hours and then dissolves.

The lens also explains Snowden's own phrasing. Acumen "executed collectively, often without conscious direction" is assemblage language without the name. And the claim that acumen is not a cognitive process running on neutral hardware is the anti-Cartesian commitment Deleuze, Ingold and Juarrero share.

Here the critique of Movement 10 returns. Acumen Incited says network intelligence must be engendered, which means creating the substrate. A refrain cannot be engendered from outside the dark. The child sings because she is afraid; no consultant gives her the song. What an outside party can do is less and more modest: not break the conditions from which refrains arise, and leave room for the strangers who start them. "Creating the substrate" risks becoming the striating move it means to oppose: the designed platform that captures the smooth space it claims to nurture.

Sixth lens: acumen on a wet Tuesday (Movement 31)

The receivership case of Movement 31 gives the triad a working shape. Salience on site is Turing's Glass: the receiver's eye for the once-seen anomaly, logged by kind. Sapience is the discipline of keeping Path apart from Place, the exit question apart from the valuation question, and reading the legal duty as a governing constraint. Sentience is taking the tenants, the contractor's unpaid subcontractors and the lender's credit officer as people with stakes, not as data. A receiver strong in two of three is one of the edge cases of Figure 36. Without sentience, a technically optimal sale that wrecks the tenancy base. Without sapience, a sympathetic delay that loses the best price reasonably obtainable. Without salience, a sound process that misses the defect in the basement.

Disputatio: four objections and their answers

Objection 1. The framework undoes the example. Natalia is an ostensive definition: "this is what acumen looks like". An acronym is a specification. Moving from one to the other turns a shown capacity into a checklist, which is the codification the Cynefin school spent two decades opposing.

Response. Snowden anticipates this in so many words. He writes that acumen needs not a formal but an ostensive definition, and offers the acronym as a description of what acumen looks like when it is functioning. He also separates conditions from observables and says the two are not in competition. Read in that light, ACUMEN works as what Herbert Blumer called a sensitising concept: it tells you where to look, not what you must find. Determinatio: the framework is sound if it is used to sensitise and fails if it is used to assess. The test is whether anyone is ever scored on it.

Objection 2. Collective acumen cannot be harvested. If acumen is executed collectively and often without conscious direction, then asking individuals to report on it, in surveys or signifiers, captures only its residue. Feeding that residue into machine learning, as Cynefin offerings propose for sense-making data, is the flattening into a training data set that Acumen Incited forbids.

Response. SenseMaker collects micro-narratives, not self-ratings, and narratives carry more of the implicit than any scale. Determinatio: the objection holds in part. Narrative is the best available trace, but it is a trace. A school that says acumen cannot be encompassed by an algorithm should say plainly which uses of its harvested data respect that limit and which do not.

Objection 3. "Creating the substrate" is design by another name. If network intelligence must be engendered by creating the substrate, then someone designs the substrate. That is the move Movement 10 named: an outside architect shaping the conditions of emergence and calling it non-design.

Response. Every intervention shapes conditions; the question is how lightly and how reversibly. Determinatio: admit the design openly, keep it minimal, and make it removable. A substrate that cannot be switched off without loss has become a dependency, not a commons.

Objection 4. The triad is itself a triad. Salience, sapience and sentience arrive in the same three-cornered form as SenseMaker signifiers. As shown above, that geometry encodes trade-off, not conjunction. The figure fights the claim.

Response. In the February post Snowden lists the three as conditions, not as corners. Replicatio: in Don't Forget the Suspenders he reports arguing in Brazil for degrees of human–AI hybridisation using the salience, sapience and sentience triad overlaid on the output of Estuarine Mapping. The triad is already being used as a geometry. Determinatio: the objection stands. If the triad is used to locate a situation, it measures the balance of the three and is blind to their strength. Use a conjunctive form instead: three independent scales, or the weakest-link reading in Figure 36.

Obligatio

In the medieval game of obligatio the respondent accepts a proposition and must defend it consistently. The treatise accepts: acumen cannot be installed. The opponent then asks: "Can it be trained?" Answer: it can be exercised. Practice in situations that matter builds habit and experience, which feed sapience; sentience cannot be supplied by the trainer. "Can it be measured?" Answer: its traces can be read. Its score cannot be set without Goodhart following. "Can a machine have it?" Answer: a machine can have salience in the form of detection and sapience in the form of inference. On the QBist reading it lacks the stake, so it lacks sentience, so it lacks the conjunction. "Then can a machine help?" Answer: yes, on the left edge of Figure 36, provided a human supplies the missing vertex. The respondent has kept faith with the proposition.

Snowden has done something valuable here. He has taken an ordinary word that management language had worn smooth ("business acumen") and sharpened it back to its needle point. He has tied it to empathy, proximity and embodiment, and he has given it a human example rather than a model. Part VII's lenses strengthen his case at every point but one. Wherever acumen is described, the lenses confirm it. Wherever acumen is turned into an instrument (named observables, harvested signals, an engendered substrate), the lenses predict the same reflexive drift that Movement 28 traced in every other measure. The suspenders of the title hold: as Movement 33 shows, sharpness of wit, the front half of the definition, and the small courtesies that tie the clever part together are exactly what an instrument cannot hold for you.

Acumen is a needle. It goes through the cloth only when a hand is behind it.

Notice first. Judge in the middle. Let it matter. Do not score the refrain.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part SixteenLiber II · Part Twelve

Liber Secundus reaches the barycentric conclusion from Snowden's own May 2026 trialectic, and the acumen conclusion from 'the manual and the training'.

Altius Enactivism and sense-making

Varela, Thompson and Rosch's enactivism (1991), extended by Di Paolo and De Jaegher's participatory sense-making, gives Snowden's triad a philosophical home. Salience is what a sense-making organism brings forth as relevant; sentience is the self-concern that makes anything relevant at all; sapience is skilled adjustment within a history of coupling. Participatory sense-making adds that meaning can arise in the coordination between agents, not inside either, which is collective acumen exactly. The enactivist lineage also supports Snowden's strongest claim: an organism without precarious self-maintenance has nothing at stake, and so nothing is salient to it in the full sense.

Woven · Liber Tertius The Body That Knows

Merleau-Ponty's primacy of perception grounds the sentience in Snowden's triad.

Movement 33 · De Sagacitate

The Mariner Inside the Whale: Wit, Sagacity and the Grating

In Don't Forget the Suspenders Snowden goes back to the half of the definition he had passed over: sharpness of wit. He reaches it by two routes, a translation and a whale. In Brazil, acumen was rendered as sagacidade, sagacity. The second route is Kipling's Mariner, a man "of infinite-resource-and-sagacity", who is swallowed by a Whale and stops its appetite from inside with a grating tied by his suspenders. This movement reads that post through Part VII. It finds that the Mariner is the treatise's figure of the observer inside, drawn eighty years before Wigner.

The two triads, and where acumen sits between them

Anthro-complexity 1/5 sets out two triads and insists they are one entangled reality seen at two levels. The 3Is (intelligence, identity, intention) are what human agents have. The 3Ss (sapience, salience, sentience) are what they do with it. Snowden pairs them: intelligence shapes sapience, and sapience corrects intelligence so that reflexive abstraction does not become clever service of bad ends; identity shapes salience, so who we take ourselves to be decides what we notice; intention shapes what sentience registers as significant. His practical conclusion is that neither triad can be addressed alone. Attend only to the 3Is and you misread how meaning moves. Attend only to the 3Ss and you get rich phenomenology with no leverage on structure.

Read the pairings as Part VII would. "Identity shapes salience" is the QQ result of Movement 26 put in human terms: the basis in which a person measures is set before the question is asked. "Intention shapes what sentience registers" is QBism's stake: what I feel as significant depends on what I am trying to do. And "sapience corrects intelligence" is Boyd's destruction and creation, in which judgement breaks apart the clever constructions that reflexive intelligence builds.

The six letters read through the six lenses

With the full text of Acumen revisited in hand, each letter can be read through Part VII. Snowden offers the letters as an ostensive description: what acumen looks like when it works. The table asks what each looks like once the observer is inside.

From deciding back to sensing

Snowden notes that the OED's parenthesis, "(now esp.)", records a drift. The older senses of acumen are about perceiving and discriminating; the modern sense is about deciding. By the time we reach "business acumen", sensing has shrunk to an input to the decision. He calls this a small instance of a larger drift he has long opposed: the collapse of sense-making into decision-making.

Part VII has a name for this collapse. It is what happened to Boyd's loop when it was taught as four boxes of equal weight and read as a decision cycle (Movement 30, Figure 34). Boyd's own sketch puts the weight on Orient and gives Decide a modest, optional role beside the implicit path to Act. "Business acumen" is the four-box OODA of the word. Recovering the front half of the definition is the same move as recovering Boyd's final sketch.

Sagacity begins in the nose

The Brazilian translation recovered something English had mislaid. Latin sagax was used of hunting dogs: keen-scented, quick to pick up a trail. Snowden draws the conclusion that sagacity is perception before reasoning, the body noticing before the mind has a story.

The quantum uncertainty compass of Part VI already contains this figure. A scent trail is a weak measurement par excellence: the dog reads a gradient without stopping the quarry, sampling often and lightly, never collapsing the field into a single fix until the last moment. It is also a dérive. The Situationist drifter follows the psychogeographic pull of streets as a hound follows a trail: attention led by gradients of attraction and repulsion, not by a plan. Sagacity, on this reading, is the faculty that the Pyxis Incerta (Movement 24) was built to train: reading tendency before forming intention.

Wit is not a letter

Snowden maps the OED clauses onto the acronym. Penetration of perception is Nuanced Perception; keenness of discrimination is Contextual Wisdom; good judgements draw on Understanding and Moral Judgement. But sharpness of wit has no letter of its own, and he thinks that is right: wit is not one capacity among six but runs through all of them.

He finds the shape of this in Locke. In the Essay (II.xi.2), wit lies in assembling ideas quickly and finding resemblance between them; judgement lies in separating ideas carefully wherever the least difference can be found. Snowden's gloss is exact: discrimination without wit becomes audit, everything carefully distinguished and nothing connected; wit without discrimination is mere cleverness. Acumen is the tension between them, and it does not resolve. He then turns to Koestler's The Act of Creation (1964): bisociation, two incompatible frames colliding, is one mechanism behind the joke, the discovery and the work of art, which Koestler called the ha-ha, the aha and the ah. Humour is one of the ways intelligence senses that its frame is wrong. A group that can laugh at its assumptions can see them.

Part VII adds one identity. Locke's two faculties are Boyd's two moves. Judgement, separating ideas wherever the least difference appears, is destructive deduction: breaking concepts into particulars. Wit, assembling ideas by resemblance, is creative induction: recombining particulars from shattered domains. Boyd's snowmobile is a bisociation: skis and outboard motor, two frames that should not meet. Koestler's jester and Boyd's fighter pilot do the same thing. And Snowden's remark that the tension "does not resolve" is Boyd's claim that the cycle of destruction and creation never ends.

The live model below makes Snowden's two failure modes measurable in a toy world. Wit proposes connections between ideas; judgement tests them. With low wit, few true connections are found (audit). With low judgement, false connections flood in (mere cleverness). The score is high only when both are high, and it does not stay high when either is turned into a target alone.
Live model
Audit, cleverness and acumen

A toy world of 140 possible connections between ideas. Wit proposes links by surface resemblance (the shaded band); judgement tests them against their real depth. Points above the dashed line are real links. Teal: real links accepted. Rose: false links accepted. Low wit gives audit; low judgement gives mere cleverness.

Humour as a test of the six conditions

Snowden tests his six conditions against humour. Jokes depend on shared meanings, so they translate badly (social embedding). Timing is bodily: a joke told a beat late is a different joke (embodiment). Children learn humour by getting it wrong in public (growth through failure). A joke can fall flat, offend or cost you the room (existential consequences). A large language model, he writes, can produce things in the shape of jokes, some good. What it cannot do is risk one.

Part VII sharpens both halves. "A beat late is not the same joke" is the order effect of Movement 26 in time: the same content, projected at a different moment, rotates the room differently. And "cannot risk one" is the QBist stake of Movement 27. A probability is an agent's own because her experience will settle it; a joke is a teller's own because the room's response will land on her. Retrieval without risk is the clearest line Snowden knows between wit and its imitation. It is also the line between Wigner, who can describe, and the friend, who must live with the outcome.

The Mariner is inside

Snowden draws three things from Kipling's story. First, the Mariner works with what is to hand: raft, knife and braces, nothing designed for the purpose and everything repurposed. That is Lévi-Strauss's bricolage and, in evolution, exaptation. Second, he does not defeat the Whale; he changes a constraint. The grating limits what can pass the throat and so permanently changes what the Whale can do. Snowden states the general rule: one intervenes in a complex system by modulating actants, including constraints, not by targeting outcomes. Third, and decisive for Part VII, he is inside. He is not an observer with a model of the Whale. He has existential stakes in getting it right, and his sagacity cannot be separated from that position.

This is the observer inside, drawn in 1902. Wigner stands outside the sealed laboratory and writes a description. The friend is inside and records a fact. Kipling's Mariner is the friend who does not wait for Wigner. He stumps and jumps and dances until the Whale has hiccups, a perturbation from inside that changes the host's behaviour. Then he fits a structure that changes the host's constraints permanently. In Deleuzian terms the grating is an assemblage of raft and braces. In Situationist terms it is a détournement, the repurposing of existing elements against the order that produced them. In Juarrero's terms it is a context-sensitive constraint that becomes a governing one. And in the vocabulary of Movement 31, it is the receiver's craft: walking inside the asset, using what the site already affords, changing what can pass, and going home.

Snowden adds an Odyssean frame. "Infinite resource and sagacity" renders Homer's Odysseus, polytropos and polymētis, the man of many turns and many wiles. The Greek name for the capacity is mētis. Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant (1974) reconstructed it as the cunning intelligence of the fox and the octopus, used in situations that are shifting, ambiguous and unfit for exact measurement. James C. Scott (1998) set mētis against the state's appetite for legibility: practical, local knowledge that schemes of standardisation flatten and then fail without. Sagacity, mētis and acumen are one family. Movement 36 below returns to Scott's other figure, the state that sees.

Snowden's argument against frictionless adoption is that many listed "obstacles" are gratings: checkpoints that require sensing before deciding, channels that keep weak signals alive, places where judgement must be exercised rather than outsourced. Remove them for efficiency and the whale eats everything in the sea. Movement 23 adds the opposite warning. A grating at every joint is constant measurement, and constant measurement freezes evolution. Requisite friction has a mesh, and setting it is itself an act of acumen.

Escape, conquest and the grating

Snowden notes that most public argument about AI offers two options: escape (refuse it, regulate it out) or conquest (align it, control it, design it to obey). The Mariner does neither. He fits a constraint made of human material, which limits what the system can swallow and so changes what it becomes. In Brazil, Snowden says, he rejected the binary and argued for degrees of hybridisation. He also notes where the material comes from: the raft and braces were already there. The capacity to constrain such systems is already distributed through organisations and communities, in habits, relationships and practices. It needs conditions that let it become operative more than it needs an expert to supply it.

StanceObserver positionKind of interventionPart VII riskDeleuzian reading
EscapeOutside, refusing to enterProhibition, distanceWigner without the friend: describes from outside and learns nothing the friend knowsFlight that leaves the striated space intact
ConquestAbove, steeringTarget outcomes; align and controlGoodhart and Lucas: the steered system learns the steering (M28)The apparatus of capture, applied to a new body

Disputatio

Objection 1. The allegory is pressed too hard. Kipling wrote a joke for a child. Snowden himself warns that an allegory pressed too hard stops being funny, which would lose the very thing he defends.

Response. The treatise uses the story for its constraint logic, not for its allegory. That the Whale "is" AI is a reading to hold lightly. That one intervenes from inside by changing a constraint, with material to hand and with stakes, is a claim that stands without the Whale. Determinatio: keep the joke, and keep the logic.

Objection 2. The grating concedes design. Movement 10 charged the Cynefin instruments with designing a "substrate" from outside while disclaiming design. The Mariner plainly designs: he cuts, ties and fits a device.

Response. This is the strongest answer the Cynefin school has given to Movement 10, and the treatise accepts it. The Mariner designs a constraint, not an outcome. He does it from inside, with existential stakes. He uses what is to hand, not a purpose-built system brought by a specialist. Determinatio: design of constraints by insiders with stakes and local material is legitimate. What Movement 10 opposed is design of substrates by outsiders with products. The difference is not whether one designs but where one stands and what one brings.

Objection 3. If wit has no letter, the acronym is incomplete. A framework that admits its central capacity is missing from it is a strange framework.

Response. It is the right kind of incompleteness. What can be listed can be assessed, and what can be assessed can be gamed (M28). Wit, unlisted, is protected. Determinatio: Snowden has built a framework with a deliberate hole in it, and the hole is where the acumen lives. This is the best defence of the acronym available, and it is his own.

Objection 4. "Wit and judgement do not resolve" cannot be an instrument. Snowden says he may need to make the tension into a trialectic.

Response. If he does, Movement 32's caution applies: a three-cornered form will show balance, not strength. Determinatio: represent the tension as a cycle in time (Boyd), not a point in a triangle.

Movement 33 changes the treatise's verdict on one point. The first six movements of Part VII found that every instrument placed inside a human system becomes an actor in it. Snowden's own definition says the same: the framework itself becomes an actor within the system. The Mariner shows what follows when one accepts this fully. Instead of pretending to stand outside, one acts as an insider, with material to hand, on constraints rather than outcomes, and does not forget the suspenders. That is an anthro-complexity practice the treatise can endorse without reservation. The remaining question, taken up in Part VIII, is what happens when many Mariners act at once.

The grating gets the credit. The suspenders hold it in.

Keep your wits. Work from inside. Change the constraint, not the beast. Remember the braces.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part TwoLiber II · Part Twenty-Four

The appointed trickster and the holy fool: Liber Secundus on the wit that cannot be licensed.

Altius Mētis and the limits of legibility

James C. Scott's analysis of high-modernist schemes shows a recurring pattern: states simplify complex practices to make them legible, then fail because the simplification removed the mētis that made the practice work. Scientific forestry, planned cities and collectivised farms all followed this path. Kipling's Mariner is mētis in action, and his grating is a constraint built from local material, the opposite of a legibility scheme. The treatise's verdict on instruments follows: those that make an organisation legible to an outside buyer risk exactly the failure Scott documented, unless they leave room for the practitioner's grating.

Pars Octava
群 · 勢 · 鯨

The Crowd and the Leviathan

Four movements on what moves many people at once. Three things give leverage in a living system: agency, adjacency and tendency. Together they drive decomposition and recombination. A flash mob and a starling murmuration both show scale without an algorithm, yet they behave in opposite ways. To see how a spontaneous tribe hardens into an institution, the treatise turns to Hobbes's Leviathan, read as a dynamic, energetic and kinetic ontology, and to Deleuze and Guattari's apparatus of capture.

Movement 34 · De Tribus Vectibus

Three Levers: Agency, Adjacency, Tendency

Archimedes is supposed to have said: give me a place to stand and I will move the earth. The saying names three things, not one. There is the lever, which someone must lift. There is the place to stand, the fulcrum, which must be next to the load. And there is the weight of the load itself, its own inclination under gravity, without which the lever would have nothing to work with. In a living system the three become agency, adjacency and tendency. The treatise's proposition is that these, and only these, give leverage, and that all three work by driving decomposition and recombination.

The three defined

Agency is the capacity to act otherwise: to choose, to refuse, to begin. Snowden's anthro-complexity locates it in intention, the ability to act toward imagined futures in ways that alter the conditions acted upon. Hobbes locates it lower down, in endeavour, the small beginnings of motion within the body before they appear as walking, speaking or striking. On the quantum uncertainty compass, agency is the act of measurement: the walker's decision to look, to commit, to collapse the lobes of the needle into a path. Leverage through agency is choosing when and how strongly to measure.

Adjacency is who and what is next to whom: the neighbourhood through which any act propagates. It has two senses, and both matter. In the first, it is Kauffman's adjacent possible, the set of states one step from the actual. In the second, it is topological: the starling attends to six or seven nearest neighbours, whatever the distance between them. On the compass, adjacency is the ring of next steps around the walker and the network of entangled companions. Leverage through adjacency is changing the neighbourhood: who meets whom, what lies one step away. Snowden's practice of throwing trios at a problem, and of nudging people to a nearby weak attractor rather than a distant goal, is leverage of this kind.

Tendency is the inclination of the whole: the propensity of a configuration, Chinese 勢 shì, Popper's propensities, Snowden's "dispositional state". Hobbes gives the best definition in the history of political thought. War, he writes, consists not in actual fighting but in the known disposition to it, as the nature of foul weather lies not in a shower or two of rain but in an inclination to it over many days together. On the compass, tendency is the shape of the lobes: where the needle leans before anyone looks. Leverage through tendency is tilting the field, not pushing the agents. Kipling's Mariner does exactly this: he does not fight the Whale; he changes what can pass its throat.

Why only all three together

Each lever fails alone. Agency without adjacency is a shout in an empty room: an act with no neighbourhood to carry it. Adjacency without tendency is a network with nothing flowing through it: everyone connected, nothing moving. Tendency without agency is weather without sailors: the field leans, but no one tacks. Leverage, like acumen in Movement 32, is a conjunction. It is strongest where a small act (agency) lands in a dense neighbourhood (adjacency) that is already inclined (tendency).

All three drive the same deeper motion: decomposition and recombination. Agency breaks a frame by acting against it; adjacency recombines by bringing particulars next to one another; tendency decides which recombinations hold. This is Boyd's destruction and creation (Movement 29), Deleuze and Guattari's deterritorialisation and reterritorialisation, Locke's judgement and wit (Movement 33), and, in Thomas Nail's kinetic ontology, the unfolding and refolding of flows. It is also the shape of every living collective: crowds gather and disperse, flocks split and re-merge, institutions break into factions and recompose.

The compass panel makes one practical point. Most interventions push on one ring only. A campaign pushes agency (exhortation). A reorganisation pushes adjacency (new reporting lines). A strategy deck describes tendency (the market is moving). Leverage appears only where the three rings line up: a small act, among the right neighbours, in the direction the field already leans.
Table 25 · The three levers across the treatise's traditions

The table is a concordance, not an equation. Its claim is narrower: in each tradition, leverage requires something that acts, something adjacent that carries the act, and something already inclined that amplifies it. Snowden, in conversation, has named his own triad as agency, affordance and assemblage. The treatise keeps agency, reads affordance as one face of adjacency (what the neighbourhood offers), and replaces assemblage with tendency, because an assemblage without a tendency is a diagram, not a motion.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part TwentyLiber II · Part Twenty-Two

Tendency as weather and agency as a hand in a river: Liber Secundus's two images for two of the three levers.

Altius Leverage points revisited

Donella Meadows ranked twelve places to intervene in a system, from parameters at the bottom to paradigms and the power to transcend them at the top. Her list maps onto the three levers. Parameters and buffers are low-grade agency; information flows and rules reshape adjacency; goals, paradigms and self-organisation work on tendency. Her famous warning, that people push leverage points in the wrong direction, follows from the conjunction: an act aimed at the wrong lean amplifies the wrong motion. The three-lever reading adds what her list lacks: leverage is not a point but a configuration of act, neighbourhood and lean.

Movement 35 · De Turba et Sturnis

The Flash Mob and the Murmuration

Two collectives reach scale without anyone running an algorithm. On 17 June 2003, around a hundred people gathered on the ninth floor of Macy's in Manhattan and told the bewildered staff they were shopping for a "love rug" for their commune. Ten minutes later they were gone. On a winter evening over a reedbed, thousands of starlings turn as one, split around a falcon, and re-form. The flash mob and the murmuration both show coordination at scale. They are opposites in almost every other respect, and the difference is the difference between anthro-complexity and computational complexity.

The flash mob: a spontaneous tribe with a script

The flash mob was the deliberate invention of Bill Wasik, then a senior editor at Harper's Magazine. In 2003 he emailed about sixty friends and acquaintances proposing a pointless gathering as a social experiment. His first attempt was foiled because the store had been tipped off. For the second he sent participants to staging areas in four Manhattan bars, where they received their instructions just in time. Wasik later revealed himself in "My Crowd, or, Phase 5" (Harper's, March 2006), describing the project as an experiment on hipster conformity. His mock FAQ gave the motive in one line: why join an inexplicable mob? Because tons of other people are doing it. The experiment ended, he wrote, with its absorption into corporate advertising.

Read through the three levers, the flash mob is all agency and adjacency, with a borrowed tendency. Each participant chooses to come and can defect (agency). The network is a forwarded email: a web of weak ties, in Granovetter's sense, linking strangers who become adjacent only at the rendezvous (adjacency). The tendency is play, conformity and the pleasure of the bystander's bewilderment. The instructions are not an algorithm; they are a score, interpreted by bodies in a room. And the mob has its own idea of levers: the absurd act that briefly jams the striated space of a department store. It is a crew in Snowden's sense, a group that temporarily aligns identity with a role for a collective purpose, and a spontaneous tribe with its own laughter.

The murmuration: scale-free correlation without a leader

The starlings have no script, no organiser and no rendezvous time. Michele Ballerini and colleagues reconstructed the three-dimensional positions of birds in flocks of up to 2,600 European starlings (PNAS, 2008). They found that each bird interacts with a fixed number of neighbours, about six or seven, regardless of distance: the interaction is topological, not metric. They argued that this keeps the flock cohesive under the large density changes caused by predators. Andrea Cavagna and colleagues then showed (PNAS, 2010) that the correlations in the flock are scale-free: a change in one bird's behaviour affects and is affected by every other bird, however large the flock. That extends each bird's effective perception range to the whole group and suggests the flock behaves like a system poised near a critical point. George Young and colleagues (2013) later showed that six or seven neighbours optimise the trade-off between group cohesion and individual effort.

Read through the three levers, the murmuration is all adjacency and tendency, with agency distributed to the point of disappearing. Adjacency is the seven-neighbour topology. Tendency is criticality: a flock poised to respond maximally to a perturbation. Agency, in Snowden's sense of reflexive intention, is absent: no bird theorises the flock. This is exactly the contrast his anthro-complexity draws when it says humans are "not ants, or birds".

The live model below runs both. In the murmuration, each bird aligns with its nearest neighbours; drop a falcon and watch the flock split and re-form by itself. In the flash mob, nothing happens until the text goes out; then strangers converge, perform, and disperse on the clock. Turn up "crystallise" and a residue stays behind after each mob. That residue is where Movement 36 begins.
Live model
Starlings and strangers

Left: 130 birds, each aligning with its k nearest neighbours whatever the distance, with some noise. Send a falcon through and watch the flock split and re-form by itself. Right: 70 strangers going about their day. Send the text and they converge, perform in sync, then disperse on the clock. Raise "crystallise" and a few stay behind after each mob.

No algorithm in sight

Both collectives are routinely modelled by algorithms. Reynolds's boids (1987) and Vicsek's self-propelled particles (1995) reproduce flocking with a few local rules. But the birds do not run the model; we do. The flock has coupling, not code. The flash mob has a script, but a script is not an algorithm: it is a score that bodies interpret, with timing, improvisation and laughter. The SwarmCompass brochure examined in Part I sells "human-AI swarm intelligence". Neither of the two great natural examples of swarm coordination contains an AI, and the human one contains something no algorithm supplies: participants who know they are in a swarm and can decide what it is for.

Reading both on the quantum uncertainty compass

Part VI's compass gives each collective a precise place. The murmuration is a critical system: near a phase transition, susceptibility is maximal and the smallest disturbance propagates across the whole. Its correlations are classical, not quantum, but its tendency has the shape of the needle's lobes: poised, many-directioned, waiting for the falcon. The flash mob is the Pyxis rendezvous (Movement 23) made flesh. Its participants share a prior "entangled" resource, the script and the synchronised clock, and act separately until the meeting. No signal passes between them in the moment; the correlation was prepared in advance. Like the entangled compasses of the no-communication theorem, they discover their harmony only when they meet. Then they decohere: the ten-minute dispersal is the mob's own decoherence rule.

The decisive difference lies in the outside. The falcon is the murmuration's measurement apparatus: the predator's approach is what collapses the flock's many directions into one turn. The bystander is the flash mob's: the mob exists to be seen being inexplicable. Part VII's thesis that the observer is inside applies twice. The falcon is inside the starlings' ecology. The bystander is inside the mob's meaning. Without the bewildered sales assistant, the love rug is not funny.

The last row is the hinge of Part VIII. Starlings never found a state. People do, and a flash mob carries the seed of one: a convener, a list, a reputation, a sponsor. Wasik's own account ends with capture by advertising. Flash mobs elsewhere ended in curfews. Both are forms of the apparatus that Hobbes described and Deleuze and Guattari anatomised. To see how a ten-minute tribe becomes a standing body, one must read Hobbes as a physicist.

Altius Criticality and its human analogues

Starling flocks appear poised near a critical point, where correlation length diverges and response to perturbation is maximal. Human systems show signatures of criticality too: power-law cascades in retweets, avalanches in financial markets. Bak's self-organised criticality offered a mechanism for reaching such states without tuning. The difference Part VIII emphasises is reflexivity: humans can recognise approaching criticality and act on it, damping or amplifying a cascade deliberately. A flash mob is a designed avalanche with a stop rule. A market crash is an undesigned one without. The ethics of convening live in that difference.

Movement 36 · De Leviathan Moto

Leviathan in Motion: Hobbes, Deleuze and the Kinetic Ontology of Institutions

Hobbes is usually read as a theorist of sovereignty and contract. He was first a natural philosopher of motion. De Corpore (1655) builds everything from bodies in motion, and Leviathan (1651) begins not with politics but with sense, imagination and the small motions inside the body. Read that way, the Leviathan is not a thing at all. It is a pattern of motion: a dynamic composition of endeavours, an energetic store of power, and a kinetic circulation that lasts only as long as it keeps moving. That reading explains how a flash mob becomes an institution, and why Deleuze and Guattari thought the State is "always already there".

Hobbes the physicist

The introduction to Leviathan sets out the programme. Life is but a motion of limbs. Why may we not say that all automata, engines that move themselves by springs and wheels as a watch does, have an artificial life? For what is the heart but a spring, the nerves but so many strings, the joints but so many wheels, giving motion to the whole body? Then the decisive step: by art is created that great Leviathan called a Commonwealth or State, which is but an artificial man.

The atoms of this artificial man are motions, not people. In chapter 6 Hobbes calls the small beginnings of motion within the body, before they appear in walking, speaking, striking and other visible actions, endeavour. De Corpore defines endeavour (conatus) as motion made in less space and time than can be given: an infinitesimal motion, a tendency at a point. Appetite is endeavour towards; aversion is endeavour away. In chapter 10, power is a man's present means to obtain some future apparent good. In chapter 11, mankind's general inclination is a perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceases only in death. In chapter 13, war is a disposition, like foul weather. Every one of these definitions is kinetic. Hobbes's political philosophy is a dynamics of human motion.

What Leviathan really is: three ontologies

Dynamically, Leviathan is a resultant. Each subject's endeavours point in different directions. Fear of violent death and hope of commodious living redirect them, and the covenant composes them into one motion, as forces compose into a single vector. In chapter 16 Hobbes states the mechanism: a multitude of men are made one person when they are by one man or one person represented. Representation is the operation that turns many vectors into one.

Energetically, Leviathan is a store. Power is present means to future good: it is potential, not motion. In chapter 17 the multitude confer all their power and strength upon one man or assembly, and the Leviathan is generated, which Hobbes, more reverently, calls a mortal god. The sovereign is an accumulator. Canetti's crowd exists at the moment of discharge, when differences are shed and all feel equal. The Leviathan is the opposite device: it stores the discharge and releases it only through law, sword and office.

Kinetically, Leviathan is a circulation. In chapter 24 Hobbes describes money as going round the commonwealth, nourishing every part as it passes, and calls this the sanguification of the commonwealth. He was writing a generation after Harvey's account of the circulation of the blood. The artificial man lives only while its blood moves: money, commands, obedience, representation. When circulation stops, the body dies. Chapter 29 lists the diseases that lead to dissolution, among them the great number of corporations, which are as it were many lesser commonwealths in the bowels of a greater, like worms in the entrails of a natural man.

Thomas Nail's kinetic ontology (Being and Motion, 2018) supplies the general terms. Matter flows; flows fold into relatively stable bodies; folds are distributed into fields, metastable patterns of circulation that sustain themselves. Nail treats conatus, in Hobbes and Spinoza, as the internalisation of motion: a flow released from one field and folded into another. On this reading the multitude is flow; the covenant is the fold; the commonwealth is the field. Leviathan is a standing wave, a vortex that persists while matter passes through it. It is not a container of people. It is a pattern in their motion.

The frontispiece, etched by Abraham Bosse after long discussion with Hobbes, shows a giant whose torso and arms are made of more than three hundred small figures. In the printed edition they face inward, towards the sovereign. In the manuscript prepared for Charles II, as Horst Bredekamp has shown, the faces look outward, towards the reader. Part VII gives the difference a sharp sense. Inward-facing subjects make the sovereign the single observer whose description counts: the Wigner of the commonwealth, a "single source of truth" imported as governance. Outward-facing subjects are each observers in their own right, looking out of the body at the world and at the reader. The same giant can be built either way, and the two ways are two ontologies of the institution.

Deleuze and Guattari: the apparatus of capture

Deleuze thinks against the State throughout his work. In A Thousand Plateaus (1980), "7000 B.C.: Apparatus of Capture" refuses the evolutionary story in which States grow gradually out of tribes. With Guattari he argues that there have been States always and everywhere: the State springs up fully formed and seems always to presuppose itself (the Urstaat). Capture happens wherever a social organisation can compare abstract quantities and appropriate a surplus: rent from land, profit from labour, tax from money. The "war machine", by contrast, is exterior to the State: nomadic, smooth-spaced, a form of organisation that the State repeatedly tries to appropriate.

The decisive anthropology is Pierre Clastres's. In Society against the State Clastres argued that so-called primitive societies are not societies that have not yet reached the State. They are societies that actively ward it off. Deleuze's 1979 seminar summarises the thesis: these societies have mechanisms that prevent concentration and condensation, and so prevent the division between governing and governed. Among them, for Clastres, is war between segments, which keeps any one segment from gathering enough matter for a State.

Deleuze's sympathies lie with Spinoza rather than Hobbes. Spinoza told a correspondent that the difference between his politics and Hobbes's is that he keeps natural right intact: the power of the multitude is not transferred to the sovereign but persists in it. Deleuze's Spinoza thinks of power as a capacity to affect and be affected, which grows by composition with other bodies. That is the flash mob at its best: bodies composing into a greater capacity, without surrendering their natural right to leave.

How a flash mob becomes a Leviathan

Put Hobbes, Deleuze and Guattari, Clastres and Canetti together and the morphing of a flash mob into an institution has a describable sequence. It is not a smooth evolution. At each stage a threshold is crossed, and at each stage a warding-off mechanism could have stopped it.

1. Flash. A broadcast, a rendezvous, an act, a dispersal. Agency and adjacency are high; tendency is play. This is Canetti's discharge: the moment when all differences are shed and everyone feels equal.

2. Refrain. The mob repeats. Repetition makes a rhythm, and the rhythm marks a territory (Movement 32's refrain). Regulars appear. Canetti notes that the crowd also hides another tendency, one that seems to lead to new and higher kinds of formation.

3. Crystal. A small, rigid, constant group forms around the convener: Canetti's crowd crystal, the small, strictly delimited group of great constancy that serves to precipitate crowds. Closed crowds, Canetti observes, give up growth for staying power, and they often turn into institutions.

4. Representation. Someone begins to speak for the mob: to the press, to the store, to the police. At this moment Hobbes's chapter 16 operates. The multitude becomes one person because it is represented by one person. The mob now has a face, and the face can make promises.

5. Capture. Comparison and appropriation arrive. A sponsor prices the mob's attention; a city prices its disruption; an agency sells the format. Wasik's experiment ended in an advertising campaign. Flash mobs in other cities ended in curfews. Both are the apparatus of capture: one by the market, one by the State.

6. Leviathan. A standing body with offices, budget and a story about itself. It persists while circulation continues (money, membership, reputation) and dies when it stops. Weber called the passage from 3 to 6 the routinisation of charisma; Victor Turner traced spontaneous communitas hardening into normative and then ideological forms.

At each step a Clastrean mechanism can ward the State off. Wasik's ten-minute rule and his first-name-only anonymity were exactly such mechanisms: dispersal before concentration, no face to represent. Critical Mass, the monthly bicycle ride begun in San Francisco in 1992, has long described itself as an "organised coincidence" with no leaders to negotiate with, a deliberate refusal of stage 4.

The live model below runs the sequence as a toy dynamical system. Set how often the mob repeats, how readily someone speaks for it, how strong the pull of capture is, and how hard the group wards off concentration. Watch the crowd, the crystal and the institution evolve over fifty cycles, and see which stage it settles in. It illustrates the logic, not any measured data.
Live model
Will it become a Leviathan?

A toy dynamical model of the six thresholds over fifty cycles of gathering. Repetition grows the crowd and its core; a core invites a spokesperson; a represented crowd can be captured; capture builds an institution. Warding off, in Clastres's sense, disperses the core and refuses representation.

The compass reading of the covenant

The quantum uncertainty compass gives one more image, offered as analogy and not as physics. Before the covenant, the multitude is a field of many headings, each subject's endeavours pointing its own way: a superposition of wills. Representation is a projection. It selects one basis, the sovereign's, and projects every subject's state onto it. Part VII's decoherence (Movement 23) supplies the rest. The apparatus of the commonwealth, its courts, offices and coin, works like an environment that selects stable "pointer states": the roles, titles and properties that survive continual observation. Zurek called this einselection. The Leviathan einselects social life.

The analogy also shows the limits. A sovereign who measures constantly freezes the commonwealth, as the quantum Zeno effect freezes a watched system. And the Leviathan is, in Hobbes's own words, a mortal god. Like every field of motion it runs down unless energy keeps flowing through it. Boyd's second law (Movement 29) applies: a closed system decays. The flash mob and the Leviathan are two ends of one spectrum of folded motion. One disperses before it can be captured; the other captures and then must keep circulating to survive.

Disputatio

Objection 1. Hobbes is a mechanist, not a complexity thinker. His clockwork automaton is the very image anthro-complexity rejects.

Response. The clockwork is Hobbes's metaphor; his ontology is motion. Endeavour as infinitesimal tendency, war as disposition, power as stored means and money as circulation make up a dynamic, dispositional account. Determinatio: read the automaton as a field of motion, not a machine of parts, and Hobbes becomes a forerunner of the kinetic reading. What survives of mechanism is the claim that the artificial body can be made. That claim is the one this treatise disputes.

Objection 2. Deleuze and Guattari deny that the State emerges from crowds. If the State is "always already there", the six-stage sequence is the evolutionism they reject.

Response. The sequence is a series of thresholds, not a gradual growth. Each is a bifurcation that the State's form "springs" across, and each can be warded off. Determinatio: the stages describe the conditions under which capture can take hold, not a developmental law. That is consistent with Clastres's "anticipation-warding off".

Objection 3. The flash mob is trivial. A ten-minute prank tells us nothing about states.

Response. Its triviality is the point. It is the smallest human collective that shows all three levers at work, the clearest case of a deliberate warding-off rule, and a documented case of capture. Determinatio: the flash mob is to institutions what the fruit fly is to genetics: short-lived enough to watch the whole cycle.

For the instruments under disputation, Movement 36 sharpens one charge. SwarmCompass convenes a "swarm" with an organiser, a list, an assessment and a harvest of data. In this movement's terms it is a flash mob that begins at stage 3, with a crystal (the consultancy) already in place, and is designed to reach stage 5, where the collected material is compared and appropriated. That is not a criticism of commerce. It is a description of where the swarm sits on the path to a Leviathan, and therefore of which warding-off mechanisms it would need to remain a swarm.

The flash mob disperses before anyone can speak for it. The Leviathan is what happens when someone does.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part EightLiber II · Part Seventeen

Lukes, Mouffe and the thermodynamics of agreement: Liber Secundus on the politics and the energetics of the room.

Altius Biopolitics and the society of control

Foucault's lectures on biopolitics traced how modern power shifted from the sovereign's right to take life to the management of populations through statistics. Deleuze's 'Postscript on Societies of Control' (1990) extended this: power now works through continuous modulation, codes and data rather than enclosure. Read kinetically, this is the Leviathan's circulation going digital: the blood is data, the representation is the profile, and the store is the dataset. The flash mob's dispersal rule faces a new adversary here, since dispersed bodies remain represented in records. Warding off the State now includes warding off the permanent record.

Movement 37 · Pyxis Vectium

The Leverage Compass: Reading Agency, Adjacency and Tendency

Part VI built the Pyxis Incerta, an uncertainty compass with seven rules. Part VIII adds three dials and six rules. The aim is a practical instrument for anyone convening many people: a facilitator, a receiver calling a creditors' meeting, an organiser, or a consultant selling a "swarm". It reads where leverage lies, how close the gathering is to capture, and what would keep it alive without hardening it.

Three dials

The agency dial asks who can act otherwise here, and how strongly they are being measured. It reads from frozen (constant observation, the Zeno condition) through weak (light, frequent glances) to committed (one decisive look).

The adjacency dial asks who is next to whom, and what is one step away. It reads from isolated through seven (the starling optimum, enough neighbours for cohesion without exhaustion) to saturated (everyone connected, nothing distinct).

The tendency dial asks where the field leans before anyone pushes. It reads the weather, not the shower: the disposition over many days.

Rule 12 is the one most instruments lack. Every crowd one convenes needs a dispersal rule written before it starts, as Wasik's mobs had ten minutes. Without one, a gathering drifts towards stages 3 to 5 of Figure 44 by default, because the convener is already a crystal and the harvested material is already a stock.

Applying the compass

The second and third rows carry a criticism of WRAS. Its vertical axis, natural versus stimulated emergence, maps onto the murmuration and the flash mob. But in human systems there is no murmuration without someone's gesture. Every human emergence is "stimulated" by someone, as Mead's gesture–response showed (Movement 9). The axis is not a choice between two kinds of emergence. It is a gradient of how visible the instigator is. Movement 36 adds that the visibility matters, because the visible instigator is the first crystal.

Part VIII began with three levers and ends with a warning that runs against the instruments' grain. Leverage is real, but it is never the property of the one who pulls. It lives in the conjunction of an act, a neighbourhood and a lean. Collectives that keep that conjunction alive, without being captured by whoever convenes them, are rare and valuable. Flash mobs keep it for ten minutes. Starlings keep it every evening without knowing. Human institutions can keep it only by declaring their form, dating their limits and remembering the suspenders.

Agency lifts. Adjacency carries. Tendency decides. And whoever speaks for the crowd has begun to build a whale.

Measure lightly. Change the neighbours. Read the weather. Write the dispersal rule.

Woven · Liber Secundus Liber II · Part NineLiber II · Part Nineteen

The discipline of declared form and the convener's many coats complete the leverage compass.

Altius Instrument design as mechanism design

Mechanism design, the 'reverse game theory' of Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson, asks how to set rules so that self-interested agents produce a desired outcome. The leverage compass suggests a humbler variant: not designing outcomes but designing gatherings whose rules keep options open and power reversible. The dispersal rule is a mechanism-design device: it removes the payoff to capturing the crowd, because the crowd will not exist long enough to be captured. Rule 13, watch for crystals, is an incentive audit: it asks who gains from the gathering's persistence, and whether they wrote its rules.

Movement 38 · Concordantia

The Compass, the Jacket and the Living Map: A Concordance of Three Books

This volume now holds three works. Book I, The Compass and the Loom, disputes two Cynefin instruments through complexity science, quantum navigation and the observer inside. Liber Secundus, To the Strait-Jacketed, the Other Always Seems Baggy, disputes two essays on how gatherings should be formed. Liber Tertius, The Living Map with Chaos Puzzles, sets out a single practice of improvisation, reflexive cartography and immersion. They were written separately. Read together, they turn out to be one argument made three times at three scales: the instrument, the room and the practice.

One proposition, three scales

The proposition is this: no one sees the form they are standing in, and every form one stands in shapes what one sees. Book I states it as physics: the measurement basis is set before the question is asked (Movement 26), and facts may be relative to observers (Movement 27). Liber Secundus states it as sociology: to the strait-jacketed, the other always seems baggy. Liber Tertius states it as epistemology: everyone who writes against maps is drawing one, and the map may come to precede the territory.

Each book also gives the same practical answer, in its own words. Book I: measure lightly, change the neighbours, read the weather, write the dispersal rule, and work from inside on constraints, as Kipling's Mariner did. Liber Secundus: declare your form in three registers, at threshold, breakdown and close, and judge it by its fruits. Liber Tertius: hold the framework as an offer, play status consciously, and draw the map in the act of traversal. These are three dialects of one discipline.

The concordance explorer below lets you pick a theme and jump straight to where each book treats it. It is the treatise's index in motion: thirty themes, each with its places in all three books.

What the weaving changes

Three findings emerge only when the books are read together. First, the triad problem is general. Book I found that a barycentric triad shows balance rather than strength; Liber Secundus found that Snowden's own trialectic convicts "neither baggy nor boxed" of being a midpoint; Liber Tertius insists its trivium is a unity in which each alone fails. All three refuse the midpoint for the same reason: what matters is conjunction, not compromise.

Second, the convener is the first crystal. Book I traced how a flash mob becomes a Leviathan once someone speaks for it. Liber Secundus found every convener claiming to hold power lightly. Liber Tertius found that status cannot be abolished, only played. Together they say: the person who convenes is already on the path to representation, and the honest response is to declare it and write the dispersal rule.

Third, the map is an offer. Book I's instruments are actors in the systems they measure. Liber Secundus's jackets are forms one can learn to see. Liber Tertius's frameworks are offers, improvisation or block depending on how they are made. A framework offered lightly, inside the room, with stakes, is the Mariner's grating. The same framework prescribed from outside is the whale's appetite.

Three books, one confession: the map is drawn from inside, and it changes what it maps.

Altius Triangulation as method

Social science calls the use of several methods on one question triangulation (Denzin, 1970), valued because convergent findings from different methods are less likely to share a bias. The three books are a triangulation of a single proposition by physics, sociology and epistemology, and their convergence is evidence of a kind. The caution Part VII supplies is that triangulation assumes the methods' biases are independent. All three books share an author's orientation and an imprint's jacket. Their agreement is real but not independent, which is why the concordance names the shared jacket rather than hiding it.
