Part Twenty-TwoThe hand that enters the river: agency, structure, and the two strokes of facilitation

Where we areWe have looked at rooms. Now we look at the people acting in them — at agency itself.
What this asksPart Twenty-Two draws on the imprint’s treatise on agency and asks whether facilitation and its opposite are really opposites at all.
In brief 22 min read
  • The imprint’s treatise The Hand That Enters the River (October 2026), seventeen questions on human agency read through Donald Innes Davies, holds that agency is not a possession but a process: the hand that acts is always already in the river of structure, energy and other people.
  • Its account of the structure–agency debate — Giddens’s duality of structure, Sewell’s transposable schemas, Archer’s morphogenetic cycle and stored potential — shows that the baggy and the boxed are two conflations: one sees agency drowned in structure, the other structure dissolved in agency.
  • Its fifteenth quaestio holds that facilitation and anti-facilitation are not opposites but the two strokes of a single respiration. Each, held alone, becomes its own shadow: facilitation without anti-facilitation breeds dependency; anti-facilitation without facilitation breeds Freeman’s tyranny of structurelessness.
  • The boxed room is facilitation without its second stroke; the baggy room is anti-facilitation without its first. Each tradition sees the other’s shadow and mistakes its own single stroke for breathing.

TakeawayAgency lives in the rhythm between making things easier and refusing to make them too easy — and in complex rooms, that rhythm cannot be held by one convener. It must be distributed.

Woven · Book I M34 agencyM36 stored powerM23 weak measurement

Archer's stored potential is Hobbes's power as present means (M36). The two strokes of facilitation are a measurement rhythm: constant facilitation freezes the group (Zeno), none lets it scatter. Agency, adjacency and tendency (M34) are the three things the two strokes act upon.

Altius Morphogenesis and the two strokes

Archer's morphogenetic cycle runs structural conditioning, social interaction, then structural elaboration, and repeats. Facilitation acts in the middle phase, and its two strokes shape whether the cycle elaborates or merely reproduces the structure. Facilitation alone tends to reproduction: the group is helped to do what it already does. Anti-facilitation alone risks fragmentation. The respiration of the two strokes is the condition under which interaction can elaborate structure rather than repeat it, which is the only route by which a gathering changes anything that outlasts it.

In October 2026, a few days before the Mowles and Snowden essays came out, the imprint finished a scholastic treatise on human agency, The Hand That Enters the River. It’s written as seventeen questions in the same form this book uses, and read through the chapter on agency in Donald Innes Davies’s work. Its title brings together two images. Machiavelli’s river, in the twenty-fifth chapter of The Prince, is fortune: a torrent that floods the plains when it rises, against which a sensible ruler builds dykes and embankments while the weather is calm. Heraclitus’s river is the world itself, which you can’t step into twice because the water is always new. The hand that enters the river is the human agent: never outside the flow it acts on, always already shaped by the currents it hopes to steer. The treatise’s first finding is that the possessive model of agency — agency as something an individual owns — isn’t so much wrong as partial: it sees the hand and forgets the river.

That finding bears directly on the baggy-and-boxed argument, which is at heart an argument about where agency lives in a gathering. The designer puts it partly in the method: the right structure lets participants act well. The traditionalist puts it in the participants’ own relating: the right openness lets their agency emerge. Both, the treatise would say, have seen the hand and forgotten the river. This Part draws out what the treatise adds.

§ 1. Seven words

The treatise is built round a sentence of Davies’s that describes agency as active energy that turns intention into responsive participation, and it reads the sentence word by word. Active, not passive: agency is a doing, not a state. Energy: not a faculty but something you can gain and lose, top up and run down. Turns: a verb of conversion, changing one thing into another. Intention: heir to Aristotle’s prohairesis, to Elizabeth Anscombe’s Intention (1957), to Michael Bratman’s planning theory. Into: a word of entering and direction. Responsive: answerable to others and to circumstances. Participation: Plato’s methexis, having a share in something. Read slowly, the treatise notes, the sentence doesn’t put agency in the will alone. It says intention has to be turned — converted — into participation, and that the turning is the agency.

Through this book’s idea, Davies’s sentence gives a test both rooms can be judged by. A gathering serves agency if it helps participants turn their intentions into responsive participation. The boxed room risks stopping the turning. People arrive with intentions, and the method channels their participation along lines the designer chose, so what gets turned into participation is more the designer’s intention than theirs. The baggy room risks stopping it another way. People arrive with intentions, and with no form to turn them, the intentions of the established, who already know the idiom, get converted into participation while the newcomer’s stay unturned. Neither room abolishes agency. Each converts some intentions and not others, and this book’s idea predicts that each will only see the other’s failures to convert.

§ 2. The three-note chord

The treatise’s second question draws on Mustafa Emirbayer and Ann Mische’s influential article “What Is Agency?” (American Journal of Sociology, 1998), which describes agency as a chord of three notes sounding together. The iterational note faces the past. It works through selective attention, recognising types, filing a situation under a category, keeping expectations steady and settling into habit. It’s how the past is made present. Its vice is rigidity — and without it nothing could get done, because someone who had to think through every gesture from scratch would be paralysed. This, the treatise notes, is the territory of Bourdieu’s habitus, Giddens’s practical consciousness, the submerged continent of the taken-for-granted. The projective note faces the future: anticipating, building narratives, rearranging symbols, hypothesising and experimenting. The practical-evaluative note faces the present: spotting problems, describing situations, deliberating, deciding and carrying out.

The iterational note is the jacket. Emirbayer and Mische’s description of it — selective attention, recognising types, filing a situation under a category — is an exact account of how a practitioner walks into a rival’s room and sees it through the categories her tradition has made habitual. Snowden recognises the conference as a type, files it under “unstructured”, and pays attention selectively to what that category predicts. Mowles recognises the workshop as a type, files it under “over-designed”, and pays attention selectively the same way. The iterational note isn’t a flaw; without it, as the treatise insists, nobody could act. But it works below awareness, so it’s the note through which this book’s idea does its work. The cure isn’t to silence it but to bring in the other two: the projective note, which can imagine the rival’s room differently, and the practical-evaluative note, which can attend to this particular room right now rather than to its type.

§ 3. Two ways of collapsing the problem

The treatise’s third question asks whether structure constrains agency or makes it up, and sets out the three positions Margaret Archer picked out in the long argument of social theory. Downward conflation collapses agency into structure: individuals carry structures, and their actions are fixed by positions they didn’t choose. Upward conflation collapses structure into agency: social structures are nothing but the sum of individual actions and interactions. Central conflation fuses the two. Anthony Giddens’s theory of structuration, in The Constitution of Society (1984), holds that structure — rules and resources — is both the medium and the outcome of the practices it organises, over and over: when I speak English I draw on its grammar, and in doing so I keep it going.

The treatise records two refinements. William Sewell, in a 1992 article, pressed on a weak spot in Giddens: if structure only exists as it’s played out in practice, how do we explain the stubborn, material weight of institutions? His revision held that structures are made of cultural schemas and resources that hold each other up; that schemas can be carried into new situations and resources read more than one way; and that agency arises exactly in that ability to carry schemas across and reinterpret resources — agency lives in the transposability of schemas. Archer went further. If structure and agency are fused in every instant, we can never ask how much of an outcome is due to which, so we can never explain why some societies change fast and others hardly at all. Her morphogenetic cycle separates them in time: structural conditioning at one moment, social interaction at the next, structural elaboration after that — so structures built up at one time lie dormant until conditions release them at another. The treatise links this to Davies’s idea of stored potential: structure built up in the past, waiting to be released.

Through this book’s idea, baggy and boxed show up as two typical kinds of collapse. The traditionalist, looking at the designed room, sees downward conflation: participants turned into carriers of the designer’s structure, their agency drowned in roles and sequences. The designer, looking at the open room, sees upward conflation: structure dissolved into whatever participants happen to do, with no form to shape it. Each sees one of Archer’s collapses in the other’s room, and neither sees the one in his own. The traditionalist’s tradition is a structure that shapes every conversation at the conference — downward conflation, unadmitted. The designer’s method is presented as if its effects were just the participants’ agency set free — a subtle upward conflation, in which the designer’s structure disappears into what the participants achieve.

Sewell’s version offers a way through. If agency lives in carrying schemas across, then a gathering serves agency to the extent that it lets participants carry their schemas — bring the categories of their own experience into new arrangements, and reinterpret the resources the gathering offers. The designed room may help by offering new arrangements, and may hinder by fixing the arrangement in advance. The open room may help by leaving arrangements open, and may hinder by supplying only the established tradition’s schemas, so the newcomer’s can’t be carried in at all. And Archer’s stored potential names what both essays miss: every room carries, from its history, built-up structure that lies dormant and can be released. The club carries decades of stored potential in its tradition; the triopticon carries the stored potential of its designer’s long practice. Neither is a fresh start. Both are rivers already in flood.

§ 4. Breathing in and breathing out

The treatise’s fifteenth question asks whether making things easy serves agency, and its answer is the single most useful thing the imprint’s work offers this argument. Facilitation and anti-facilitation, it argues, aren’t opposites. They’re breathing in and breathing out. Facilitation, from the Latin facilis, “doable”, makes action possible by lowering its cost. Anti-facilitation makes agency possible by refusing to lower the cost too far — by holding back, disrupting or reversing ease, so that people and groups have to build their own agency. And in complex settings, both have to be shared out among everyone present.

The treatise grounds this in six traditions, and each deserves a quick look. In ecology, facilitation means the positive interactions by which one organism makes conditions better for another — the nurse plant whose shade lets seedlings take root in a desert. Mark Bertness and Ragan Callaway’s stress-gradient hypothesis (1994) proposed that facilitation matters more as environmental stress rises. But as the facilitated seedling grows, it finds the nurse plant turning into its competitor for light and water. Facilitation that never ends becomes suppression. In social psychology, Robert Zajonc’s 1965 resolution of seventy years of conflicting findings on social facilitation showed that other people’s presence boosts well-practised responses and hampers new ones: every shared space makes the habitual easier and the new harder, whether anyone means it to or not. In neurophysiology, Charles Sherrington’s The Integrative Action of the Nervous System (1906) showed that coordinated movement depends on the interplay of excitation and inhibition across the whole nervous system: pure excitation is a spasm, pure inhibition is paralysis. In group relations, from Bion’s refusal to lead the groups he chaired to the Tavistock conferences begun at Leicester in 1957, consultants have deliberately declined the role of the one everyone depends on, so that members could take up their own authority — anti-facilitation as a disciplined presence that refuses to rescue. In adaptive leadership, Ronald Heifetz’s Leadership Without Easy Answers (1994) asked leaders facing adaptive challenges to give the work back to the people who have to do it, keeping them in a productive zone of disequilibrium within what Winnicott called a holding environment. Here, the treatise notes, facilitation and anti-facilitation merge in one act: the leader makes the container easy and the content hard. And in complexity, Juarrero’s enabling constraints give the theoretical key. Facilitation, properly understood, is providing enabling constraints; anti-facilitation is removing governing constraints that have outlived their use, so that new constraints suited to the context can organise themselves among participants. Owen’s Open Space, the treatise suggests, is a near-perfect example: a minimal set of enabling constraints and an almost total refusal of governing ones.

§ 5. Each breath alone turns into its own shadow

The fifteenth question’s key finding is that each practice, on its own, turns into its own shadow — and each shadow can only be corrected by the other practice. Facilitation without anti-facilitation breeds dependence: the group that can’t meet without its facilitator, the team that can’t decide without its consultant, the professional who can’t reason without the tool. Anti-facilitation without facilitation breeds Freeman’s tyranny of structurelessness, or Heifetz’s distress with nothing to hold it: people thrown into uncertainty with no container, who then grab the nearest strong voice. Agency, the treatise concludes, lives in the rhythm between them.

That’s this book’s twin idea stated as a theory of practice, and it explains the Snowden–Mowles argument unusually precisely. The boxed room — the sticky-dot workshop Mowles describes, and in a more refined form any method that fixes its sequence in advance — is breathing in without breathing out. It makes action easy, and in doing so risks dependence on the form and the facilitator. The baggy room — the conference where nothing is fixed but start and finish — is breathing out without breathing in. It refuses to make things easy, and in doing so risks leaving the newcomer in a structurelessness where the established win. Each tradition sees the other’s shadow. Mowles sees the workshop’s dependence and calls it turning participants into drones. Snowden sees the conference’s structurelessness and calls it the domination of recognised power. Each is right. And each mistakes his own half-breath for breathing.

That has a corollary for the triopticon, which Snowden presents as the cure for both shadows. Does it breathe? Partly. Its roles and sequences make things easier: they lower the cost of taking part for people who might otherwise be silenced. Keeping the Ravens quiet, refusing early consensus, appointing a Coyote — these make things harder on purpose: they hold back ease where ease would lead to entrainment. But the designer holds both breaths, fixes them in advance and runs them to schedule. The rhythm is composed, not breathed. The fifteenth question’s demand is that in complex settings no single role can hold the rhythm, because no single position can see enough of the field to time it well.

§ 6. Sharing out the rhythm

If making things easier and making them harder have to alternate, who decides when? In a simple setting, the treatise answers, a designated facilitator can judge. In a complex one, no single position can see enough to time the rhythm, so the rhythm has to be shared: everyone present carries some responsibility for when to make things easier and when to stop. At its best, the group breathes. Someone holds the silence instead of filling it. Someone refuses to rescue the colleague looking to them for the answer. Someone names the hidden transcript the meeting has been dodging. Someone else makes it safe enough for that naming to be heard. No one person does all of it.

Sharing has its own shadow, the treatise admits: John Darley and Bibb Latané’s 1968 bystander studies, where the more people present at an emergency, the less likely any one of them was to act. And here again the two breaths correct each other. Shared anti-facilitation interrupts the spreading-thin of responsibility: when someone deliberately refuses to carry the function for the others, it becomes visible that nobody is carrying it — which is what has to happen before everyone can. The treatise points to Liberating Structures, the set of small facilitation formats developed by Henri Lipmanowicz and Keith McCandless. Their formats make things easy in structure and hard in content: everyone gets a slot to speak, and nobody gets the right to answer for the others.

The shared rhythm is the practical form of the discipline of declared form. A gathering whose members know that both breaths are needed, and that any of them can take up either, has made its form visible in the deepest sense — not as a procedure pinned to the wall, but as a shared understanding of what the gathering needs and who can supply it. It answers Snowden’s charge against the process tradition — that it can’t account for the practitioner’s specific contribution — by spreading the practitioner’s contribution across the room. And it answers the process tradition’s charge against Snowden — that the designer takes back the observer’s standpoint — by refusing to let any one person hold the standpoint from which the rhythm is timed.

§ 7. Heron’s three modes

The treatise recalls John Heron’s Complete Facilitator’s Handbook (1999), which distinguishes three modes of facilitation: hierarchical, where the facilitator directs; cooperative, where facilitator and group share direction; and autonomous, where the facilitator respects and protects the group’s own self-direction. Heron argued that good facilitation moves between these over a group’s life, ideally towards autonomy. The autonomous mode, the treatise notes, is the door anti-facilitation comes in through: if the aim of facilitation is a group that no longer needs a facilitator, then at some point the most facilitative thing you can do is stop facilitating.

Heron’s modes reframe the argument in the dimension Part Six found decisive: time. The boxed room is facilitation stuck in the hierarchical mode, never moving towards autonomy, because the method is run again for each new group and no group stays long enough to graduate. The baggy room is facilitation that starts in the autonomous mode — right for a mature group whose members went through the hierarchical and cooperative stages together long ago, and wrong for the newcomer who hasn’t. Each form is right for some moment in a group’s life and wrong for others. This book’s idea predicts that each tradition will treat its own mode as right for every moment, because its members live in that moment and can’t remember the others, or never went through them. The designer, who meets each group once, can’t see what a group becomes over years. The traditionalist, who has belonged for years, can’t remember what it was like to arrive.

§ 8. Designing so you can undo it

The treatise’s twelfth question asks whether agency can be designed, and answers in terms of keeping options open and decisions reversible: institutions serve agency to the extent that they do both, guarding against what Sidney Dekker called drift into failure. It draws on David Collingridge’s dilemma (1980). Early in the life of a technology or institution, change is cheap but information about its effects is scarce. Later, information is plentiful but change has become expensive, because the institution has set hard. The moment you can most easily shape an institution is the moment you least know how it should be shaped.

Applied to gatherings, Collingridge’s dilemma suggests that the triopticon and the open conference sit at different points on that curve. The open conference is old. Its form has set over decades; there’s plenty of information about its effects — Mowles knows its patterns of inclusion and exclusion well — and change is expensive, because the form has become the tradition’s identity. The triopticon is younger and more pliable: its designer could revise it tomorrow, though the evidence about its effects is still thin. Each is caught by the dilemma differently. Read through Collingridge, the discipline of declared form is a way of keeping both kinds of gathering reversible: declaring the form so it can be revised, and recording its effects so revision can be informed. Part Twelve’s double declaration — to participants during, to outsiders after — is a defence against drift.

§ 9. Answering for what you can’t control

The treatise’s thirteenth question asks whether you can answer for what you can’t control, and its tenth introduces Madeleine Clare Elish’s idea of the moral crumple zone: the way responsibility in complex socio-technical systems gets dumped on the human operator nearest the failure, who absorbs the blame for outcomes produced by the design of the whole. The idea has an uncomfortable application to designed gatherings. When a method fails — when the triopticon produces a shallow consensus, or the workshop a list of platitudes — the blame tends to land on the participants (who didn’t engage) or the convener on the day (who didn’t run it well), not on the design. The method itself is protected, with a crumple zone of people absorbing its failures. The open room has its own crumple zone: when the conference shuts a newcomer out, the blame lands on the newcomer, who didn’t understand, rather than on the tradition, whose form shut her out.

For an account of responsibility that fits complexity, the treatise turns to Iris Marion Young’s Responsibility for Justice (2011) and its social connection model. Responsibility for structural injustice is shared by everyone who takes part in the processes that produce it — not because any one of them caused it, but because they’re connected to it through taking part. Applied to gatherings, Young’s model says the designer, the convener, the established members and the newcomers all share responsibility for what the gathering’s form produces — not equally, since power and position differ, but genuinely. Nobody is the crumple zone. That’s the ethical ground for the shared rhythm: if responsibility is shared, so must be the ability to change the form that shares it out.

§ 10. The hand and the river, again

The treatise closes its first question where Davies closes his orientation: agency is ecological; it belongs to patterns of interaction rather than isolated actors. The possessive model sees the hand and forgets the river. In that light, this argument has been a quarrel between two ways of forgetting the river. The designer forgets that his method enters a river already flowing — a stream of participants’ histories, habits and stored potential that his roles and sequences can’t reset. The traditionalist forgets that his tradition is a river too, with banks, a channel and a current, and that the newcomer standing at its edge sees not open water but a torrent she doesn’t know how to get into. Both are hands in rivers. The question is never whether to enter the flow, because every hand is already in it. It’s whether you know the current — and whether you’re willing, with the others in the water, to take turns holding still and swimming.

§ 11. Things that act

The treatise’s eighth question asks whether things act, and answers, with Bruno Latour and Jane Bennett, that agency is spread across humans and non-humans alike. Latour’s actor-network theory, set out in Pandora’s Hope (1999) and elsewhere, treats anything that makes a difference to a course of action as an actant: the speed bump that slows the driver acts just as surely as the police officer it replaces. Bennett’s Vibrant Matter (2010) took the thought into a political ecology of things, arguing that materials, objects and assemblages have powers of their own that human projects have to reckon with. The treatise adds that once beliefs and mental frameworks are understood as physical arrangements of matter and energy, as John Challoner’s account requires, there’s no principled reason to stop at the skull: notebooks, databases, procedures and models do part of the work of thinking.

The rooms in this argument are full of such actants, and neither essay notices them. The flip chart where outputs are written up, the sticky dots used to vote, the wall where the triopticon’s clusters go, the circle of chairs in Open Space, the table at the Friday supper, the online platform through which Mowles’s clinician broadcast the aside she meant to keep private — each makes a difference to what can be said, by whom, and with what result. The sticky dot turns a conversation into arithmetic of preferences. The clustered wall turns a deliberation into a classification. The supper table turns strangers into companions before a word of substance has been said. The platform turns a hidden transcript into a public one at the press of a key. These are jackets made of things. They’re invisible to the people using them for the same reason as every other jacket: they work by being taken for granted. A full audit of a gathering’s form would ask not just what the convener designed and what the tradition supplies, but what the furniture does.

§ 12. The ironies of facilitation

The treatise’s tenth and eleventh questions turn to automation and to software agents acting on our behalf, drawing on Lisanne Bainbridge’s classic paper “Ironies of Automation” (1983). Bainbridge saw that the more a process is automated, the more vital the human operator’s skill becomes at the moments automation fails — and the less chance the operator gets to practise that skill, since the automation does it the rest of the time. The operator is left watching a system she rarely controls, and is expected to take over, expertly, in exactly the situations that are hardest and least rehearsed. The treatise reads these ironies through Davies’s psychological energy: the steady draining of mastery, autonomy and attention in people who supervise what they no longer do.

The ironies of automation have a direct parallel in the ironies of facilitation. The more completely a method structures a group’s deliberation — who speaks when, how contributions are clustered, how conclusions are reached — the less participants practise the judgement deliberation needs, and the worse they’ll be at deliberating when the method isn’t there, which is most of the time. A group that has met for years under a skilled facilitator may find, when she leaves, that it can’t hold a meeting. That’s breathing in without breathing out, seen from the side of skill. The designed room, run for groups that never meet without it, risks producing people who can only deliberate inside a method. The open room, by contrast, practises judgement all the time — but only among people who already have it, leaving the newcomer to fail in exactly the situations she’s never rehearsed. Bainbridge’s cure wasn’t to abandon automation but to design it so operators kept the skills it might call on — to keep them in practice. The parallel is the move from the hierarchical towards the autonomous mode that Heron described, deliberately built into a group’s life, so the method makes itself steadily less necessary.

§ 13. The “we” that acts

The treatise’s fourteenth question asks whether a “we” can act, and surveys the main philosophical accounts of collective agency. In Margaret Gilbert’s On Social Facts (1989), a plural subject is formed by the joint commitment of its members, each obliged to the others to act as a body. In Bratman’s Shared Agency (2014), shared intention is built from interlocking individual intentions and mutual responsiveness. And Raimo Tuomela, in Social Ontology (2013), distinguishes acting in the I-mode, as an individual who happens to be in a group, from acting in the we-mode, as a member of a group whose ends are your own. Its finding, drawing on Saras Sarasvathy’s account of how ventures form, is that in complex situations collective agency is less often a “we” that already exists and then acts, and more often a “we” that assembles itself while acting.

The baggy-and-boxed argument is, among other things, an argument about how a “we” gets made. The open conference assumes a “we” already made — a plural subject formed by years of joint commitment to a tradition — and its conversation is carried on in the we-mode by those who belong. The newcomer arrives in the I-mode and somehow has to be drawn into a “we” whose commitments she hasn’t made yet; the conference’s unspoken form gives her no explicit way in. The triopticon assumes no “we”. It brings strangers together and, through its roles and sequences, builds a temporary plural subject for the length of the event. Its “we” is built by design, and it may dissolve when the event ends. Each room sees the other’s “we” through its own jacket. To the traditionalist, the designed “we” is a simulation — a set of I-modes coordinated by a procedure. To the designer, the traditional “we” is a closed circle — a plural subject that can’t let new members in without falling apart. Gilbert’s account suggests the bridge: you can enter a joint commitment explicitly, by declaring that you’ll act as a body with others. A gathering that wanted to make a “we” out of strangers and members alike would invite that declaration — would say, at the threshold, what the members are committed to, and ask the newcomer whether she’ll commit too.

§ 14. The crazy quilt

The treatise’s sixteenth question takes up Sarasvathy’s theory of effectuation (2001), drawn from studies of expert entrepreneurs. It contrasts causal reasoning — setting a goal and choosing the means to reach it — with effectual reasoning, which starts from the means at hand and lets goals emerge from what can be done with them. Sarasvathy named several principles of effectuation. Start with the bird in hand: the means you already have. Commit only what you can afford to lose. Build a crazy quilt of partnerships, each partner bringing new means and new goals and reshaping the venture. Turn surprises into opportunities — make lemonade from lemons. And be the pilot in the plane, controlling what can be controlled rather than predicting what can’t. The treatise reads effectuation as turning uncertainty into possibility, and sets it beside Weick’s sensemaking and Snowden’s sensing as three ways of acting well without knowing what your action will do.

Effectuation gives the argument a model of form that’s neither designed in advance nor left to chance. The effectual gathering starts with the means at hand — the people who’ve come, what they know, what they’re committed to — rather than with a method picked to hit a goal. It commits only what it can afford to lose, probing rather than plunging. It builds its form like a crazy quilt, each participant who commits bringing something that changes the shape of the whole. It treats surprises — the newcomer’s unexpected question, the Eagle’s unlooked-for disagreement — as material, not disruption. And its convener acts as a pilot, attending to what can be steered now rather than to a plan. A gathering like that isn’t baggy, because it has principles and a discipline. And it isn’t boxed, because its form is put together during the meeting out of what participants bring. The crazy quilt is Part Fourteen’s joiner in cloth: a form made of declared pieces, seams showing, whose pattern nobody designed and everybody made.

Facilitation makes the act doable; anti-facilitation refuses to make it too doable; and agency lives in the breathing between them. The boxed room breathes in forever; the baggy room holds its breath. A room that knows it has to do both, and lets everyone in it take the breath, has started to live.

Agency lives in the breathing between two strokes. And breathing is close to play — which has its own wisdom about rules.

Part Twenty-ThreePlay, cabaret and the drift: ludology, the carnival and the Situationist critique of the room

Where we areThe argument has been serious for a long time. Time to bring in play.
What this asksPart Twenty-Three asks what game theory of the human kind — finite and infinite games, carnival, the Situationist drift — reveals about the rules of a gathering.
In brief 14 min read
  • The imprint’s framework of organisational ludology draws on Carse, Böhme, Gadamer and temporal inversion. James Carse’s distinction between finite games, whose rules may not change, and infinite games, whose rules must change, is the clearest available statement of the contestable frame.
  • Roger Caillois’s axis from paidia (free, turbulent play) to ludus (rule-bound play) is the baggy-and-boxed axis in the theory of games — and Caillois held that ludus disciplines paidia without abolishing it.
  • Bakhtin’s carnival suspends hierarchy, but its critics note that licensed misrule can protect the order it inverts; the imprint’s idea of the organisational cabaret, with its porous boundary between performer and audience, is an attempt to keep the inversion live.
  • The Situationists supply the sharpest critique of both rooms: the facilitated workshop as spectacle, the conference as recuperated refusal — and the dérive, a drift with rules, as a model of structured openness.

TakeawayThe question is not whether a gathering has rules but whether it is a finite game, played to win within fixed rules, or an infinite game, played to keep the play going by changing them.

Woven · Book I M22 dériveM35 flash mobM36 capture

The flash mob is a late descendant of the Situationist construction of situations, and its fate, recuperation by advertising, is exactly the capture the Situationists predicted. Carse's infinite game is a warding-off mechanism: change the rules before anyone can own them.

Altius Recuperation as capture

The Situationists called recuperation the process by which subversive ideas are absorbed into the spectacle and sold back. Boltanski and Chiapello's 'new spirit of capitalism' (1999) documented the same process in management: the artistic critique of the 1960s, demanding autonomy and creativity, became the vocabulary of project-based organisation. Flash mobs repeated it in a decade. Book I's apparatus of capture names the mechanism, and Carse's infinite game names the defence: change the rules faster than they can be packaged.

One of the frameworks the imprint has developed under its own name is what it calls organisational ludology: an account of organisational life as play. It combines James Carse’s finite and infinite games, Gernot Böhme’s atmospheres, Hans-Georg Gadamer’s philosophy of play, and a device borrowed from the film Tenet — time running backwards, so that events are read in reverse from their consequences. The complexity corpus stretches the framework into what it calls the organisational cabaret and the carnivalesque, drawing on Henri Lefebvre, the Lettrists and the Situationists. And the imprint’s earlier essays — “All Coherence Gone”, on Situationist theory, and “Everything Is Incoming / No Original — No Copy”, on sampling and borrowing — are written in the same spirit. This Part reads the baggy-and-boxed argument through play.

§ 1. Finite and infinite games

James Carse’s Finite and Infinite Games (1986) opens with a distinction that has had a long life in management writing, much of it shallow, and that deserves reading in its original sharpness. A finite game, Carse wrote, is played to win; an infinite game is played to keep the play going. Finite games have fixed boundaries, agreed players and rules settled before play starts, and they end when someone wins. Infinite games have no fixed boundaries, let new players in, and change their rules as they go — precisely so the play can continue, since a rule that would end the game has to be changed for the game to go on. Carse put the contrast in one sentence: the rules of a finite game may not change; the rules of an infinite game must change.

That sentence is the most compact version going of Part Nine’s sixth question: how can participants challenge and change the form itself? A gathering whose form is fixed before it starts and can’t change during it is, in Carse’s terms, a finite game, however open its content. The triopticon, with its roles and phases settled in advance, is a finite game played to produce outputs. A gathering whose form changes during play so the play can continue is an infinite game. Does the open conference count? In one sense yes: its conversation goes where it goes, and participants can take it anywhere. But Carse would ask whether its rules — the tradition’s unspoken norms, the idiom, the liturgy — can change during play, or whether they’re as fixed as the triopticon’s, just invisible. An open conversation held inside unchangeable unspoken rules is a finite game that doesn’t know it is one. The infinite game isn’t the absence of rules. It’s a game whose rules are always in play.

Carse added a second distinction that bears on this book’s idea: finite players play within boundaries; infinite players play with boundaries. The finite player sees the boundary as a given and plays inside it. The infinite player sees it as one more piece of the game, to be moved when moving it keeps the play alive. Each tradition in this argument plays within its own boundaries — the designer within his method, the traditionalist within his idiom — and sees the other’s boundaries as the other’s prison. An infinite player would see both sets of boundaries as playable. That’s the disposition the jacket audit is trying to grow.

§ 2. Paidia and ludus

Roger Caillois’s Man, Play and Games (1958), a critical extension of Johan Huizinga’s Homo Ludens (1938), sorted games into four kinds — agon, competition; alea, chance; mimicry, make-believe; ilinx, vertigo — and set them all along one line running from paidia to ludus. Paidia is free improvisation, turbulence, spontaneous and uncontrolled fantasy: a child tumbling in the grass. Ludus is play bound by rules, conventions and deliberately cultivated difficulty: chess, or the crossword. Caillois held that ludus disciplines paidia — rules give shape to the raw energy of play and make it a game — and that, broadly, civilisation moves from paidia towards ludus.

The line from paidia to ludus is the baggy-and-boxed line in the theory of games, and Caillois handles it more subtly than either essay. He didn’t set paidia and ludus against each other as the free and the confined. He held that ludus is paidia given shape, and that the pleasure of ludus depends on the paidia energy it channels. A game with rules but no turbulence is dead; turbulence with no rules never becomes a game. Every good game has both. So Caillois anticipated, in the language of play, the breathing Part Twenty-Two described: one breath opens space for turbulence, the other gives it shape, and neither alone is play.

Huizinga, for his part, gave the theory of play its most famous image: the magic circle, the marked-off space — the arena, the card table, the stage, the law court — inside which the rules of play hold and the rules of ordinary life are suspended. Every gathering is a magic circle in Huizinga’s sense: a space set apart from ordinary life, with special rules inside. The open conference is a magic circle whose boundary is its membership; the triopticon is a magic circle whose boundary is its procedure. Neither lacks a circle. The question, again, is whether the circle is drawn where everyone can see it.

§ 3. The game that plays the players

Gadamer, in Truth and Method (1960), made play the key to understanding what art is, and his account bears on this argument in a way neither essay sees coming. Play, Gadamer argued, isn’t mainly something a person does. It’s a movement — a to-and-fro — that players get drawn into, and it has a life of its own. The players don’t so much play the game as get played by it. The game takes priority over the player’s awareness; a player absorbed in play is no longer in charge of what happens, and that absorption is what makes it real play. A player who stood outside the game, deciding moment by moment whether to join in, wouldn’t be playing.

At first glance Gadamer’s account sides with Mowles. The living present of conversation, where participants get drawn into a movement nobody controls, is play in Gadamer’s sense, and the designer who stands outside it arranging its conditions isn’t playing. But Gadamer was just as clear that play has a structure — that the to-and-fro is shaped by the game’s own form, and the player’s absorption is absorption into that form. A child at play is absorbed in the rules of a game she invented a minute ago; a chess player is absorbed in the rules of chess. Play isn’t formless. It’s the experience of form from inside, as movement rather than restriction. That’s the jacket become body, in Gadamer’s terms: the form of the game, fully lived in, feels not like a rule but like the play itself. The designer’s method, fully lived in by participants who’ve practised it, could feel the same way. The conference’s tradition feels that way to its members. The newcomer, not yet absorbed, feels both as rules.

§ 4. Running it backwards

The imprint’s ludology borrows from Christopher Nolan’s Tenet (2020) the device of time inversion: objects and people moving backwards through time, so effects come before causes and a bullet flies back into the gun. The framework uses it as a way of reading organisational events backwards from their consequences, so that what looked like accident going forwards looks like pattern going backwards.

Applied to this argument, running it backwards is a useful exercise. Read forwards, each essay tells the story of a gathering and then judges its form: Mowles describes the workshop and then condemns its structure; Snowden describes the conference and then condemns its openness. Read backwards, the verdict comes first. Each author arrived with a judgement already formed by his tradition, and the story was put together afterwards to support it. Running it backwards exposes the iterational note of agency — the selective attention and recognition of types Part Twenty-Two described — as the hidden cause of the perception it seems to follow. The bullet of the verdict was already in the chamber. That isn’t an accusation of bad faith. It’s a description of how all perception works, and a reminder that the forward story of any gathering is always partly projected backwards from the verdict you brought into the room.

§ 5. Carnival and its licence

Mikhail Bakhtin’s Rabelais and His World, written in the 1930s and 1940s and published in 1965, made the medieval carnival a figure for hierarchy suspended: a time when the official order of church and state was turned upside down, the fool was crowned, the high were brought low, and people laughed together in a second life outside authority’s rule. Bakhtin read carnival as a utopian taste of freedom and equality, and as the source of the grotesque, double-edged, renewing laughter he found in Rabelais.

The complexity corpus takes up the carnivalesque, alongside Lefebvre’s festival, as a deliberate renewal of organisational energy: the crack in the managed order where aliveness gets in. But Bakhtin’s critics have long pointed out what Part Two noted through Max Gluckman’s rituals of rebellion: licensed misrule can protect the very order it turns upside down, by giving discontent a safe channel and then putting the hierarchy back intact when the festival ends. Terry Eagleton put the objection bluntly when he called carnival a licensed affair, a permitted break in the dominant order. The triopticon’s appointed Coyote is a carnival figure in exactly this sense: a licensed fool, crowned for the length of the phase, whose upending of assumptions leaves the method untouched.

The imprint’s idea of the organisational cabaret is, in this light, an attempt to keep the upending live rather than licensed. The cabaret, as the corpus describes it, is a kind of social encounter where the line between performer and audience is deliberately blurred, where the content is satirical and serious at once, and where the emotional charge of the performance is the analysis. The Weimar cabaret the image comes from wasn’t a licensed festival but a nightly provocation, carried on under constant threat of censorship, in which the audience was caught up in the satire it was watching. As the corpus uses them, the difference between carnival and cabaret is the difference between an upending granted by authority for a season and an upending seized by performers every night, with the audience made part of the act. Carried over to gatherings, the cabaret asks whether challenging the frame is a role the designer hands out, or a possibility open to anyone at any moment, with everyone present implicated.

§ 6. The spectacle

Guy Debord’s The Society of the Spectacle (1967) opens by claiming that in societies where modern conditions of production rule, all of life shows up as a vast pile of spectacles, and everything that was once lived directly has retreated into representation. Its fourth thesis states the crux: the spectacle isn’t a collection of images but a social relationship between people, mediated by images.

Read through Debord, Mowles’s account of the facilitated workshop describes a spectacle: flip-chart outputs read out, applause on cue, energy performed, participation represented rather than lived. The participants are spectators of their own participation — a social relationship mediated by the images of participation the method produces. That’s the Situationist critique of the boxed room, and it’s severe: the designed gathering doesn’t just constrain participation; it replaces it with a picture of itself.

But Debord’s critique doesn’t spare the open room. The conference can turn into a spectacle of a different kind: a performance of depth, reflectiveness and critical seriousness, where members show each other how well they can notice dynamics and sit with ambiguity, and where the tradition’s picture of itself — Part Twenty-One’s group charisma — is reproduced as an image. A spectacle of authenticity is still a spectacle. Debord’s point was that the spectacle swallows everything, including the critique of the spectacle — which brings us to the Situationists’ sharpest idea.

§ 7. Recuperation

The Situationists called it récupération: the process by which radical ideas, gestures and practices get absorbed by the order they oppose — neutralised, packaged and sold back. The rebel’s style becomes a fashion; the critique of consumerism becomes a product; refusing work becomes a lifestyle brand. Recuperation isn’t repression. It’s absorption, and it works better than repression because it leaves the radical believing he’s been heard.

Every tradition in this argument is exposed to recuperation, and this book’s idea predicts each will see the other’s and not its own. The process tradition’s refusal of managerial method was a radical gesture, and it has been absorbed into a doctoral programme, a conference, a reading list, a professional identity and a market where its graduates sell their services. The refusal of method has become a method you can buy. The anthro-complexity tradition’s critique of systems thinking and naïve complexity was a radical gesture too, and it has been absorbed into a company, a set of licensed methods, a certification and a brand. The critique of frameworks has become a framework you can buy. Jackson’s critical systems thinking took its name from the Frankfurt School’s critique of instrumental reason, and has been absorbed into a practitioner’s guide. This imprint’s own Situationist streak — its post-punk prophetic voice, its manifestos and broadsides — is published on GitHub and promoted on LinkedIn: the same LinkedIn where, as Mowles noted, thought collectives police their members. Recuperation is the jacket the radical picks up on the way to market, and the wearer can’t see it because it feels like success.

§ 8. The dérive

Debord’s “Theory of the Dérive” (1956, revised 1958) described the Situationist practice of drifting through a city: moving quickly through different atmospheres, letting yourself be drawn by the pulls of the terrain and the encounters you find, and dropping for a while your usual reasons for going anywhere. The dérive is often misremembered as aimless wandering. Debord insisted it wasn’t. It involved playful-constructive behaviour and awareness of psychogeographical effects, and chance played a smaller part than you might think. The drifters were paying disciplined attention to the currents and eddies of the city’s atmospheres — the way some streets pull and others push away — and they wrote down what they found. The dérive had rules: a length of time, a number of people, a terrain, a habit of noting. It was a drift with a method.

The dérive is the Situationist answer to baggy and boxed, and it anticipates Part Twenty-Two’s breathing. It isn’t the commuter’s planned route, moving through the city along lines fixed in advance — the boxed. Nor is it the idle stroll of someone going wherever impulse leads — the baggy. It’s disciplined openness: a practice whose structure exists to make the drifter available to whatever the terrain offers. Psychogeography — the study of how geographical surroundings affect people’s feelings and behaviour — was its science; the dérive was its method. Carried over to gatherings, the dérive suggests a form whose rules exist not to fix where the conversation goes but to make participants available to where it might go: a length of time, a terrain, a habit of noticing, and a willingness to be pulled. That’s close to what the best open conversations achieve, and close to what the best designed methods intend. The Situationists named it, and named what it needs: the drift has to be done with your eyes open to its own currents.

§ 9. All coherence gone

The imprint’s essay on Situationist theory took its title from John Donne’s An Anatomy of the World (1611), written as the new astronomy took hold: “’Tis all in pieces, all coherence gone.” Donne was mourning the collapse of the medieval cosmos under Copernicus and Galileo — the loss of a single frame where everything had its place. The imprint uses the line, in a post-punk and Situationist key, to turn the lament into a condition. The single frame has gone, and with it any chance of a view from nowhere. What’s left is a world of fragments, samples and partial views, which each practitioner has to put together into whatever coherence the moment allows.

The imprint’s manifesto “Everything Is Incoming / No Original — No Copy” carried the same insight into the aesthetics of sampling: every work is put together from earlier works; there’s no original that copies come from, just a constant circulation of material, re-cut and recombined. Applied to the forms of gatherings, that’s freeing and sobering at once. The triopticon samples the Tavistock conference, the expert panel, the small-group exercise and the totem menagerie. The open conference samples the group-analytic session, the academic colloquium and the weekend retreat. Jackson’s grid samples Habermas and operational research. None of these forms is original. Each is a remix, and each tradition’s claim that its form is the one true answer to the problem of structure is a DJ’s claim that his mix is the only music. In a world where all coherence has gone, the honest practitioner does what the post-punk musician did: makes the form himself out of what’s to hand, says where it came from, and accepts that someone else will re-cut it tomorrow.

Ninth Interlude · On the Drift

The commuter knows his route and sees nothing. The idler follows his whims and sees only himself. The drifter sets out with a time, a terrain, a notebook and a companion, and lets the city tell him where to turn — and because he has rules, he can be surprised. That’s the secret the boxed room and the baggy room both forget: openness isn’t the absence of form but a form whose purpose is to make you available. The street that pulls you is only felt by someone who has agreed, for an afternoon, to be pulled.

The infinite game changes its rules to keep the play alive. The Church learned something similar, over two millennia, about order and the Spirit.

Part Twenty-FourTry the spirits: the long Christian argument about order and the wind that blows where it lists

Where we areThe oldest institution in the West to argue about structure and spontaneity is the Church.
What this asksPart Twenty-Four asks what two thousand years of argument about order and Spirit can teach two management theorists — and finds that it taught the lesson long ago.
In brief 14 min read
  • The imprint’s theological works — on the discernment of spirits, on pneumatology and holy fools, on incarnational reality, on soul friendship — enter a quarrel the Church has conducted for two thousand years: between the Spirit that blows where it lists and the order that lets all things be done decently.
  • Paul’s instructions to the Corinthians hold both in a single chapter; the Rule of Benedict calls itself a little rule for beginners; Quaker meetings discern the sense of the meeting in a silence that is rigorously ordered; Ignatius adapts a structured set of exercises to each person. None is baggy or boxed.
  • The holy fool, unlicensed and uninvited, is the true trickster that the appointed Coyote imitates; C. S. Lewis’s “inner ring” names the desire that sustains the established group; and the anam cara shows a constitutive form held in friendship rather than procedure.
  • Discernment — trying the spirits by their fruits — is the audit of jackets in its oldest form: not asking whether a form is structured or open, but testing what spirit it serves.

TakeawayThe Church learned long ago that the Spirit is not opposed to order, and that a form can be tested only by its fruits. The baggy and the boxed are two ways of failing to discern.

Woven · Book I M33 the unlicensed trickster

The holy fool, unlicensed and uninvited, is the wit that has no letter in ACUMEN (M33). An appointed Coyote is wit given a job description, and so ceases to be wit.

The imprint’s work reaches beyond complexity and organisation into theology. Several of its biggest treatises — on the discernment of spirits, under the title Try the Spirits; on the Holy Spirit, three Chinese theologians and the holy fools, under the title Seeing the Invisible; on incarnational reality, drawing on Leanne Payne and C. S. Lewis, under the title Another Is In Me; on soul friendship and the Celtic tradition of the anam cara — take up a question that the baggy-and-boxed argument restates in secular terms. The complexity corpus, too, has a thread about the Spirit, which reads the living present through the breath that organises social life. This Part asks what the oldest institution in the West to have argued about structure and spontaneity can teach the newest.

§ 1. The wind and the order

The Christian tradition carries both poles of this book’s idea in its founding texts. The Gospel of John records Jesus telling Nicodemus that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit (John 3:8, in the Authorised Version). The Spirit is the baggy principle above all others: unpredictable, uncontrollable, refusing every container. And the same tradition built, over two thousand years, the most elaborate institutional order the West has known — offices, councils, canons, liturgies, rules of life — and justified it as the work of the same Spirit.

The tension shows up in the earliest Christian writings. Paul’s first letter to the church at Corinth, written around the middle of the first century, is addressed to a community whose worship had got chaotic, with members speaking in tongues all at once and prophets talking over each other. His answer holds both poles in a single chapter. On one side: “How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation” (1 Corinthians 14:26). The gathering is open; every member brings something; nobody is the only speaker. On the other: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (14:40), “for God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (14:33). Prophets are to speak two or three at a time, with the others weighing what’s said; if a revelation comes to someone sitting by, the first speaker is to hold his peace. Paul doesn’t choose between openness and order. He gives openness an order: a sequence, a limit on numbers, a practice of weighing what’s said, a rule of giving way to the person with something new. The gathering at Corinth is neither baggy nor boxed. It’s ordered openness, two thousand years before anyone used the phrase.

§ 2. Prophecy and office

In the second century the tension turned into a split. The movement later called Montanism, which arose in Phrygia around the 160s, held that the Spirit was speaking directly through new prophets — Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla — whose ecstatic words carried an authority that could correct the bishops. The emerging order of bishops rejected the claim, and that rejection helped settle an understanding of authority as resting in office, tradition and the canon of Scripture rather than in charismatic speech. Historians have long argued about the episode, and sympathetic readers have seen in Montanism a silenced voice of the Spirit against a hardening institution. This book doesn’t need to settle that. What matters is that the Church faced, right at its foundation, exactly the quarrel this book has been following: between people who saw the institution as a box smothering the Spirit and people who saw the prophets as a disorder endangering the community. Each saw the other’s jacket. And the Church’s eventual settlement didn’t abolish either. It kept prophecy within an order, and kept the order answerable, at least in principle, to the Spirit it claimed to serve.

§ 3. A little rule for beginners

The monastic tradition faced the same tension in the desert. The earliest Christian monks of Egypt and Syria, in the third and fourth centuries, were hermits — the Desert Fathers and Mothers, whose sayings are among the great documents of Christian spirituality — and in this book’s terms their life was the baggy extreme: each alone with God, guided by an elder, under no shared rule. In the early fourth century Pachomius founded communities living under a common rule, and the communal tradition he started culminated in the West in the Rule of Benedict, written in the sixth century for the monastery at Monte Cassino.

Benedict’s Rule is the most successful constitution in the history of Western institutions — it has governed communities without a break for fifteen centuries — and the way it describes itself is revealing. In the prologue Benedict says he hopes to set up a school for the Lord’s service, in which nothing harsh or burdensome is laid down. In the last chapter he calls it a little rule for beginners, and points anyone who wants to go further to the Fathers and the Scriptures. The Rule is detailed — it lays down the hours of prayer, the psalms to be sung, the shape of the day, how the abbot should behave, how guests should be received — and yet it presents itself as a minimum, a beginning, a trellis rather than a cage. And it’s full of provisions for adapting itself. The abbot is to adjust it to each monk’s strength, to the season, to the needs of the sick and the old. The community is to be consulted on important matters, and the abbot is to listen even to the youngest, since the Lord often shows what’s better to the younger.

So the Rule contains, fifteen centuries early, almost every element of the discipline this book has proposed. Its form is declared: it’s written down and read aloud to the community regularly, so nobody can claim not to know it. It’s fitted to people: not applied uniformly but adjusted for each. It can be challenged within limits: the abbot has to consult and listen. It understands itself as a beginning, a scaffold for formation rather than a replacement for it. And it’s lived over a lifetime, so that its forms become, for those who stick with it, the shape of their days — the jacket become body in the most literal sense, since the monk’s habit is the garment he wears until he dies. Benedict didn’t ask whether his community should be structured or open. He asked how a structure could serve the freedom of the people living inside it, and he answered by writing a rule that knew it was a rule.

§ 4. The sense of the meeting

The Religious Society of Friends, the Quakers, offers the most striking modern Christian example of ordered openness, and one that bears directly on this argument because it’s about how gatherings are run. In a traditional Quaker meeting for worship, Friends gather in silence, with no minister, no liturgy and no programme. Anyone can stand and speak if they’re moved to, and the meeting may pass entirely in silence. To an outsider nothing could look baggier. Yet the silence is strictly ordered by long-standing practice. Friends are to speak only when genuinely moved, not to reply to each other, to leave time between contributions, and to test whether what they feel prompted to say is for the meeting or just for themselves. Long-standing members carry the form without saying it, and newcomers are taught it, gently.

The Quaker meeting for worship for business, where decisions get made, is more remarkable still. There’s no voting. A clerk listens to what’s said and tries to discern what Friends call the sense of the meeting — not a majority, not a compromise, but the direction the gathered community is being led in — and proposes a minute recording it, which the meeting can accept, change or reject. A single Friend who can’t unite with the sense can stand aside or, in serious cases, hold the meeting back. The clerk isn’t a chair who directs or a facilitator who designs. The clerk serves the meeting’s discernment, and her authority depends entirely on the meeting recognising that the minute is true. The practice has its own failures — meetings can be dominated by weighty Friends whose view gets mistaken for the meeting’s, an established–outsider pattern in plain dress — but its form is fully declared, its clerk is answerable, and its way of discerning is open to the whole community.

The Quaker practice is neither the triopticon nor the open conference. It has no designed roles beyond the clerk, and its silence is as open as anything Mowles describes. But its openness sits inside a declared discipline newcomers can learn, and its decisions are reached through a discernment answerable to everyone present. It may be the closest thing in existing practice to the formative encounter Snowden named in May: a process whose outcome belongs not to the clerk or any member but to the meeting, and which changes the people who take part.

§ 5. The Exercises, adapted

Ignatius of Loyola’s Spiritual Exercises, published in 1548, are among the most structured tools of formation in the Christian tradition: a sequence of meditations, contemplations and examinations, laid out over four “weeks” and carried out under a director’s guidance. Yet the introductory notes Ignatius put at the start insist again and again on adapting them. The exercises are to be fitted to the age, education and ability of the person making them; someone who can’t benefit from the full sequence is to be given less. The director isn’t to lean towards one choice or another but to let the Creator deal directly with the creature, standing like the needle of a balance, tilting neither way. The structure is elaborate, and its purpose is to make the person free — free, in Ignatius’s word, to be indifferent to everything except what serves the end for which human beings were made.

So Ignatius resolves this book’s idea in his own terms: the Exercises are a box that exists to produce freedom, and a director who imposed them uniformly, or steered the person towards his own preferences, would betray them. The director’s self-restraint — tilting neither way — is the Ignatian version of the convener who stays out of the content, and it carries the same risk this book has pointed out: claiming not to lean can hide leaning. Ignatius knew this, which is why his rules for discerning spirits pay such close attention to deception.

§ 6. The angel of light

Ignatius’s rules for discernment, attached to the Exercises, distinguish consolation — movements of the soul that draw it towards God, with peace, joy and growing faith — from desolation — movements that draw it away, with turmoil, darkness and a pull towards low things. In the rules for the second week he adds a warning drawn from Paul’s remark that Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). With a soul that’s making progress, the enemy doesn’t tempt it with obvious evils. He starts by suggesting good and holy thoughts that fit its devotion, and then little by little leads it towards his own ends. The test, Ignatius says, is to watch the whole course of the thoughts — beginning, middle and end — and notice whether they end in something less good, or in disquiet and lost peace.

The warning applies uncomfortably well to ways of gathering. A designed method that presents itself as freeing — sharing out voice, protecting the unexpected, cutting across hierarchy — may be exactly what it says. Or it may begin with good thoughts and end by bringing back the designer’s authority under a new name. An open conversation that presents itself as the place of authentic relating may be exactly that. Or it may begin with good thoughts and end by shutting out everyone who doesn’t share its idiom. The test isn’t how the form describes itself, which will always sound attractive, but the whole course of what it produces. The angel of light is the jacket that looks like freedom. Discernment is the practice of watching where it leads.

§ 7. Try the spirits

The first letter of John gives the imprint’s treatise on discernment its title: “Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1 John 4:1). And the Gospels give the test: “Ye shall know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16). Discernment doesn’t ask whether a teacher is eloquent or a movement impressive. It asks what it produces in the lives of the people it touches. Paul’s list of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance (Galatians 5:22–23) — is a set of tests any spirit, and any form, can be tried by.

Discernment is the jacket audit in its oldest form, and it corrects the baggy-and-boxed argument in a way the argument badly needs. Snowden and Mowles argue about forms — structured versus open — and each judges the other’s form by how it looks: the conference looks baggy, the workshop looks boxed. Discernment refuses to judge by appearances. It asks what each form produces. In whom does it grow patience, gentleness, faithfulness, self-control? Whom does it leave in turmoil and darkness? Whom does it draw in, and whom does it drive away? A structured gathering that leaves the least powerful heard and the newcomer welcomed has borne good fruit, whatever its structure. An open gathering that leaves its members renewed and its newcomers shut out has borne mixed fruit, whatever its openness. This book’s idea makes the test hard, because each tradition’s jacket shapes what it sees as fruit. But the test itself is clear, and it’s older than any of the traditions in the room.

§ 8. The holy fool

The imprint’s treatise Seeing the Invisible gives sustained attention to the holy fools — the saloi of Byzantium and the yurodivye of Russia — who pretended to be mad for Christ’s sake, mocked the pieties of the respectable, disrupted the liturgy, rebuked tsars and lived outside every institution. Symeon of Emesa in the sixth century, who came into the city dragging a dead dog and threw nuts at the candles in church, and Basil the Blessed of Moscow in the sixteenth, who went naked through the Russian winter and is said to have rebuked Ivan the Terrible, are among the best known. The holy fool stands for the Spirit’s freedom against the institution’s order: unlicensed, uninvited, disruptive, and recognised as holy precisely because his disruption can’t be contained.

Part Two argued that an appointed trickster is a contradiction in terms: the triopticon’s Coyote, licensed to challenge in a designated phase, is a court jester rather than a trickster, and his challenge protects the frame it seems to question. The holy fool is the real figure the appointed Coyote imitates. Nobody appointed Symeon. No method gave Basil his phase. Their challenge reached the frame itself — the liturgy, the throne — and it was dangerous, which is why it was holy. You can’t design a holy fool into a gathering. You can only put up with him, recognise him and, sometimes, listen. A gathering that wanted to make room for him wouldn’t appoint a Coyote. It would make its frame open enough that someone moved to challenge it could do so, and humble enough to ask whether the challenger was mad or sent.

§ 9. The inner ring

C. S. Lewis, whose work the imprint’s treatise on incarnational reality draws on, gave a memorial lecture at King’s College London in 1944 called “The Inner Ring”. Lewis noticed that in every institution, alongside the official hierarchy, there are unofficial circles — inner rings — whose membership is never formally announced but always keenly felt, and whose edges shift as people are drawn in and left out. He didn’t condemn such rings, which he thought inevitable and sometimes harmless. What he warned against was wanting to be inside them: the passion for the inner ring, which he thought one of the most powerful and most corrupting human motives. It leads good people to do bad things for the sake of belonging, and it can never be satisfied, because every ring you get into reveals another one beyond it. The cure, Lewis suggested, was to seek the company of people you genuinely love and the work you genuinely value, and let any ring that forms around those things be a by-product rather than a goal.

Lewis’s inner ring is Elias’s established group described from inside, by a moralist rather than a sociologist. The open conference, the anthro-complexity community, the critical systems school and this imprint all have inner rings, and wanting to belong to them shapes what their members see as good work, good conversation and good thinking. The newcomer feels the ring before she can see it; the member doesn’t feel it, because he’s inside. Lewis’s cure is the one Part Twelve reached through the master and the manual: let belonging follow from love of the work rather than come before it. A gathering ordered by love of the work it exists to do, rather than by its members’ wish to stay inside, will have rings — every human gathering does — but they’ll be porous.

§ 10. The soul friend

The imprint’s treatise on soul friendship takes up the Celtic tradition of the anam cara — the soul friend, the person you share the deepest things with — made popular by John O’Donohue’s Anam Ċara (1997), and examines Stephen Cope’s Soul Friends (2017), which reads friendship as a path of development through Winnicott and attachment theory. In the early Irish Church, the anam cara was a spiritual companion and confessor, and the saying credited to Brigid — that a person without a soul friend is like a body without a head — expresses the conviction that nobody is formed alone.

Soul friendship is a constitutive form held in a relationship rather than a procedure. It has no method, no sequence, no designed roles; to an outsider it might look completely baggy. Yet it’s one of the most demanding human forms, with its own disciplines of honesty, confidentiality, faithfulness and patience, learned over years and lived in until they become the shape of the friendship itself. It’s the jacket become body at the scale of two people. And it suggests, in the end, where formation actually happens: not mainly in gatherings, baggy or boxed, but in the long-term relationships that gatherings are only occasions for. The open conference forms its members because they’ve known each other for years; the triopticon, met once, can’t. Part Sixteen’s formative encounter, Part Twelve’s masters, Part Nine’s forming people rather than designing events — all point to the same conclusion, which the Celtic Church reached in a proverb. Nobody is formed by a form. People are formed by people, inside forms that serve their friendship.

The wind blows where it likes, and the Church learned to let it blow inside a rule that knew it was a rule. Try the spirits by their fruits, not their clothes: the spirit dressed in structure and the spirit dressed in openness are known alike by whom they leave at peace and whom they drive away.

Try the spirits by their fruits. Strategy, too, has learned that forms must keep moving to stay true.
