Epigraphs

Nine Voices on the Map

A map is not the territory it represents, but, if correct, it has a similar structure to the territory, which accounts for its usefulness.Alfred Korzybski, Science and Sanity (1933)
As you push the question back, what you find is an infinite regress, an infinite series of maps. The territory never gets in at all.Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)
It is the map that precedes the territory — precession of simulacra — that engenders the territory.Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)
Only partial perspective promises objective vision. It allows us to become answerable for what we learn how to see.Donna Haraway, Situated Knowledges (1988)
An offer is anything an actor says or does. The improviser has to be like a man walking backwards. He sees where he has been, but pays no attention to the future.Keith Johnstone, Impro (1979)
It is the conversations that flow from the use of the frameworks that are important, not the frameworks themselves.Chris Rodgers
Human thought has always been paradoxical acts of immersing and abstracting at the same time.Ralph Stacey, quoted by Chris Rodgers
We have no option but to muddle through the practical implications of the immersion–abstraction paradox.Chris Rodgers
We cannot stand outside our commitments, although we only fully realise what they are through articulating them and encountering others’ difference.Chris Mowles
Abstract

The Argument in Brief

This paper takes up a problem that has shadowed organisational thought for a century and the complexity sciences for three decades: the relation between the map and the territory. It does so in order to reconcile three families of practice that are usually treated as rivals — improvisation, reflexive cartography, and immersive process — and to argue that they are not three things at all but one practice falsely divided.

The argument proceeds historically and then constructively. It traces the map–territory question from Alfred Korzybski’s 1931 dictum, through Lewis Carroll’s one-to-one map and Gregory Bateson’s infinite regress, to Jean Baudrillard’s unsettling inversion in which the map comes to precede and generate the territory. It then turns to Donna Haraway’s situated knowledges, which replace the impossible “god-trick” of the view from nowhere with the accountable view from somewhere; to the later Wittgenstein, for whom meaning is use and the territory is itself a form of life; and to Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Gilles Deleuze, who relocate knowing in the body’s pre-reflective, haptic engagement with the world.

Against this philosophical backdrop the paper reads the practical traditions: Pierre Wack’s “gentle art of re-perceiving” and the discipline of scenario thinking; the improvisation literature of Keith Johnstone, Henry Larsen, Frank Barrett and Karl Weick; and the complex responsive process tradition of Ralph Stacey, Chris Mowles and Kevin Flinn. It gives particular weight to Chris Rodgers’ pragmatic dissent — his insistence that the problem is never the framework itself but the false concreteness with which it is held.

The synthesis is named the living map: a map drawn in the act of traversal, by a practitioner who arrives with orientation rather than a script, who treats every framework as an offer rather than an answer, who works consciously with the status dynamics that no facilitation can abolish, and who holds the immersion–abstraction paradox open rather than collapsing it. Improv, on this account, is not a set of theatre games imported into management. It is the oldest available grammar of the living map — the discipline of receiving what the territory offers before knowing what to do with it.

Introduction

OpeningThe Cartographer’s Confession

❖
Woven · Book I M20 inverse instrumentLiber II, Part 18

Everyone who writes against maps is drawing one. Book I meets the same confession in the quantum uncertainty compass, which is offered explicitly as an inverse instrument: a map of what cannot be mapped, honest about being a map. Liber Secundus read this essay in its Part Eighteen; here it is in full.

Begin with an admission that the organisational complexity literature has been slow to make out loud. Everyone who writes against maps is drawing one. The critic of the cartographic reflex produces a cartography of cartography’s limits. The theorist of emergence produces a theory of emergence. The professor who rejects frameworks delivers a lecture organised by the unstated framework of rejection. This is not hypocrisy. It is the structure of the problem, and it will not be escaped by trying harder to escape it.

Chris Mowles, in his 2024 essay “Complexity and Inside-Out Thinking,” names the reflex with diagnostic precision. Most of the thinking aimed at helping organisations, he observes, concerns maps and frameworks of a world thought to exist “out there” — the two-by-two grids, the parts-and-whole charts, the imagined estuaries, all of them “more or less realist and representationalist.” He is right. And the companion essay to this one — the cyberpunk critique titled 悖论, Chaos Puzzles, reproduced in full as the companion volume to this one — pressed his diagnosis to its first paradox: any consistent rejection of frameworks is itself a framework, performed at a higher level of abstraction.

That paper proposed, as its solution, a deepening: not the abandonment of the map but the discovery that the map was always already phenomenological — a structure of experience rather than a picture of a system. This is correct as far as it goes. But it leaves a practical question unanswered. If the practitioner cannot stand outside the territory, and cannot do without orientation inside it, what exactly is the competent thing to do, moment by moment, in a room full of people?

The answer this paper develops is improvisation — understood not as a metaphor borrowed from jazz or the theatre, and not as a workshop technique, but as an ontology and an epistemology: a disciplined way of being in a situation that holds the map and the territory in living tension. The improviser arrives with something. They are not empty-handed; they carry a trained vocabulary of forms, an ear for status, a capacity to recognise an offer. But they do not arrive with a script. They draw the map as they move, and they let the territory redraw it.

Three traditions converge on this point without quite recognising one another. The first is reflexive cartography: the family of thought, from Korzybski to Haraway, that has learned to use maps while remaining honest about their partiality. The second is immersive process: the complex responsive process tradition of Stacey, Mowles, Flinn and their colleagues at Hexford, who insist that organisations exist only in the ongoing local interaction of the people who constitute them. The third is improv: the practical discipline, articulated by Johnstone and carried into organisations by Larsen, Barrett and Weick, of generating coherent meaning in real time without a predetermined plan.

This paper argues that these three are facets of a single practice, and that naming the practice — the living map — resolves the paradox the Chaos Puzzles essay — reproduced in full as the companion volume that follows — could only deepen. The structure is as follows. Parts One to Four lay the philosophical foundation: the archaeology of the map, the view from somewhere, the territory as practice, and the body that knows. Parts Five and Six turn to the practical traditions of re-perceiving and improvising. Part Seven recovers Chris Rodgers’ pragmatic dissent and the immersion–abstraction paradox. Part Eight retrieves an unlikely resource — the medieval trivium — as a meta-map of the whole. Part Nine offers the synthesis. A coda asks what remains when the voyage returns you.

Part OneThe Archaeology of the Map

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M28 performativityM11′ compression

Baudrillard's precession of simulacra is performativity in its strongest form: the map engenders the territory. Book I's Movement 28 adds the sequel MacKenzie found in markets, counter-performativity: the territory eventually breaks the map that made it.

Altius Performativity's two directions

MacKenzie distinguished generic, effective and Barnesian performativity: a model used, a model that makes a difference, and a model that makes reality more like itself. Baudrillard's precession is the Barnesian case taken to its limit. The counter-case, counter-performativity, is equally important for The Living Map: a map used so heavily that the territory breaks it. Practitioners need both concepts. The map that eats the territory is a risk; the territory that bites back is the signal that the map has been believed too long.

1.1Korzybski and the Conjecture

The sentence that founds the modern discussion was delivered to the American Mathematical Society in New Orleans in 1931, in a paper on the necessity of a non-Aristotelian system for rigour in mathematics and physics. Alfred Korzybski — an aristocratic Polish engineer who had settled in the United States after the First World War and reinvented himself as an independent philosopher — there proposed three propositions about maps that have outlived almost everything else he wrote.

A map may have a structure similar or dissimilar to the structure of the territory. A map is not the territory. An ideal map would contain the map of the map, the map of the map of the map, and so on, endlessly — a fact first noticed by Royce.Alfred Korzybski, paraphrased from the 1931 address and Science and Sanity (1933)

The decisive refinement came in Science and Sanity two years later. A map, Korzybski wrote, “is not the territory it represents, but, if correct, it has a similar structure to the territory, which accounts for its usefulness.” Three things are being said at once, and all three matter. First, the map and the territory are not identical — to treat them as such is an error of the most fundamental kind. Second, the map is nonetheless useful, and useful precisely because of a structural correspondence. Third — in the conditional “if it could be ideally correct” — the perfect map is impossible, because perfection would require the map to contain itself, and then to contain its containing, without end.

Korzybski’s target was a habit of mind he called the confusion of orders of abstraction: mistaking the word for the thing, the belief for the reality, the model for the world. The pain of a stone dropped on the foot is not the stone; one’s opinion of a politician is not the politician; the abstraction never captures all the facets of its source. He held that a great many people live inside this confusion, and that a non-Aristotelian re-training of perception — a discipline of remembering that the map is not the territory — was a precondition of sanity. The claim was extravagant. The underlying observation was exact, and it has never been refuted.

Korzybski gave the discipline a name: consciousness of abstracting — the trained, habitual awareness that in every act of perception and naming, characteristics have been left out. He even proposed a working attitude to carry it, the phrase “I don’t know; let’s see,” an orientation of provisional, experimental engagement that this paper will meet again, much later, in the practice of the improviser. And he chose for the epigraph of Science and Sanity a sentence of Alfred North Whitehead’s that states, decades early, the danger this whole paper is concerned with:

A civilisation that cannot burst through its current abstractions is doomed to sterility after a very limited period of progress.Alfred North Whitehead, quoted by Korzybski as the thesis of Science and Sanity (1933)

The abstraction that cannot be burst through is the map mistaken for the territory: the framework that has hardened into the unquestioned shape of the real. Whitehead’s “sterility” is the precise fate the rest of this paper sets out to forestall.

1.2Carroll’s Useless Perfection

Korzybski credited the philosopher Josiah Royce with first noticing the regress of the self-containing map. But the most vivid statement of the problem is older and stranger, and it comes from a writer of children’s books. In Lewis Carroll’s last novel, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893), a German Professor describes his nation’s cartographic ambitions.

We very soon got to six yards to the mile. Then we tried a hundred yards to the mile. And then came the grandest idea of all! We actually made a map of the country, on the scale of a mile to the mile! It has never been spread out, yet. The farmers objected: they said it would cover the whole country, and shut out the sunlight! So we now use the country itself, as its own map, and I assure you it does nearly as well.Lewis Carroll, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893)

The joke is also a theorem. A representation that omits nothing, simplifies nothing and organises nothing has ceased to be a representation; it is merely a duplicate, and a duplicate is useless because it is no easier to handle than the original. The utility of a map is identical with its infidelity. It is useful because it leaves things out. The cartographer’s craft is the disciplined practice of strategic omission — deciding what to make visible so that the rest can be left, productively, in shadow.

This has a sharp implication for the organisational practitioner, which the complexity literature states but rarely dwells on. Every framework — every two-by-two, every maturity model, every culture typology — is a theory of salience. It is a decision, usually unexamined, about what counts and what does not. The Stacey Matrix makes certainty and agreement visible and renders the relational history of the people in the room, the power dynamics that govern what may be said, and the emotional weather of the conversation, invisible. This is not a flaw to be corrected by a better matrix. It is the price of having a matrix at all. The question is never whether the map omits — it must — but whether the cartographer knows what has been omitted, and can feel its absence pressing back.

1.3Bateson and the Infinite Regress

Gregory Bateson took Korzybski’s regress and turned it from a curiosity into an epistemology. In the 1970 lecture “Form, Substance and Difference,” collected in Steps to an Ecology of Mind, Bateson asked the question that the dictum invites and then refuses to answer.

We say the map is different from the territory. But what is the territory? Operationally, somebody went out with a retina or a measuring stick and made representations which were then put on paper. What is on the paper map is a representation of what was in the retinal representation of the man who made the map; and as you push the question back, you find an infinite regress, an infinite series of maps. The territory never gets in at all. Always the process of representation will filter it out so that the mental world is only maps of maps, ad infinitum.Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)

This is not scepticism and it is not despair. It is a precise account of the situation of any knower. The territory, as an unmediated fact available for inspection, is not something anyone has ever had. What we have is representations of representations: the retinal image is already a map; the perception built from it is a map of that map; the words we use to report the perception are a map of the perception. There is no first floor to the building. There is no point at which the map gives way and the bare territory shows through.

Bateson’s deeper move — and the reason his version matters more than Korzybski’s for our purposes — is the relocation of the territory from substance to difference. “What gets onto the map,” he wrote, “is difference.” A map records contrasts, edges, distinctions that make a difference to the mapper. The territory is not a stuff to be copied; it is a field of differences, and which differences register depends on the perceiving system. Bateson compressed the whole point into the sentence for which he is most quoted:

Information is a difference that makes a difference.Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)

A difference becomes information only when it makes a difference to some observer — when it changes a perception, a behaviour, an understanding. There is no neutral, observer-independent inventory of differences; there is only the selection that a particular perceiving system, with its particular interests and history, is equipped to register. Bateson drew the consequence with unusual bluntness, and it is the seed of everything that follows in this paper:

We create the world that we perceive, not because there is no reality outside our heads, but because we select and edit the reality we see to conform to our beliefs about what sort of world we live in.Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature (1979)

This is not idealism — Bateson is explicit that there is a reality outside our heads. It is a claim about selection and editing. If the territory is a field of differences and the map is a selection among them, then the act of mapping is not the passive copying of a pre-given world. It is an active, selective, interested engagement — and the question of who is doing the selecting, from where, with what equipment of attention, becomes unavoidable. Bateson himself doubted that Korzybski’s cure could fully succeed: speaking as a philosopher, Korzybski urged people to discipline their thinking, “but he could not win,” Bateson observed, because when the dictum is applied to the actual natural history of human mental process “the matter is not so simple.” We do not, any of us, achieve rigour. The map cannot be escaped; it can only be held with more or less honesty.

1.4Borges, Baudrillard and the Map That Eats the Territory

Carroll’s fable was rewritten, almost certainly unknowingly, by Jorge Luis Borges in the one-paragraph story “On Exactitude in Science” (1946), attributed to a fictitious seventeenth-century traveller. In Borges’ empire the cartographers’ guild draws a map of the empire that coincides with it point for point. Succeeding generations, less devoted to the study of cartography, find the enormous map cumbersome and abandon it to the deserts and the weather, where tattered fragments survive, inhabited by animals and beggars.

Jean Baudrillard, opening Simulacra and Simulation (1981), seized this fable and inverted it — and the inversion is the single most important development in map–territory thinking since Korzybski. For Baudrillard the modern condition is not that our maps fail to capture the territory. It is that the map has come first.

Today abstraction is no longer that of the map, the double, the mirror, or the concept. It is the generation by models of a real without origin or reality: a hyperreal. The territory no longer precedes the map, nor does it survive it. It is the map that precedes the territory — the precession of simulacra — that engenders the territory.Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

Strip away the polemical gloss and what remains is a description that any organisational practitioner will recognise. Baudrillard’s “precession of simulacra” is what happens to a framework that has been institutionalised for long enough that it is no longer experienced as a framework. Kotter’s eight stages began as a representation of a pattern observed in change efforts. Through repetition, training, consultancy and the slow sedimentation of habit, the representation became a prescription, and the prescription became the shape that change actually takes in organisations that have internalised it — not because that shape is the best available, but because it is the shape the organisation has equipped itself to see, to talk about, and to act within.

This is a subtler and more pervasive thing than the cartographic reflex Mowles diagnoses. The cartographic reflex is the act of reaching for a map. The hyperreal map is the framework that has stopped being visible as a map at all because it has become the texture of the organisation’s reality. The practitioner who proudly rejects the McKinsey 7-S model is not thereby free of it; they are free of it in the way a fish leaping from water is free of water — briefly, conspicuously, and in urgent need of another medium. What is required is not a further map and not the heroic abandonment of all maps. What is required is a change in the practitioner’s relation to the map: a practice that can make the framework visible again as a framework, hold it as provisional, and keep it answerable to the territory it was always only approximately catching. That practice has a name in the philosophy of science, and it is reflexivity. It has a name in the theatre, and it is improvisation. The rest of this paper argues that these are the same name.

Part TwoThe View From Somewhere

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M27 relative factsLiber II, Part 14

Haraway's god-trick has a physics in Book I: the Local Friendliness theorem shows that no observer-independent set of facts need exist. Situated knowledge is not a concession to politics; it is how facts work.

2.1Haraway and the God-Trick

In 1988 the historian of science Donna Haraway published “Situated Knowledges: The Science Question in Feminism and the Privilege of Partial Perspective.” The essay was written as a commentary within feminist philosophy of science, but folded inside its argument is the most exact account of reflexive cartography available in the English-language tradition, and it supplies precisely the element the Chaos Puzzles essay — the companion volume to this one — left missing.

Haraway’s target is what she names, with deliberate irreverence, the “god-trick”: the claim that knowledge counts as objective only when it is produced from nowhere in particular, by no one in particular — the conjuring of a disembodied, placeless, all-surveying eye. Scientific writing, she observes, performs this trick as a matter of convention, presenting its findings “as if it did not matter where it came from.” Against the trick she sets a different account of objectivity.

I am arguing for politics and epistemologies of location, positioning, and situating, where partiality and not universality is the condition of being heard to make rational knowledge claims. Only partial perspective promises objective vision. Feminist objectivity is about limited location and situated knowledge, not about transcendence and splitting of subject and object. It allows us to become answerable for what we learn how to see.Donna Haraway, Situated Knowledges (1988)

The paradox in the phrase “only partial perspective promises objective vision” is deliberate and exact. The knowledge most worth trusting is not the knowledge that claims to see everything from nowhere. It is the knowledge that is explicit about where it stands, candid about what its standpoint reveals and conceals, and therefore accountable — correctable, answerable, locatable. The god-trick produces knowledge that is universally applicable and locally useless. Situated knowledge produces knowledge that is particular, partial, embodied and actionable, because it is produced from inside the situation it describes.

2.2The Map That Knows Itself

Haraway’s situated knowledge is the map that knows it is a map. It is neither of the two failures that the map–territory problem invites. It is not the god-trick of the master framework, claiming to picture the whole from outside. And it is not the relativism that, having noticed that all perspectives are partial, concludes that all maps are therefore worthless and should be abandoned. Haraway is sharp about why relativism is no improvement on the god-trick:

Relativism is a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally. The ‘equality’ of positioning is a denial of responsibility and of critical enquiry.Donna Haraway, Situated Knowledges (1988)

Relativism and the god-trick are mirror images — both are refusals of location, and therefore both are refusals of accountability. The situated map is the third thing. It is partial, located and answerable. It knows its own edges. It knows what it foregrounds and what it pushes into shadow. And — this is the part that matters most — it is therefore genuinely open to revision when what it cannot see makes itself felt. Haraway’s further and more radical claim is that the partial perspective is not merely the humble option but the epistemologically productive one. The view from somewhere generates knowledge that can act, because it is generated from within the relations it describes and remains entangled with them.

Mowles’ inside-out thinking, at its best, is an attempt to produce situated knowledge in exactly Haraway’s sense. A group that attends to its own local patterns of relating, that treats its own conversation as the material of inquiry, is not claiming a view from nowhere. It is claiming a view from here: from inside this configuration of relationships, with this relational history, in this moment. The Foulkesian hypothesis that such a group is a microcosm of wider social dynamics is itself a situated claim — not a universal law, but a wager whose validity is tested through what the group actually finds. This is why the Stacey Matrix is defensible read one way and indefensible read another. As a grid applied from outside — locate yourself on the axes of certainty and agreement — it is the god-trick in miniature: the manager standing outside their own complexity to diagnose it. As a structure through which the practitioner’s own experienced situation presents itself, it is a situated map: the report of someone who says “this situation presents itself to me as uncertain,” and who knows that the sentence is a confession of location, not a measurement of a system.

Part ThreeThe Territory Is Practice

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M9 gesture–responseM10 meshwork

Meaning as use is Mead's gesture–response seen from the side of language. A framework, like a gesture, means what the response to it makes of it.

3.1Wittgenstein’s Two Pictures

Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote two philosophies, and the relation between them is the relation at the centre of this paper. The early Wittgenstein of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) proposed what is now called the picture theory of meaning: a proposition is meaningful because it pictures a possible state of affairs, sharing a logical form with the fact it represents. Language, on this account, is a map; meaning is structural correspondence between proposition and world. It is, almost exactly, Korzybski’s cartography stated as a theory of language.

The later Wittgenstein of the Philosophical Investigations (1953) dismantled the picture theory — his own — with patient and devastating care, and replaced it with something that the organisational literature has borrowed in fragments and never fully absorbed. Meaning, the later Wittgenstein argues, is not picturing. Meaning is use.

For a large class of cases of the employment of the word ‘meaning’ — though not for all — this word can be explained in this way: the meaning of a word is its use in the language.Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (1953), §43

A word does not mean by corresponding to an object. It means by the part it plays in a shared, rule-governed, embodied human activity — what Wittgenstein calls a language-game. And a language-game is intelligible only against the background of a form of life: the whole interwoven fabric of practices, habitual responses, shared judgements and cultural understandings within which the game is played. “To imagine a language,” he wrote, “is to imagine a form of life.” “What has to be accepted, the given, is — one might say — forms of life.”

Wittgenstein also saw, with unusual clarity, why the earlier picture had been so hard to escape — and his diagnosis is the exact diagnosis this paper gave, in Part One, of the hyperreal map:

A picture held us captive. And we could not get outside it, for it lay in our language, and language seemed to repeat it to us inexorably.Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (1953), §115

The picture that held the early Wittgenstein captive was the picture theory itself — the map mistaken for the structure of the world, lying so deep in the language that the language kept handing it back. This is Baudrillard’s precession of simulacra and Korzybski’s unburst abstraction, restated as the predicament of a philosopher trapped inside his own framework. Wittgenstein’s later work is the long, patient labour of getting outside the picture — and his name for the philosophical work that does it is worth holding onto: “philosophy,” he wrote, “is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language.”

3.2From Correspondence to Participation

This is not a theory of language only. It is an epistemological revolution, and the revolution can be stated in a sentence: it is the shift from a picture of knowledge as correspondence — map matched to territory — to a picture of knowledge as participation in a form of life. To know is not, fundamentally, to hold an accurate inner representation of an outer world. It is to be a competent participant in the practices through which a community establishes what counts as evidence, what counts as a sound move, what counts as an appropriate response.

For organisational complexity thinking this carries an implication that has not been drawn out with enough force. The territory the practitioner is trying to map is not a fixed reality lying in wait, prior to and independent of all maps. The territory is a form of life — a set of interlaced practices, habitual responses and enacted routines that constitute organisational existence. The territory is the practice. And the practice is always already shaped by the frameworks through which it is conducted, communicated and made sense of.

Here Wittgenstein and Baudrillard meet, and Wittgenstein explains what Baudrillard only describes. The precession of simulacra — the map coming to precede the territory — is not a peculiar pathology of late capitalism. It is the ordinary condition of meaning, seen from inside the workshop where meaning is made. The Kotter framework does not merely represent change dynamics; it organises the language-game of change management, fixing what shall count as a step, what shall count as success, what shall count as resistance. Those who have learned to play the Kotter game inhabit a different form of life from those who have not, and the difference is not a difference of vocabulary only. It is a difference in what they are able to see, because seeing, for the later Wittgenstein, is already shot through with the grammar of the practices one has been trained into.

3.3Commanding a Clear View

The implication appears, at first, to be a counsel of imprisonment. If meaning is use, and use is governed by the grammar of a form of life, and one cannot step outside one’s form of life to inspect it from a neutral vantage — then the practitioner seems trapped inside the language-games they have inherited, with no leverage for change. This is where the later Wittgenstein’s gift becomes precise, and where he parts company decisively from Mowles’ via negativa.

Wittgenstein does not offer escape. He offers something more demanding and more useful: the capacity for what he called an übersichtliche Darstellung — a perspicuous, surveyable representation — the capacity to “command a clear view of the use of our words.” One cannot leave the language-game. But one can learn to see the game as a game: to notice the moves one is making, to feel the grammar one is obeying, to hold the rules with the lightness of a player who knows they are rules rather than the weight of someone who takes them for the iron furniture of reality.

This is not the via negativa’s stripping-away of frameworks until nothing remains. It is the harder discipline of being inside the framework and aware of it at the same time — inhabiting the form of life fully while retaining the reflexive distance that makes revision possible. The framework is not abandoned; it is played consciously. And the capacity to play a structured activity with full awareness of its grammar, while remaining genuinely responsive to what the moment offers, is not an abstraction. It is the specific, trainable, embodied competence of the skilled improviser. Wittgenstein, who never used the word, described the improviser’s mind exactly: a man walking backwards, who sees the form of what has been done and pays attention not to a planned future but to the next move the game makes available.

Part FourThe Body That Knows

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M32 sentienceM33 sagacity

The body that knows is Snowden's sentience and the Mariner's sagacity, the hunting dog's nose before the story. Merleau-Ponty's primacy of perception is the philosophical ground of Book I's claim that acumen is not a cognitive process running on neutral hardware.

4.1Merleau-Ponty and the Primacy of Perception

If the territory is a form of life and knowing is participation, then knowing cannot be a purely intellectual affair conducted in the head. It must be carried, at least in part, by the body. This is the contribution of Maurice Merleau-Ponty, whose Phenomenology of Perception (1945) is the most thorough account available of how a body knows a world before the mind has formed a proposition about it.

Merleau-Ponty’s quarrel is with two opposed errors that nonetheless share a prejudice. Empiricism treats perception as the passive reception of sensory data, the body a camera feeding pictures to a brain. Intellectualism treats perception as the mind’s active imposition of order onto chaos, the body a mere occasion for judgement. Both, Merleau-Ponty argues, presuppose a fully determinate objective world lying ready-made, and then try to explain consciousness as either its effect or its spectator. Against both he asserts the primacy of perception: that our basic, founding relation to the world is a pre-reflective, embodied engagement that precedes and grounds all reflection, all science, all explicit theory.

The key concept is the lived body — le corps propre — sharply distinguished from the objective body studied by anatomy. The objective hand is a mass of bone and tissue. The lived hand is a repertoire of powers: the ability to grasp, point, reach, steady, with what Merleau-Ponty calls motor intentionality — a directedness toward action that needs no explicit mental command. The skilled driver, the pianist, the dancer, he writes, know the world “not through maps or syllogisms, but through their limbs.” Before we think about the cup, the hand already knows how to receive it. Merleau-Ponty’s compressed formulation has become the motto of the whole position:

The body is our general medium for having a world.Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Phenomenology of Perception (1945)

This pre-reflective bodily knowing, Merleau-Ponty insists, “is the foundation of all thought.” And he was withering about the alternative — the stance of the detached intellect that builds models and mistakes them for the world. His description of that stance is, almost word for word, a description of the cartographic reflex:

Science manipulates things and gives up living in them. It makes its own limited models of things, and, operating upon these indices, comes face to face with the real world only at rare intervals.Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Eye and Mind (1964)

To give up living in things in order to manipulate models of them: that is the exact gesture this paper has been tracking since Korzybski. Merleau-Ponty’s corrective is not to abolish the model but to remember that it is built on, and answerable to, a prior and richer bodily inhabitation of the world — what he called, simply, our anchorage. “Our body,” he wrote, “is not in space like things; it inhabits or haunts space.”

4.2Palpation: Knowing by Pressing Back

The Chaos Puzzles essay — reproduced as this volume’s companion — gave this embodied knowing a name borrowed from clinical medicine — palpation — and the name is worth holding onto, because it captures something the word “perception” does not. To palpate is not merely to receive. It is to press, and to read the territory by the quality of its pressing back. The physician’s hands on the abdomen feel for the liver’s edge, the unexpected mass; the diagnosis emerges from the contact itself, in advance of any diagram, distributed across a history of trained encounter that the physician’s conscious mind has not yet caught up with.

Palpation is a two-way transaction, and this is its decisive feature for organisational practice. The practitioner who enters a group does not scan it as a detached instrument scans a sample. They press into the field and read what presses back — and their pressing is itself felt by the field, alters it, contributes to it. There is no palpation that does not also leave a fingerprint. The Stalker in Tarkovsky’s film does not merely read the Zone; the Zone, the film insists, reads the Stalker. The quality of the encounter depends on what both parties bring. This is the embodied form of Haraway’s situated knowledge: the knower is in the picture, touching and touched, and the knowledge produced is the knowledge of a contact, not the knowledge of a spectator.

4.3Deleuze and Guattari: Smooth Space and the Haptic

Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, in the fourteenth plateau of A Thousand Plateaus (1980), give this embodied, contact-based knowing its most developed conceptual geography. They distinguish two kinds of space, and the distinction maps with uncanny exactness onto the two relations to the map this paper is tracing.

Striated space is gridded, metric, organised, optical. It is the space of the settled, the measured, the administered — the space seen from above and from a distance, structured by a central perspective, parcelled into the homogeneous units that allow comparison and control. Smooth space is its other: open, intensive, vectorial, haptic. It is the space of the desert, the steppe, the ice, the sea — a space, as Deleuze and Guattari put it, whose “orientations, landmarks, and linkages are in continuous variation,” a space “occupied by intensities and events” rather than carved into measured forms.

Smooth space is a field without conduits or channels. It is haptic rather than optic — a close-range vision, as distinguished from a long-distance vision. One is occupied by points and the other by lines; one is striated and the other smooth.Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1980)

The crucial term is haptic. Deleuze and Guattari draw it from the art historian Alois Riegl: haptic vision is a seeing that functions like touch, a close-range engagement in which the eye does not survey from a distance but feels its way across a surface, point by point, with no fixed perspective and no invariant scale. Striated space is navigated by the map and the compass — instruments that pre-exist the journey. Smooth space is navigated by the nomad, who has no instruments transcending the territory and must read orientations immanent to it, as they change with the vegetation, the wind, the ice. Their celebrated emblem is the contrast between two games: chess, whose pieces have fixed identities and move across a gridded, striated board, against Go, whose identical stones acquire their value purely from position and relation, played across a smooth field of pure exteriority.

Mowles’ cartographic reflex is the compulsion to striate — to grid the organisational field in advance so it can be surveyed and administered from a distance. The practice this paper is reaching for is the capacity to move in smooth space: to navigate by haptic, close-range, immanent reading of a territory whose landmarks will not hold still. But — and this is the point at which Deleuze and Guattari are more useful than a simple preference for the smooth would allow — they insist the two spaces exist only in mixture, passing constantly into one another. “Smooth space is constantly being translated, transversed into striated space; striated space is constantly being reversed, returned to a smooth space.” The nomad does not abolish the map. The practitioner does not abolish the framework. The living map is precisely the disciplined passage between the two — striating just enough to orient, smoothing just enough to feel — which is the geography, in Deleuze and Guattari’s own vocabulary, of improvisation.

Two further Deleuzian formulations belong here, because each names something the synthesis will need. The first concerns the body. Deleuze, reading Spinoza, made a deceptively simple claim into what he called “practically a war cry”:

We know nothing about a body until we know what it can do — what its affects are, how they can or cannot enter into composition with the affects of another body.Gilles Deleuze & Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1980)

To know a body — a person, a group, an organisation — is not to hold an accurate picture of what it is, but to have felt what it can do: its capacities, its thresholds, the compositions it can and cannot enter. This is knowledge by palpation, raised to a principle, and it cannot be obtained from outside or in advance. The second formulation concerns the little word that will become decisive in Part Seven. Deleuze prized, in Spinoza, the means of “thinking with AND rather than thinking for IS” — of replacing the verb of essence and identity, which fixes and striates, with the conjunction of relation and addition, which connects and keeps open. When Ralph Stacey and Chris Rodgers insist, later in this paper, that the practitioner must hold “both ‘ands’ at the same time,” they are — without naming him — making Deleuze’s move: choosing the AND of living relation over the IS of fixed abstraction.

4.4Bohm: Thought, Participation and the Implicate Order

One more thinker is needed to complete the foundation, because the embodied knowing described so far is still largely individual, and organisations are not individuals. David Bohm — the theoretical physicist who, late in his life, turned from quantum theory to the nature of thought and dialogue — supplies the collective dimension.

Bohm’s first relevant claim is that thought is not the private possession of individuals but a largely collective, largely tacit process. “Thought,” he wrote, “is a system. That system not only includes thoughts and feelings, but it includes the state of the body; it includes the whole of society.” Most of our thoughts, he observed, are not ours; they are inherited, collective representations into which each of us makes only a small contribution and which very few of us ever change very much. And much of what passes for thinking is not thinking at all — Bohm put the point with a bluntness worth quoting:

A great many people think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices.David Bohm

Thought, moreover, is reflexive in a way it conceals from itself: it produces results and then, forgetting its own authorship, perceives those results as independent realities — which is precisely Baudrillard’s precession of simulacra restated as a fact about cognition.

Bohm’s second relevant claim is the implicate order: beneath the explicate order of separate, observable, stable forms lies an enfolded order of undivided movement — the holomovement — from which the explicate forms continuously unfold and into which they enfold again. “What we observe as stable structure,” the idea runs, is always the temporary crystallisation of a deeper, enfolded, ceaseless movement. The organisational chart, the strategy deck, the culture-survey result, the matrix on the whiteboard — each is an explicate freeze of an implicate flow that none of them captures.

From these two claims Bohm derived a practice — dialogue — and the practice is improvisation’s nearest cousin in the literature of collective inquiry. Bohmian dialogue is not debate, not negotiation, not the contest of opinions. Its discipline is the suspension of assumptions: holding one’s own thought up where it, and others, can look at it, without defending it and without suppressing it. “If we can all suspend our assumptions,” Bohm wrote, “and simply listen and watch and let them be, and observe what they mean — then we may be able to move more freely.”

In dialogue each person does not attempt to make common certain ideas or items of information that are already known to him. Rather, it may be said that two people are making something in common, creating something new together. Out of creating a larger field of more coherent shared meaning, truly new and penetrating understandings may emerge, often unexpectedly.David Bohm, On Dialogue (1996)

“Making something in common, creating something new together” — this is, word for word, a description of improvisation. Bohm gives the complex responsive process tradition its philosophy of collective thought: a group palpating its own implicate order, suspending the explicate certainties long enough for what is enfolded to unfold. He was precise, too, about where genuine understanding comes from, and where it does not: “Truth does not emerge from opinions,” he wrote; “it must emerge from something else — perhaps from a freer movement of this tacit mind.” And he names the failure mode exactly. A group that cannot suspend its assumptions has each member defending a different content, fighting or deflecting the assumptions of the others; a group that can do so begins to share a content, and “that thought,” Bohm noted, “is probably latent in the group as a whole, implicit.” Improvisation, in the chapters that follow, will turn out to be the trainable, embodied grammar of exactly this suspension.

Part FiveThe Gentle Art of Re-Perceiving

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M26 order effectsM24 Pyxis

Wack's re-perceiving is a change of measurement basis. Scenarios did not predict the oil shock; they rotated the managers' attention so that the shock was salient when it came, as question order rotates a respondent.

5.1From Forecasting to Re-Perceiving

The philosophical foundation is now laid: the territory is a form of life, the map is an honest partiality, knowing is embodied palpation, and collective inquiry is the suspension of assumptions in dialogue. The next two parts turn from philosophy to the practical traditions that have, often without naming their philosophy, worked out how to act on these terms. The first, and the older, is the discipline of scenario thinking, and its decisive figure is Pierre Wack.

Wack — a French intellectual of unusual range, a student of mysticism and gardens as much as of economics — led the scenario team at Royal Dutch/Shell through the 1970s. He is remembered, in the conventional telling, as the man whose scenarios allowed Shell to perceive the 1973 oil shock before it struck, and then a second shock after it. But Wack himself was impatient with that telling, because it mistook the achievement. The scenarios had not predicted the future. Their value lay elsewhere, and naming where became the work of his unpublished 1984 Harvard manuscript and his two celebrated 1985 Harvard Business Review papers.

Wack drew a sharp line between forecasting and what he called re-perceiving. A forecast tries to get the future right. It is a map asserted in advance of the territory, and — because the future of any genuinely complex system cannot be derived from its present — it is almost always wrong, and wrong in ways that are most dangerous precisely when it is trusted most. A scenario, in Wack’s hands, does something categorically different. It does not compete to describe the future more accurately. It works on the perceiver.

5.2The Microcosm and the Predetermined

The true object of scenario work, Wack insisted, is not the future at all. It is what he called the manager’s microcosm — the inner model, usually tacit and usually unexamined, of how the business world works. Strategists do not act on the world; they act on their picture of the world. And the picture, once formed, becomes self-confirming: it determines what counts as a signal and what is dismissed as noise, what is seen and what is structurally invisible. This is, in the vocabulary of this paper, the hyperreal map of Part One and the form of life of Part Three, observed inside the head of a single decision-maker.

Scenarios succeed, on Wack’s account, not when they forecast but when they re-perceive — when they break the grip of the existing microcosm and let the strategist see something that was always present and had been rendered invisible by the map through which they had been looking. The decisive event of good scenario work is not a more accurate prediction. It is a change in the perceiver: the moment the manager’s inner model is loosened enough that the present itself looks different. Wack’s phrase for the whole discipline is the one this part takes as its title — the gentle art of re-perceiving — and the gentleness is not incidental. A microcosm cannot be demolished by assertion; a frontal attack on someone’s map only hardens it. It can only be loosened, gently, by an experience that the existing map cannot quite contain.

Wack paired this with a second discipline that has been widely misunderstood. He insisted on the rigorous identification of predetermined elements — the features of the situation that are, for the relevant horizon, genuinely settled: demographic facts, infrastructure already built, consequences already in train — and on separating them with great care from the genuine, irreducible uncertainties. This is not a retreat into prediction. It is the disciplined striation that makes smooth navigation possible. The practitioner who has distinguished the predetermined from the uncertain has just enough orientation to move, and has cleared the genuine open field where the real improvisation must happen. It is precisely the move Part Four found in Deleuze and Guattari: striate enough to orient, and no more, so that the smooth space remains genuinely open to be felt.

5.3Conversations with Remarkable People

The third of Wack’s practices is the one the Rodgers document explicitly invokes, and it is the practice that most directly anticipates this paper’s synthesis. Wack made a deliberate discipline of seeking out conversations with what he and his colleagues called remarkable people — individuals chosen, and sought out at some effort, from beyond the organisation’s normal spheres of engagement. Not the usual experts, not the recognised authorities in the firm’s own field, but people whose vantage was genuinely other: a person who saw the situation from somewhere the organisation’s own form of life could not reach.

The logic of the practice is exact, and it can be stated in the vocabulary already built. A microcosm cannot re-perceive itself from inside. A form of life cannot, by its own resources, generate the offers that would disturb it, because what it can generate is precisely what its grammar already permits. Re-perceiving requires an offer from outside the language-game — a contribution the existing map has no slot for, made by someone standing somewhere the organisation does not stand. Wack understood, decades before the vocabulary of offers and situated knowledge existed, that the strategist’s task is less to compute the future than to remain genuinely, deliberately, structurally susceptible to being surprised by the present — and that this susceptibility must be engineered, because a settled organisation will not stumble into it by chance.

Wack’s three practices, taken together, form a complete miniature of the living map. The microcosm is the map that must be held as a map. Re-perceiving is the disciplined loosening of that map by an experience it cannot contain. The predetermined elements are the minimal, honest striation that makes orientation possible without foreclosing the open field. And the remarkable people are the deliberate cultivation of offers from outside the form of life. Scenario thinking, read through Wack rather than through the proceduralised industry it later became, is not a forecasting technique at all. It is a discipline of re-perception — and re-perception, this paper will argue through its remaining parts, is what improvisation does, moment by moment, in the room.

Part SixThe Offer

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M35 the script as offerM36 representation

Johnstone's offer meets the flash mob's script: both are scores that bodies accept, advance or block. Status that cannot be abolished is the seed of Hobbes's representation: someone always ends up speaking for the scene.

Altius Status as a dynamical variable

Keith Johnstone's status work has an empirical counterpart in the study of dominance hierarchies, where status signals are exchanged in milliseconds through posture, gaze and voice. Tiedens and Fragale (2003) found that people tend to complement rather than mimic dominance displays: high status elicits low and vice versa. Johnstone's see-saw is that complementarity. It implies that a facilitator cannot lower the room's status by lowering their own alone; the room will rise to complement. Conscious status play means choosing the pairing, not abolishing the game.

6.1Johnstone: Improvisation as Ontology

Keith Johnstone’s Impro: Improvisation and the Theatre (1979) is one of the most penetrating books ever written about how human beings generate meaning together in real time, and it appears on almost no organisational complexity reading list. The omission is itself instructive — a small demonstration of Wittgenstein’s point that a form of life sees what its grammar equips it to see. The complexity field has its authorised canon, its recognisable genre; Johnstone, writing about status and spontaneity and masks from inside the practice of theatre, does not look like complexity theory from outside the game. From inside the game — inside the lived attempt to be genuinely present to another person without a script — his work is not adjacent to complexity theory. It is complexity theory, reported by a practitioner.

Johnstone’s foundational concept is the offer. An offer, in his vocabulary, is anything a partner does — and the breadth of the definition is the substance of it. An offer is not merely a verbal proposal. It is a glance, a posture, a hesitation, a chosen word, an unexpected silence. The environment makes offers. The history between two people makes offers. The mood of the room makes offers. The skilled improviser is, before anything else, someone who has trained the capacity to receive offers — to register what is actually being given, in its full particularity, rather than overwriting it with what they had planned or expected.

Good improvisers seem telepathic; everything looks pre-arranged. This is because they accept all offers made — which is something no ‘normal’ person would do.Keith Johnstone, Impro (1979)

The apparent telepathy is the whole point. What looks, from outside, like prearrangement is in fact the disciplined, total acceptance of whatever the situation gives. Johnstone pressed the discipline further still, into a counsel that sounds paradoxical and is in fact exact: “I tell my actors,” he wrote, “never to think up an offer, but instead to assume that one has already been made.” The improviser does not generate material from inside their own head; they turn outward, treat the situation as already brimming with offers, and respond. This is the precise opposite of the cartographic reflex, which turns inward to the framework and reads the situation through it.

This is Deleuzian palpation in the vocabulary of the theatre. It is Wack’s susceptibility to being surprised by the present. It is Bohm’s listening that suspends the assumption. And Johnstone’s account of what blocks it is equally precise. He observed that ordinary education and ordinary social life systematically train spontaneity out of us.

There are people who prefer to say ‘Yes’, and there are people who prefer to say ‘No’. Those who say ‘Yes’ are rewarded by the adventures they have, and those who say ‘No’ are rewarded by the safety they attain. There are far more ‘No’ sayers around than ‘Yes’ sayers, but you can train one type to behave like the other.Keith Johnstone, Impro (1979)

6.2Yes, And: The Epistemology of Acceptance and Advance

Johnstone’s most famous principle — usually compressed to the slogan “yes, and” — is routinely flattened into a motivational nostrum about being positive in meetings. Its actual epistemological content is far more demanding, and far more useful. The “yes” is the act of accepting the offer on its own terms, before one knows what one will do with it. The “and” is the act of advancing from what has been accepted — contributing one’s own offer in response. The sequence is not “accept, then deliberate, then respond.” It is accept-and-respond in a single movement, which is only possible if the response grows out of the acceptance rather than being retrieved from a plan held in reserve.

Johnstone’s contrasting term is the block. To block is to refuse the offer — “No, that isn’t a spaceship, it’s a chair” — and Johnstone identifies blocking as the single most common way groups suppress their own creative intelligence.

In life most of us are highly skilled at suppressing action. Bad improvisers block action, often with a high degree of skill. Good improvisers develop action.Keith Johnstone, Impro (1979)

The blocker is rarely consciously hostile. More often they are simply executing the grammar of their existing form of life, which has no slot for what has just been offered. This is exactly Kevin Flinn’s borrowed certainties, and exactly Carl Rogers’ introjected value systems: the inherited frameworks that pre-empt the acceptance of any offer inconsistent with the self-structure already in place. Mowles’ inside-out method reduces blocking by reducing the pressure of the existing structure — free association, no agenda, the group attending to its own spontaneous productions. But, as Flinn warns, removing the block is not the same as installing the skill. The via negativa clears the ground; it does not, by itself, teach the positive competence of genuine reception. That competence is what improvisation, practised seriously, builds: not merely the absence of defensive blocking, but the trained capacity to take what is offered, on its own terms, before knowing what can be made of it — and then to find what can be made.

It is worth correcting, here, the most common misunderstanding of “yes, and” — the belief that it is about the words, that one must literally avoid saying “no” or “but.” The improviser and business teacher Neil Mullarkey, who co-founded the Comedy Store Players and has spent decades carrying improvisation into organisations, is emphatic that this is a category error. The principle, he insists, has nothing to do with the actual words used; it is about accepting an offer and adding to its value — and one can do that while saying “no,” “but,” “maybe,” anything at all. A facilitator who has trained their team to swap “yes, but” for “yes, and” while still, underneath, blocking every offer has changed the vocabulary and changed nothing. “Yes, and” is a stance toward the offer, not a script for the sentence. This is the difference, once again, between holding the framework as a living instrument and holding it as a hollow form.

The reconciliation of cartography and improvisation now comes clearly into view, and it is not additive. It is not “draw the map first, then improvise around its edges.” It is simultaneous: hold the map loosely enough that an offer contradicting it can still be received, and hold the conversation openly enough that what has been mapped can be revised, in real time, by what the territory gives. The framework is not the enemy of the offer. The framework, deployed rightly, is itself an offer — a move made into the room to see what the room does with it.

6.3Status: The Furniture That Cannot Be Removed

Johnstone’s second great contribution is his analysis of status, and it bears directly on every facilitated process the complexity tradition has ever convened. Status, for Johnstone, is not a fixed property of persons or roles. It is something done — enacted, moment by moment, in every interaction, through posture, eye contact, the length and confidence of sentences, the tolerance or avoidance of silence, the small physical adjustments by which people raise and lower themselves relative to one another. “I should really talk about dominance and submission,” Johnstone wrote, “but these words are too sexy. I prefer the more neutral terms status and the playing of status.” Status, in his account, is read in the smallest physical signals:

Breaking eye contact can be high status so long as you don’t immediately glance back; if you ignore someone your status rises, if you feel impelled to look back then it falls. Thus dark glasses raise status, because we can’t see the submission of the eyes.Keith Johnstone, Impro (1979)

The point is not the eye contact as such; it is that status is unceasing, granular and physical, transmitted below the threshold of what most participants consciously notice. Johnstone made a further claim that should unsettle any facilitator: that the texture of a life is, in part, a status outcome. “Everyone,” he observed, “chooses more or less what kind of events will happen to them by their conscious patterns of blocking and yielding.” Blocking and yielding are status moves. A group’s whole climate — who speaks, who is heard, what may be offered — is the aggregate of thousands of such moves, and they do not stop because the facilitator wishes them to.

The organisational relevance is considerable and almost entirely uninvestigated. The Stacey Matrix, deployed in the ordinary consulting manner — the consultant places the framework before the group and invites them to locate themselves on it — is a high-status move: its very form positions the consultant as the holder of the organising concepts and the group as the located object. Mowles’ inside-out method tries to interrupt this: no imposed framework, free association, the group as the source rather than the recipient of organising concepts. But Johnstone sees what the inside-out account does not quite say aloud. Attempting to flatten status is itself a status move. The facilitator who announces “there is no hierarchy here” is making a high-status offer — using the authority of the facilitator’s role to declare that authority is suspended. The declaration does something; but what it does is read by the group as a status act, whatever its content claims.

The skilled improviser knows that status games cannot be switched off, only played with greater or lesser awareness. The discipline is not to abolish status dynamics but to become conscious of them — to be able to raise and lower one’s own status deliberately, to be high-status when the group needs a strong offer it must receive, low-status when it needs space and the modelled vulnerability of genuine not-knowing. This is precisely what Flinn describes as the facilitator’s “real-time, continuously calibrated intervention,” and it is what makes the difference between a facilitator executing a method and a facilitator genuinely present to the room.

6.4Larsen, Barrett, Weick: Improvisation Enters the Organisation

Johnstone wrote about the theatre. Three bodies of work carried his insight into the study of organisations, and each adds a piece the synthesis needs.

Henry Larsen — associated with the Dacapo Theatre and the Doctor of Management programme at the University of Hertfordshire, the same Hexford-centred tradition that produced Stacey, Mowles and Flinn — wrote his 2005 doctoral thesis, Spontaneity and Power, on theatre improvisation as a process of organisational change. Larsen’s decisive move was to link improvisation explicitly to the complex responsive process account of human interaction, and to introduce the concept of invitations:

By invitations we mean conscious or unconscious moves that encourage the involved people to take spontaneous moves together in a mutually improvised context.Henry Larsen & Marcel Bogers, on the role of improvisation in innovation

Invitation is Larsen’s word for the offer, theorised for organisational life. And his account of spontaneity is exact, and quietly radical: “One finds oneself in spontaneous activity,” he writes, “when one becomes unsure of the response the other will take to one’s gesture.” Spontaneity, on this account, is not the absence of structure, and not a personality trait. It is the live, uncertain, mutually improvised quality of genuine responsiveness — the state of not yet knowing how one’s gesture will land — and it is inseparable from power, because every gesture into uncertainty is also a move in a relationship of dependency.

Frank Barrett — a management scholar and working jazz pianist — gave the improvisation literature its most useful organisational vocabulary in Yes to the Mess: Surprising Leadership Lessons from Jazz (2012). Two of his concepts are indispensable here. The first is provocative competence: the deliberate act, by a leader or facilitator, of disrupting habit and pushing a group past its comfortable routines into the productive discomfort where genuine learning happens — Miles Davis tuning his band to unfamiliar territory so that they could not fall back on what they already knew. It is, as Barrett puts it, the leader’s job to create the discrepancy and dissonance that triggers people to move away from habitual patterns. The second is the principle of minimal structure, maximal autonomy: the recognition that improvisation is not the absence of structure but the presence of just enough — a chord progression, a tempo, a set of conventions — to make freedom navigable. Barrett’s jazz musician is not the opposite of the cartographer. The jazz musician is the cartographer who has learned to hold the chart so lightly, and has so thoroughly internalised its grammar, that the chart becomes a platform for invention rather than a cage. “Improvisation,” as the jazz scholar Paul Berliner put it in a line Barrett and Weick both prize, “involves reworking precomposed material and designs in relation to unanticipated ideas conceived, shaped, and transformed under the special conditions of performance.” Barrett is candid, too, about what the stance costs:

You say yes to the mess by surrendering control — by opening yourself up to the capriciousness of the crowd, with no guarantee of success for your efforts. Ultimately, that takes one quality above all others: courage.Frank J. Barrett, Yes to the Mess (2012)

Surrendering control without a guarantee of success is precisely what the cartographic reflex exists to avoid; the framework promises the guarantee. Barrett’s point is that the guarantee is false, and that the courage to proceed without it — to treat leadership, in his words, not as the rational sifting of data toward a predicted future but as pragmatic experimentation — is the actual competence that complex conditions demand.

Karl Weick — the organisational theorist of sensemaking — supplies the analytic frame and the cautionary tale. Weick’s account of organising treats it not as architecture but as a continuous, improvised, retrospective process: we act, and then we make sense of what we have done, and the sense we make shapes the next action. “How can I know what I think,” runs his most quoted line, “until I see what I say?” The reflexive twist in his account is the part that matters most for this paper:

People make sense of things by seeing a world on which they have already imposed what they believe. In other words, people discover their own inventions.Karl E. Weick, Sensemaking in Organizations (1995)

To discover one’s own inventions is the precise experience of the practitioner who finds, in the territory, exactly the pattern their framework taught them to look for — and mistakes the finding for confirmation. Weick’s celebrated and contested analysis of the 1949 Mann Gulch fire disaster — in which thirteen smokejumpers died — describes a “collapse of sensemaking”: when the situation outran every map the crew possessed, and their training offered no script, the organisation dissolved, role structure disintegrated, and most of the crew, unable to drop the heavy tools that their now-useless map told them to carry, ran and died. The foreman who survived, Wagner Dodge, survived by an improvised act for which no map existed — lighting an escape fire and lying down in its ashes. Weick drew from this four sources of organisational resilience, and the first is improvisation itself. But the Mann Gulch case also delivers a warning this paper must heed: improvisation is not a guarantee, and the romance of pure spontaneity is dangerous. Dodge improvised successfully because he had decades of fire behind him — accumulated, embodied, palpative knowledge. Improvisation without that depth is not freedom; it is panic. The living map is drawn by someone who has earned the right to draw it.
