Part SevenBoth ‘Ands’

Rodgers and the Immersion–Abstraction Paradox

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M29 destruction and creationLiber II, Part 17

Immersing and abstracting at once is Boyd's cycle in its stillest form: every abstraction partly destroys the immersion it came from, and every immersion breaks the abstraction it was carrying.

Altius Abstraction as compression

Immersing and abstracting can be read through Book I's Movement 11′: abstraction is compression, keeping the stiff directions of experience and discarding the sloppy ones. Stacey's Type 2 abstraction is aggressive compression into a few parameters; Type 1 keeps more of the history in narrative. Rodgers's dissent becomes measurable: a framework is useful when its compression keeps the directions that matter for the conversation at hand, and harmful when it discards them. The test is not abstract versus concrete but which information survives the compression.

7.1The Dissent Within the Tradition

Every synthesis needs a sceptic who belongs to the family it is trying to reconcile, and the complex responsive process tradition has one in Chris Rodgers. Rodgers writes from inside that tradition — his own work on informal coalitions is part of its literature — but on one matter he records, in his own words, “one of those very rare occasions” on which his perspective differs from Ralph Stacey’s. The disagreement is precisely about the map.

The common ground comes first, and it is the foundation of this entire part. Stacey, in Complexity and Organizational Reality, argues that abstraction is not the enemy of immersed, lived experience but its inseparable companion — that the two happen together, always, in every act of human sense-making:

Human thought has always, and quite obviously, been paradoxical acts of immersing and abstracting at the same time — people are simultaneously immersed in the experience of local interaction and abstracting from it at the same time.Ralph Stacey, Complexity and Organizational Reality, quoted by Chris Rodgers

Rodgers’ own diagram, reproduced above, states the paradox in a single image: the two great loops of immersion and abstraction are not sequential and not separable — they turn together, continuously, around the same lived centre, each feeding the other. Rodgers accepts this entirely. The immersion–abstraction paradox — the fact that we are never purely immersed and never purely abstracted, but always both at once — is, for both men, simply the truth of the human condition, and the foundation on which any honest account of practice must be built. The disagreement concerns what Stacey builds on it. Stacey distinguishes two kinds of abstraction. Type 1 abstraction, in his account, is the meaning that arises in “the simplifying, generalizing, elaborating and categorizing of experience in the form of narrative and philosophy,” with group dynamics at its core. Type 2 abstraction is “the deliberate operating on the categories of experience to construct models, based on more precise categorizing and measuring” — and Stacey associates Type 2 with the aim of “simplicity, standardization and uniformity, with the explicit intention being to exert some form of control.” In Stacey’s hands, the model-making of Type 2 abstraction is positioned as continuous with what he elsewhere calls the dominant management discourse: the complexity-denying machinery of prediction and control. Yet Stacey himself insists that both kinds of abstraction live in the same place — “it is in local interaction,” he writes, “that people perform acts of both first and second order abstraction, and it is in such local interaction that the meaning of these abstractions emerges.”

Rodgers’ dissent is quiet and consequential. Not all models, he insists, are rooted in the complexity-denying assumptions of Stacey’s Type 2 description. Many are — but the category is not destiny. A model — or, as Rodgers prefers to call it, a sense-making framework — can be designed and held in a way that is congruent with complexity rather than denying it. And if it can, then the wholesale suspicion of Type 2 abstraction throws away something the practitioner genuinely needs.

7.2The Framework Is Not the Problem

The pragmatic use of sense-making frameworks, as a way of abstracting meaningfully from the complex social reality of everyday life, is not the problem. Attributing a false sense of concreteness to them, or claiming their universal, context-free applicability, is.Chris Rodgers

This is the hinge of the whole paper, and it should be read slowly. Rodgers is not making a conservative case for the preservation of management orthodoxy — quite the reverse. It is the mainstream narratives, he insists, “with their accompanying ‘if you do this, you’ll get that’ certainties and linear, step-wise methodologies, that need to be de-bunked; not diagrams and sense-making frameworks as such.” He is making a case more demanding than Mowles’ via negativa. The instruction is not “reject the frameworks.” It is: hold the frameworks with the right kind of intelligence. The difference between a sense-making framework held as a situated, provisional, revisable instrument and the same framework held as a context-free, concrete prescription is not a difference in the framework. It is a difference in the practitioner — in their relation to their own tools, in whether they can use the map without mistaking it for the territory.

Here Rodgers reactivates Korzybski’s original insight with full precision. The question was never whether a map is useful — useful maps abound. The question is whether the mapper understands the relation between the map and the territory. A map held by someone who knows it is a map — partial, structured, foregrounding some things and shadowing others — is an instrument of orientation. The identical map held by someone who has forgotten it is a map is a hall of mirrors. Rodgers names the trap exactly: the error is “attributing a false sense of concreteness.” That is Baudrillard’s precession of simulacra stated as a practitioner’s warning. The hyperreal map is simply a framework whose false concreteness has been forgotten.

Rodgers is positive, not merely permissive, about what a well-held framework can do. A complexity-congruent framework, deployed with care, can — in his words — “potentially transform the nature and content of people’s ongoing participation,” facilitating “individual and collective sense-making in creative ways that are not consciously part of current experience, and which otherwise might not become apparent.” And he is realistic about where such work must begin. The appeal of a good framework, he notes, is partly that “it starts from where people typically are in their thinking and practice, rather than where we might like them to be” — given their constant exposure to mainstream, “do this and you’ll get that” prescriptions. The practitioner who refuses all frameworks on principle refuses, with them, the bridge from where people actually are.

Rodgers goes further, and his further step is where his work and the improvisation literature silently converge:

In all cases, it’s the conversations that flow from the use of the frameworks that are important, not the frameworks themselves. It is these that determine the meanings and actions that people make from their use — at that time, in that situation and in the specifics of that relationship.Chris Rodgers

The framework, in this account, is valuable not as a representation but as a provocation: a move that, deployed well, can — Rodgers writes — help managers “escape from unhelpful patterns of thinking, feeling and acting,” opening dialogue rather than closing it down, exposing taken-for-granted assumptions to challenge, and provoking “new insights and possibilities that might otherwise not be accessible.” The framework, for Rodgers, is an offer. He has arrived, by the pragmatic route, at Johnstone’s word.

7.3Set-Piece and Open Play

Rodgers adds one image that the synthesis needs and that the improvisation theorists, oddly, do not supply with the same clarity. He distinguishes the “set-piece” event from the “open play” of everyday interaction. Periodic, structured, group-wide gatherings — the workshop, the away-day, the facilitated intervention — are set-pieces. They matter, but they are not where organisational life mostly happens. The imaginative use of sense-making frameworks, Rodgers argues, can help “shift the focus of managers’ and others’ attention beyond periodic ‘set-piece’ events towards the ‘open play’ of everyday conversational interaction” — and it is in that open play, he insists, that organisations are actually made:

Through the widespread interplay of their small-group and one-to-one interactions — formal and informal, structured and unstructured — people are perpetually creating the future together. Every conversation is a co-creation forum.Chris Rodgers, drawing on The Wiggly World of Organization

What we think of as “the organization,” on this account, is continuously re-emerging in that ongoing interactional process — and, crucially, “the vast majority of these conversations,” Rodgers observes, “take place without the relevant manager being physically present.” Influencing the overall process of sense-making-cum-action-taking, he concludes, must therefore “go beyond the intensity of periodic, structured, group-wide interactions.”

This is a necessary corrective to a romance the improvisation literature can fall into — the romance of the brilliantly facilitated room. The living map is not drawn only, or even mainly, in the set-piece. It is drawn in the open play, in the thousands of unattended conversations through which the future is, in Rodgers’ phrase, perpetually being created together. The implication for practice is significant. The point of the well-improvised set-piece is not the set-piece. It is whether the quality of attention cultivated there — the capacity to receive offers, to suspend assumptions, to hold frameworks lightly — travels back into the open play and changes how people are with one another when no one is facilitating. A workshop that produces a peak experience and changes nothing in the open play has, in the vocabulary of the Chaos Puzzles paper reproduced as this volume’s companion, visited the Zone without undergoing it.

7.4Muddling Through as Mature Practice

Rodgers’ conclusion is the sentence this paper takes as its epigraph and its license. Viewing abstraction as either narrative-and-philosophy (good) or sense-making-frameworks (bad), he argues, “limits the possibilities available for shifting the patterning of people’s perspectives, practices and performance in organizationally beneficial and personally resonant ways.” The alternative is not to choose a side but to hold both:

If people are to ‘get to grips’ fully with organizational complexity, they need to use both ‘ands’ at the same time. From my viewpoint, we have no option but to muddle through the practical implications of the immersion-abstraction paradox.Chris Rodgers

Muddling through, taken seriously, is not a confession of failure. It is a description of competent practice in genuinely complex conditions. It is the disciplined refusal to resolve the immersion-abstraction paradox by amputating one of its poles. The practitioner who has decided, once and for all, that frameworks are bad and process is good has stopped muddling through and started reciting a doctrine — and a doctrine, however radical its content, is a Type 2 abstraction held with false concreteness. They have exchanged the living map for its simulacrum. To muddle through is to hold the paradox open: to abstract and immerse at once, to striate enough to orient and smooth enough to feel, to carry the map and let the territory redraw it. It is uncomfortable. It is theoretically untidy. It is, exactly, what this paper means by improvisation.

Chris Mowles, whose diagnosis of the cartographic reflex opened this paper, supplies its closing image of what muddling through actually feels like from inside — and it is, fittingly, an image of conversation rather than of mapping:

Organising is a continuous conversation which has no beginning and no end. It is often heated because our valuations matter to us: we cannot stand outside our commitments, although we only fully realise what they are through articulating them and encountering others’ difference. In struggling together as a community of inquiry, we discover how to take the next step, which may then give us a new perspective to keep going.Chris Mowles

“We cannot stand outside our commitments” — this is the via negativa’s own most honest sentence, and it concedes precisely what this paper has argued throughout: there is no view from nowhere, no exit from the territory, no map drawn from outside. But notice what Mowles puts in the place of the impossible external vantage. Not nothing — not the bare refusal of frameworks — but a conversational community, a community of inquiry, discovering the next step by articulating commitments and encountering difference. That is not the absence of method. It is the living map, described by the very thinker whose critique made it necessary. The next step is discovered, not derived; the new perspective is earned in the encounter, not imported from above. Mowles and Rodgers, the critic and the dissenter, end in the same place: improvisation, conducted as a community of inquiry, holding both ‘ands’ at once.

Part EightThe Trivium Recovered

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M34 three leversM33 wit and judgement

The trivium is a conjunction like Book I's levers and acumen: grammar, dialectic and rhetoric each fail alone. Rhetoric, the art of the offer, is close kin to Locke's wit; dialectic to judgement.

8.1Three Roads to Knowledge

The Rodgers document, in its final exchange, gestures toward a resource older than any so far considered: “the Medieval use of the trivium.” The gesture is worth following, because the trivium turns out to be an unexpectedly exact meta-map of the very problem this paper has been working — and a map drawn, suggestively, by a tradition that understood it to be a map.

The trivium — from the Latin tri-via, the place where three roads meet — was the first and foundational division of the seven liberal arts in the medieval curriculum: grammar, dialectic (or logic), and rhetoric. It is tempting, and not wrong, to read these three as the curriculum of language. But the medieval understanding was larger. Grammar was the art of knowledge — of the right ordering of what is given, the foundation and beginning of learning. Dialectic was the art of testing — of subjecting knowledge claims to scrutiny, contradiction and the discipline of reasoned argument. Rhetoric was the art of bringing thought to bear — of discovering and presenting it so that it could move another mind, “the adaptation of language to circumstance.”

The novelist and classicist Dorothy L. Sayers, in her 1947 Oxford lecture “The Lost Tools of Learning,” recovered the decisive point about what the trivium was for. It was not, she argued, a body of content to be memorised. It was a set of tools — and the distinction is the one this whole paper has been pressing:

The whole of the Trivium was intended to teach the pupil the proper use of the tools of learning, before he began to apply them to ‘subjects’ at all. The trivium is by its nature not learning, but a preparation for learning.Dorothy L. Sayers, The Lost Tools of Learning (1947)

A preparation for learning, not learning itself: this is exactly the status this paper has claimed for the living map. The grammar of offer and response, of situated mapping, of suspended assumption, is not a content to be applied but a readiness to be carried — a way of being equipped for whatever the territory turns out to give. The twelfth-century scholar John of Salisbury, in his Metalogicon, recorded the trivium’s other essential teaching: that the three arts are a unity, and that each, pursued alone, fails. “Dialectic,” he wrote, “if it be solitary, lies bloodless and sterile, nor can it fertilise the soul to bear the fruit of philosophy, if it conceive not from another.” Each art moderates the excesses of the others. Grammar without dialectic is the know-it-all hoarding facts; dialectic without grammar is sterile logic-chopping with nothing to chop; rhetoric without either is persuasion in the service of nothing. And — the detail that matters most — the trivium was never a solitary pursuit. Its three roads met at a crossroads, and the crossroads was public: a place of encounter.

8.2The Trivium as Map of the Synthesis

Set the trivium beside the three traditions this paper has been reconciling, and the correspondence is not forced; it is structural.

Reflexive cartography is the work of grammar. It is the art of the right ordering of what is given — the disciplined drawing of the map, the honest selection among differences, the situated knowledge that knows its own foundation. The cartographer who knows the map is a map is practising grammar in John of Salisbury’s full sense: providing knowledge while remaining answerable for how it was composed.

Immersive process is the work of dialectic. It is the art of testing — but testing understood as the complex responsive process tradition understands it, not as solitary logic but as the live, relational scrutiny of assumptions in the encounter with others’ difference. This is Bohm’s dialogue exactly; it is Stacey’s insistence that meaning is tested in local interaction; it is the group analytic session in which the borrowed certainties are subjected, painfully, to the contradiction of the room. Dialectic, the medievals knew, “cannot fertilise the soul if it conceive not from another” — which is to say, immersive process is barren without the encounter that the other two arts make possible.

Improvisation is the work of rhetoric — and here the recovery is most illuminating, because rhetoric has been the most maligned of the three arts, dismissed in the modern era as mere ornament or manipulation. The medieval understanding was otherwise. Rhetoric was “the adaptation of language to circumstance”: the art of bringing thought to bear on this audience, in this moment, in a form they can receive. That is the improviser’s art precisely. The offer is a rhetorical act in the oldest and most honourable sense — a move adapted to the living circumstance, made to land in this room, with these people, now. Johnstone’s “yes, and,” Larsen’s invitation, Wack’s conversation with remarkable people: all are rhetoric recovered as the art of timely, circumstantial, responsive contribution.

And the trivium’s deepest teaching is the one this paper has been arguing throughout: the three are a unity, and each alone fails. Cartography without process and improvisation is the hyperreal map — grammar hoarding its categories, mistaking them for the world. Process without cartography and improvisation is the magic roundabout — dialectic spinning, bloodless and sterile, testing and testing and never bearing fruit. Improvisation without cartography and process is panic at Mann Gulch — rhetoric unmoored from knowledge and untested by encounter, persuasion with no ground beneath it. The living map is the trivium restored: grammar, dialectic and rhetoric practised together, at the public crossroads where the three roads meet — which is to say, in the room, in the open play, in the conversation.

Part NineThe Living Map

The Synthesis Stated

❖ ❖ ❖
Woven · Book I M37 leverage compassM23 four laws

'The living map is drawn in the act of traversal' is the Pyxis Incerta's deepest rule restated: the compass reads only while one walks. Book I's leverage compass adds that the walker always walks among neighbours, in a leaning field.

Altius A grammar is generative

Calling the seven propositions a grammar rather than a framework has a precise sense in linguistics. A grammar is generative: a finite set of rules that produces an unbounded set of well-formed sentences, most never uttered before. A framework, by contrast, enumerates cases. The living map is generative in Chomsky's sense: its propositions do not list situations but produce appropriate moves in situations no one anticipated. That is why it can be drawn only in traversal: like speech, it exists in use.

The argument can now be drawn together. Improvisation, reflexive cartography and immersive process are not three approaches to be balanced, traded off, or sequenced. They are three aspects of one practice, and the practice has been falsely divided by a literature that inherited its divisions from the very cartographic reflex it set out to criticise. The name proposed for the undivided practice is the living map: a map drawn in the act of traversal.

What follows is not a framework. It has no quadrants, no steps, no diagnostic grid — to supply one would be to perform, at the close of an argument against false concreteness, an act of false concreteness. What follows is a grammar: a set of relations between moves that, taken together, describe what competent practitioners of genuine complexity engagement do when they are doing it well. It is stated as seven propositions.

Map and territory co-constitute each other.

Korzybski established that the map is not the territory. Baudrillard showed that, under modern conditions, the map comes to precede it. Wittgenstein revealed that the territory is itself a form of life, and that practice is always already shaped by the frameworks through which it is conducted. The synthesis of the three is that map and territory stand in a relation of mutual constitution. The map shapes how the territory is experienced and thereby shapes the territory; the territory — the embodied, relational, surprising encounter with what is — presses back on the map and thereby reshapes it. The practitioner who does not know this is trapped: either clutching a map that no longer fits, or stripped of all orientation. The practitioner who knows it is free to move between the two, using the map to orient the encounter and the encounter to revise the map, in real time, as the practice itself.

All perspectives are partial; partiality is not uselessness.

Haraway’s situated knowledge forecloses the god-trick — the master map that sees the whole from nowhere — without collapsing into the relativism that, having noticed all maps are partial, abandons mapping altogether. Every map is made from somewhere, by someone, with particular salience and particular blindness. The imperative is practical: know where your map was made, what it was built to illuminate, and what it structurally cannot see. The practitioner who holds a framework as a partial perspective can use it to see what would otherwise be invisible, without mistaking the visible for the total. The practitioner who holds it as the territory cannot be corrected by the territory, because they no longer register a distinction between the two.

Meaning is use; a framework has the meaning its use confers.

Wittgenstein dissolves the question of whether a framework is ‘true’ as a representation. The question becomes: what does the use of this framework, here, in this configuration of relationships, make possible? A framework that opens dialogue, exposes assumptions and creates room for the genuinely new is valuable not because it is accurate but because of what its use produces. A framework that closes dialogue, confirms borrowed certainties and manufactures the illusion of understanding is damaging not because it is inaccurate but because of what its use forecloses. This is Rodgers’ pragmatism given its philosophical ground: the test of a sense-making framework is the quality of the conversation that flows from it.

Improvisation is the practice in which offer and response generate living meaning.

Johnstone’s grammar — offer, accept, advance, block — describes genuine responsive engagement with the present. It is not a grammar for abandoning structure but for holding structure lightly enough that the structure can be revised by what the situation gives. The practitioner who deploys a framework as an offer — tentatively, curious about how it lands, attending to what the group does with it rather than steering the group toward the framework’s implied conclusion — is improvising. The practitioner who deploys the same framework as a prescription is blocking. The framework is identical; the relation to it is opposite. ‘Yes, and’ is not a technique but an epistemological commitment: to take the territory seriously on its own terms before attempting to map it.

Status cannot be abolished, only played consciously.

Every facilitated process enacts a status dynamic, and the facilitator who claims to suspend hierarchy is making a high-status move. This is not a problem to be solved but a condition to be worked with. The practitioner conscious of the status they are enacting can choose deliberately — high-status when the group needs a strong offer it must receive, low-status when it needs space and the modelled vulnerability of not-knowing. The practitioner unconscious of these dynamics reproduces them automatically, usually in contradiction of their stated intentions. This is Flinn’s quality of noticing applied to the register of power: tracking not only what is said but the status structure shaping who may say it.

The framework is an instrument, not a territory.

Rodgers’ pragmatic accommodation is not a retreat from complexity but an advance into its practical consequences. The practitioner who rejects all frameworks is not thereby living in the territory; they are living in the negative image of the frameworks they rejected. The practitioner who holds frameworks as situated, provisional, revisable instruments — knowing what each illuminates and what it cannot see — is doing something harder and more productive than either pure cartography or pure via negativa. The test is not the framework’s theoretical sophistication but what flows from its use: whether the conversations it generates are richer, more honest and more productive of genuine surprise than the conversations that would occur without it.

The living map is drawn in the act of traversal.

The synthesis is not a treaty assigning territories to three rival practices. It is the recognition that there is one practice. The practitioner doing it well draws the map while crossing the territory. They arrive with orientation — trained responsiveness, a vocabulary of forms, the capacity to recognise and make offers — but not with a script. They enter the territory, allow it to surprise them, let it make offers that contradict their prior maps, and revise those maps in real time, not as an afterthought but as the primary activity. They leave with a map different from the one they carried in: more detailed where the territory taught them detail, more honest about its gaps, more faithful to this particular territory as it was actually encountered. This is what the Stalker does in the Zone, what the clinician does in palpation, what the jazz musician does on the stand, what the scenario thinker does in re-perceiving the present. It is the trivium restored, the language-game played with a clear view of its grammar, the offer received before its use is known.

9.2What This Changes in Practice

Reading the room is a skill, not a gift.

When a practitioner reads the mood of a room with apparently effortless intuition, what is on display is not a gift but accumulated palpative intelligence — the capacity, built through long reflective encounter, to register what a situation is doing from inside it. The practitioner with only conceptual training reads the framework on the whiteboard. The practitioner with palpative intelligence reads the quality of attention, the energy, the weight of what has not been said, the precise moment a conversation is about to turn. This is Flinn’s quality of noticing, and it is cultivated the way the Stalker’s knowledge of the Zone is cultivated: by throwing nuts and reading where they land, over years.

The facilitator Johnnie Moore — who came to this work through improv theatre — has given the quality a name: the unhurried. The best improvisation, he observes, has an unhurried quality; the players can relate to each other and build the scene together without panic. His account of facilitation is deliberately small-scale, almost anti-heroic: facilitation, he writes, is “often about small, subtle acts of noticing and experimenting,” and what he calls “small-p presence” is simply being open to the life already in the room. Moore’s further claim is the one that matters most for the living map: that the collective intelligence a group can reach “exists between us, rather than in each of us.” Reading the room is not a private act of perception performed by a clever facilitator; it is a participation in something the group is generating together, and it is unhurried because what is between people cannot be rushed into being. This is, in a practitioner’s plain language, the same point the Rodgers comment makes when it praises Moore for two specific capacities — “reading the mood of the room,” and cultivating Pierre Wack’s network of conversations with interesting people beyond the organisation’s normal spheres of engagement.

Frameworks are opening offers, not closing answers.

Rodgers’ insight — that it is the conversation flowing from the framework that matters — transforms how a tool is introduced into a group. The Stacey Matrix offered as a diagnostic grid (where are we?) closes the conversation. The same matrix offered as a provocation (what does this illuminate? what does it miss? where does it fail to hold what we actually experience?) opens it. Same map; opposite relation to the territory. The framework deployed as offer invites the group to accept, advance, push back, or block — and the quality of that engagement is itself the most valuable data the practitioner receives.

Status dynamics are the furniture of organisational life.

They do not vanish because a facilitator declines to name them. The practitioner who can track status in real time — who notices when a particular person’s offers are systematically blocked by the room’s implicit hierarchy, when high-status participants are unconsciously silencing what the group most needs to hear — is doing developmental work that neither pure cartography nor pure via negativa can reach. Redistributing status, introducing status-disrupting offers, creating conditions in which a low-status participant can make a high-value contribution: this is skilled improvisation, and it requires both the map (the status vocabulary) and the live, responsive deployment of it in the conditions of this particular room.

Muddling through is the practice, not its failure.

The practitioner who believes they have resolved the immersion-abstraction paradox — who has settled, once and for all, whether frameworks are good or bad, whether process or structure comes first — has stopped practising and started reciting. Muddling through, understood with the seriousness Rodgers gives it, is the disciplined holding-open of the paradox: making provisional moves from partial perspectives, remaining genuinely susceptible to having one’s maps redrawn by what the territory offers, and doing all of this while remaining answerable to the people and the organisation one is working with. It is not comfortable and it is not tidy. It is what competent practice in genuinely complex conditions looks like.

Coda

ReturnWhat Remains When the Voyage Returns You

❖
Woven · Book I Book I codaM33 homecoming

Both books end with a return. Book I's canoe is held still; Kipling's Mariner goes home and marries. The Living Map's traveller returns with a map that no longer matches the one she left with.

The Chaos Puzzles essay — the companion volume that follows this coda — ended in Tarkovsky’s Zone, with Monkey moving glasses across a table by the force of her attention — changed by the Zone, the film refusing to say whether the change is catastrophe or gift. This paper ends a little differently, because its question has been not what the Zone does to those who enter it, but what competent people actually do once inside.

Every genuine voyage of inquiry ends somewhere other than it intended. The traveller sets out with a chart, encounters what the territory actually gives, and returns carrying a map that no longer matches the one they left with — because the territory refused to be mapped in advance. The organisation that has genuinely undergone the work of the living map is, in the same way, other than it was: not obviously more comfortable, but differently inhabited — less defended against the genuinely new, more able to receive what the territory actually offers rather than what the old framework predicted. Seamus Heaney’s Sweeney, cursed into the trees after the battle of Moira and composing his finest poetry from the branches, is the old emblem of this: the breakdown of the settled map as the condition of a different and truer kind of seeing.

And the practice does not stay achieved. This is the final and most demanding thing to say. The Zone is never permanently navigated; every entry is a new entry. Every group is a new configuration of offers. Every conversation is a fresh opportunity to discover that the map carried in does not hold what the territory is doing. The living map is not a competence acquired once and then possessed. It is a discipline maintained, lost, and renewed — closer to a musician’s daily practice or a clinician’s accumulating touch than to a certificate on a wall.

The traditions gathered in this paper can be set down, finally, as a single sentence each.

Korzybskithe map is not the territory.

Batesonand the territory is itself an endless regress of maps, so stop hunting for the bare ground.

Baudrillardbeware — the map can come to precede and devour the territory.

Carrollthe perfect map is useless; utility lives in what is left out.

Harawayso draw your map honestly, from somewhere, and stay answerable for what it cannot see.

Wittgensteinthe territory is a form of life, meaning is use, and you cannot leave the game — only learn to see it as a game.

Merleau-Pontyyou know it first with your body, before you know it with a proposition.

Deleuze & Guattarinavigate the smooth space haptically, by close-range feel, striating only enough to orient.

Bohmin company, suspend the assumption and let the implicate order unfold.

Wackre-perceive the present rather than forecast the future, and seek out the remarkable people who can offer what your own world cannot.

Johnstonereceive the offer before you know what you will do with it, and stop blocking.

Mullarkey‘yes, and’ is not about the words — it is accepting an offer and adding value, whatever you say.

Larsenspontaneity is the live uncertainty of genuine response, and it is inseparable from power.

Moorestay unhurried; the intelligence is between us, not in us.

Barretthold the chart lightly enough that it becomes a platform; provoke competence; minimal structure, maximal autonomy.

Weickact, then make sense of what you did — but earn the right to improvise.

Sayersthe tools of learning are a preparation, not a content.

Staceyhold both ‘ands’ at the same time.

Rodgersit is the conversation that matters, never the framework; the sin is false concreteness.

Flinncultivate the quality of noticing, because once you can see your own participation you cannot unsee it.

Mowlescome from inside, not from above — we cannot stand outside our commitments.

The living map is drawn in the act of traversal — by someone who arrived with orientation rather than a script, was willing to be changed by what they met, and held the map and the territory in a tension that neither cartography, nor process, nor improvisation alone could carry. The crash helmet is on the table. The nut is in the hand. The conversation has already begun.

Preface惖论

The Zone Is Not a Metaphor

Crossing From Sepia Into Colour

Woven · Book I M21 navigation without maps

Palpation before theory: the nervous system registers the Zone before cognition does. Book I's quantum navigators sense acceleration and rotation without any external map; the Stalker senses the Zone the same way.

There is a scene early in Andrei Tarkovsky’s Stalker (1979) that no framework can contain. Three figures — the Stalker, the Writer, the Professor — ride a flatcar through a post-industrial wasteland, passing from the sepia-toned world of the ordinary into the luminous, misted, hyper-real colour of the Zone. The transition is not announced. There is no cut, no title card, no pedagogical intervention. The world simply changes. The air changes. The quality of attention changes. And the viewer’s nervous system registers the shift before their cognition does.

This is palpation before it has been theorised. This is what Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari (1987) meant when they wrote about feeling one’s way through chaos, tracing potential, navigating the unknowable not through maps but through haptic intelligence — the body’s pre-cognitive wisdom about what a situation can do, before the analytical faculties have had time to construct their protective frameworks.

Chris Mowles’ Medium post “Complexity and Inside-Out Thinking” (2024) is a similar transition. It arrives in the reader’s phenomenal field like that flatcar ride — quietly, persistently, insisting on a different mode of engagement. But Mowles, for all his brilliance and the genuine radicalism of his project, stops at the edge of the Zone. He identifies the cartographic reflex with diagnostic precision. He proposes the choreographic alternative with philosophical rigour. And then — like the Professor in Tarkovsky’s film, who nearly detonates a bomb in the Room before weeping at his own failure of nerve — he arrives at the threshold of the deepest paradox and turns back.

This paper does not turn back. What follows is a ten-movement critical analysis expanded to its fullest extent, built around the Chinese concept of 惖论 (bèi lùn) — literally “contrary-discourse,” the paradox that re-poses itself at a deeper level each time you think you have resolved it. It is written simultaneously in the register of academic rigour and in the burning, chrome-and-neon prose of the cyberpunk tradition, because complexity — real complexity, the kind Stacey, Mowles, and Flinn have dedicated careers to thinking — cannot be adequately addressed in a single register without immediately falsifying it.

In working notes attributed to Tarkovsky [source unverified], the line appears: “In the Zone, each person encounters only what they bring with them. The Zone does not give what is desired; it gives what is true.” This paper attempts something similar. What you bring to it will determine what you find. The crash helmet is optional. The encounter is not.

Movement I惖论

Neon Entry: The Blog Post as Paradox Device

The Cartographic Reflex and Its Discontents

Woven · Book I M2 the brochureM12 I-Space

Mowles's salvo against 2×2 grids hits the WRAS matrix and the SenseMaker triad alike. Book I's Part I tested both on their own terms before agreeing.

Most of the thinking I encounter aimed at helping organisations grapple with their problems has to do with maps and frameworks of a world which is thought to exist ‘out there’. These two by two grids, parts and whole charts and frameworks, even imagined estuaries, are more or less realist and representationalist.Chris Mowles, Medium (2024)

The blog post opens with a salvo. Chrome hitting concrete. In the flickering neon underbelly of late-capitalist organisational life — where chrome-plated frameworks rust under the acid rain of perpetual uncertainty, where the consultant’s 2x2 grid hangs on the boardroom wall like a sacred icon before which executives genuflect without belief — Mowles’ text detonates. It is not a blog post. It is a 惖论. A paradox device. A bomb planted in the phenomenal field of management education.

The diagnosis is acute and philosophically well-grounded. For decades, the dominant modes of organisational consulting have operated on a single unexamined assumption: that organisations are systems that exist “out there,” separate from the people who constitute them, mappable, diagnosable, improvable through the correct application of conceptual tools. From Ansoff’s corporate planning matrices of the 1960s through the BCG growth-share grid, from Kotter’s eight-step change model to the McKinsey 7-S Framework, from the balanced scorecard to the VUCA model — all rest on what Stacey and Mowles (2016) call the “cognitivist assumption”: that a sufficiently detached and analytically skilled manager can stand outside their organisation, see it whole, diagnose its condition, and design its future.

In Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics (7th ed., 2016), Stacey and Mowles trace the genealogy of this reflex with forensic patience, showing how its internal contradictions accumulate until the model collapses under its own logical weight:

The systemic assumption — that organisations are wholes whose behaviour can be understood by analysis of their component parts and the relationships between them — generates a series of increasingly elaborate modifications once it encounters the actual messiness of organisational life. The open system, the complex adaptive system, the learning organisation: each is a patch on a model that cannot accommodate what it encounters. The patches accumulate. The model becomes baroque. And still it fails to account for the most important feature of organisational dynamics: that the people who constitute organisations are self-interpreting, reflexive, emotionally complex, politically motivated human beings whose interactions produce outcomes that none of them individually intends or controls.Ralph Stacey & Chris Mowles, Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics, 7th ed. (2016)

Mowles names this, correctly, as what Kant called “regulative ideas” — methods to think with, ambitious abstractions that attempt to understand big problems in the round. He traces the phenomenology of this approach with precision: the assumption that you cannot understand what you are dealing with unless you map the territory; that you cannot make a journey until you can identify your destination; that the relationship between parts and whole, when those parts are “self-interpreting, rationally-irrational human beings,” is “something of a mystery.”

And yet — and here the first ghost of 惖论 stirs in the circuitry — the very act of articulating this insight produces a new kind of overview. The critic of cartography draws a map of cartography’s limits. The theorist of emergence produces a theory. The professor who rejects frameworks delivers lectures structured by the unacknowledged framework of rejection. The Zone is entered, and immediately a new version of the old outside-in gaze reasserts itself, dressed now in the vocabulary of process and interaction rather than systems and design, but occupying the same structural position: the knower surveying the known, the method applied to the material.

Stacey was alert to this recursion throughout his career. In Complexity and Organizational Reality (2010), he wrote with characteristic directness about the limits of his own earlier work:

I am aware that the perspective I am developing here is itself a framework — a set of concepts, distinctions, and ways of attending to organisational life that shapes what I see and what I cannot see. I cannot step outside this framework to verify it against an unmediated reality. None of us can. The question is not whether we use frameworks but whether we hold them with the appropriate degree of tentativeness, aware of what they foreground and what they render invisible, ready to revise them when they stop illuminating and start obscuring.Ralph Stacey, Complexity and Organizational Reality (2010)

This is the Stacey who wears the crash helmet: not the triumphant demolisher of the Stacey Matrix, but the patient, self-aware thinker who knows that the demolition of one framework is always, simultaneously, the construction of another. The crash helmet is not armour against the complexity of organisational life. It is armour against the impact of his own thinking — because genuine thought, pursued with sufficient honesty, always eventually runs into the wall of its own assumptions.

惖论Chaos Puzzle #1

Any consistent rejection of frameworks is itself a framework. The anti-cartographic manifesto is a cartographic act performed at a higher level of abstraction. The critique does not escape the condition it diagnoses; it instantiates it in a more sophisticated register. The first chaos puzzle does not invalidate Mowles’ project. It deepens it. The 惖论 is an invitation to go further into the Zone.

Movement II惖论

The Stacey Matrix as Onto-Phenomenological Machine

From Grid to Animated Substrate: Husserl Enters the Zone

Woven · Book I Liber II, Part 17Liber II, Part 14

The Stacey Matrix appears in all three books: here as an onto-phenomenological machine, in Liber Secundus as a matrix with a deleted political axis and as the jacket its maker took off.

The Stacey Matrix — in its original form, a two-by-two grid plotting degree of certainty against degree of agreement — is the most famous artefact of Stacey’s intellectual career, and also the one he came to regard with the most productive ambivalence. In Complexity and Organizational Reality (2010), Stacey distanced himself from the simplified version that had circulated through management consulting with alarming speed:

The matrix as it has been taken up in management consulting practice collapses the paradox of certainty and uncertainty and so sustains the dominant discourse of managerial control that the complexity perspective was supposed to challenge. When managers use the matrix to locate themselves in the ‘complex zone’ and then ask what tool to apply to manage the complexity they have diagnosed, they have entirely missed the point. The point is that there is no tool. The point is that the manager is already inside the complexity they are trying to stand outside of and diagnose.Ralph Stacey, Complexity and Organizational Reality (2010)

This is a remarkable act of theoretical self-revision. The author of the most-used complexity framework in management education explicitly repudiates the way his framework has been used, because its use has betrayed its intention. Taken as a diagnostic grid, the Stacey Matrix reinstates exactly the managerial overview that the complexity perspective undermines: the practitioner standing outside the system looking at it, locating it on a map, deciding which tools to apply.

But the comments on Mowles’ post offer a more radical reinterpretation that rescues the Matrix from both its naive use and Stacey’s own repudiation:

The Matrix is an onto-phenomenological cartographical grid — an animated substrate running beneath the surface of all organisational dynamics, all conversation and all [psycho-dynamic] group relations. Inside-out thinking does not exist unless it is a Hertfordshire Tardis style Huddle in a room which from the outside looks like the size of a manhole. The real issue is the implicate-explicate nature of the Stacey Matrix from a phenomenological perspective.Comment on Mowles’ blog post

This is a crucial philosophical move that deserves sustained analysis. Rather than treating the Stacey Matrix as a representation of organisational territory — a picture of where you are, drawn from outside — the comment treats it as what Edmund Husserl would call a “noematic schema”: the structured intentional content through which organisational experience presents itself to any reflective practitioner at all. Not a map of the territory, but the structure of the territory’s presenting.

Husserl’s distinction between noesis (the act of intending, the directedness of consciousness toward its object) and noema (the intentional content, what the act is about as experienced) is the key. The noesis is the practitioner’s attending consciousness, felt in what Husserl called the “temporal thickness” of the living present: the retention of what has just passed, the primal impression of what is occurring right now, and the protention of what is about to occur. The noema is the organisational situation as-experienced — not as it “objectively” is (if such a thing could be independently established), but as it presents itself to this practitioner, in this moment, with this relational history.

Understood this way, the dimensions of the Stacey Matrix — certainty and agreement, or their absence — are not properties of an objective situation to be diagnosed from outside. They are dimensions of how the situation presents itself in the noematic experience of a reflective practitioner. “We are in the complex zone” is not a cartographic claim. It is a phenomenological report: this situation presents itself to me as one in which the degree of certainty about outcomes and the degree of agreement about what to do are both low, and I notice that this presentation generates in me a particular quality of anxiety and a particular temptation to reach for familiar tools that will reduce the anxiety by reinstating a false certainty.

The Husserlian analysis transforms the Tardis-huddle from whimsy into theory. The group analytic session is phenomenologically asymmetric: from outside, it appears small, bounded, contained — a room in a university building, a handful of people sitting in a circle, no products, no deliverables, no visible outcomes. From inside, in the noematic field of lived participation, it is potentially infinite: it contains, in its relational dynamics, the entirety of the social world that each participant carries within them. Every group member arrives with their entire relational history encoded in their body, their emotional patterns, their characteristic ways of registering the salience of what happens in the room.

This interior expansion is central to one account of what leadership development, at its most ambitious, attempts:

We are all meaning-making animals, embedded in social and cultural practices that shape what it is possible for us to mean. The developmental encounter is not the addition of new competencies to a pre-existing self. It is the creation of conditions in which the practitioner can encounter the assumptions, habits, and emotional patterns that have previously been operating entirely outside awareness — the automatic responses, the unexamined loyalties, the defended territories of self-concept that shape every interaction without ever appearing in the practitioner’s conscious deliberation. The group is the mirror in which these patterns become, painfully and productively, visible.[unattributed]

The group-as-mirror is the Tardis: small from outside, infinite from within. And the Stacey Matrix, in its onto-phenomenological reading, is the structure of what the mirror reflects: not a diagram of certainty and agreement plotted on axes, but the living felt sense of the practitioner’s relationship to the unknown, their tolerance for ambiguity, their capacity to remain present in the face of the genuinely uncertain. The Matrix is inside, not outside. It is the structure of experience, not the picture of a system.

David Bohm’s distinction between the implicate and explicate orders is the ontological scaffold for this reading. The implicate order is the enfolded structure of potential from which the explicate order of observable pattern continuously unfolds. In Bohm’s holomovement, what we observe as stable structure — the organisational chart, the strategic plan, the culture survey results, the Stacey Matrix plotted on a whiteboard — is always already the temporary crystallisation of a deeper, enfolded movement that cannot be reduced to any of its explicate manifestations.

In the third image from the Stalker stills: the shallow water spreading across the Zone’s post-industrial landscape is the implicate order made visible. The surface is not still. It is alive with movement that barely registers as pattern. The black dog standing at its edge reads it perfectly, without theory, without a framework, without a diagnostic grid. The dog is palpating the Zone.

惖论Chaos Puzzle #2

The Matrix cannot be transcended by abandoning it. It can only be deepened by entering it. The inside-out move does not escape cartography; it discovers that the map was always already phenomenological. What was thought to be a representation of external reality was, all along, a structure of internal experience — a noematic schema through which the Zone presents itself to whoever is patient enough to feel it.

Movement III惖论

Inside-Out Thinking and the Via Negativa Trap

Foulkes, Piaget, Jaeggi, and the Magic Roundabout

Woven · Book I Liber II, Part 4

Inside-out thinking and the via negativa trap meet Liber Secundus's charge that Mowles's conference is a liturgy resting on the undeclared frame of group analysis.

Mowles’ constructive proposal is inside-out thinking: attending to local patterns of relating in groups, through free association, no imposed agenda, and the accumulation of what Piaget calls “liberated convictions” — insights produced through group processes that “question and probe, which in turn provoke spontaneous insight based on participants’ original experience.” The method draws on S. H. Foulkes’ group analytic tradition, which holds that any group of more than eight people contains sufficient variety of deviations from the social norm to generate insights about broader social trends. The group becomes a microcosm. Local interaction yields global understanding. The fractal logic of social patterning means that what is true here, in this room, with these specific people, resonates with what is true out there, in the broader social field.

This is philosophically serious and therapeutically effective. It is also, as the comments identify with precision, a via negativa — an approach that defines itself primarily through what it rejects: not frameworks, not maps, not systems, not alignment, not managed emergence, not strategic intent, not outcome-orientation, not imposed agenda. What remains when all these are stripped away is the group in free association, attended to with reflexive precision.

The via negativa, in the mystical tradition it inherits from Pseudo-Dionysius through Meister Eckhart to John of the Cross, is the method of approaching the ineffable by successive negation. Not this, not that, not any of these things, until what remains is the unnameable itself. In Eckhart’s formulation: “To get at the core of God at his greatest, one must first get into the core of himself at his least.” The via negativa is a movement inward and downward, through successive abandonments of the surface, toward the ground of being that cannot be grasped but can be inhabited.

Mowles’ via negativa strips away the frameworks not to find God but to find the group’s own intelligence — the “liberated convictions” that cannot emerge while the agenda and the outcome-orientation and the strategic intent are pre-occupying the room’s attentional field. This is valuable. But there is a deep structural problem, identified elsewhere with characteristic directness:

There is a version of the complexity perspective — and I say this with the utmost respect for colleagues I admire — that can become a sophisticated form of learned helplessness. The practitioner learns to notice the complexity of their participation. They learn to hold their frameworks more lightly. They learn to sit with uncertainty. And then they sit with it. And sit with it some more. And the organisation around them continues to generate patterns of interaction that are harmful, unjust, or simply stuck — and the practitioner observes these patterns with increasing reflexive sophistication and decreasing practical engagement. This is not the fulfilment of the complexity perspective. It is its shadow.[unattributed]

The shadow of the via negativa is precisely the magic roundabout. The roundabout is not stupid. Its horses are made of Norbert Elias and Foulkes and Piaget and Stacey. Its music is the language of emergence and co-construction and regular-irregularity. Its operator is sophisticated and theoretically well-equipped. And it goes around. And around. And around. “This is the end, my beautiful friend.” And yet it is not the end. It is the stuck place.

Stacey himself was alert to this danger. In Managing in Uncertainty (2011), he inserted a passage that has been underemphasised by his interpreters:

We have no option but to muddle through the practical implications of the immersion-abstraction paradox. It therefore seems to me that viewing abstraction in terms of either narrative and philosophy (‘good’) or the use of sense-making frameworks (‘bad’) limits the possibilities available for shifting the patterning of people’s perspectives, practices and performance in organisationally beneficial and personally resonant ways. If people are to ‘get to grips’ fully with organisational complexity, I would suggest that they need to use both ‘ands’ at the same time.Ralph Stacey, in Managing in Uncertainty (2011)

Both ‘ands’ at the same time. Abstraction and immersion. Narrative and framework. Map and territory. Cartography and choreography. The immersion-abstraction paradox is not dissolved by choosing one pole. It is lived, muddled through, held in creative tension. This is not a synthesis that transcends the tension. It is a mature relationship to the tension — a quality of noticing:

The quality of noticing I am pointing to is not a technique. It is not a competency that can be trained and assessed. It is an attentional capacity that has to be cultivated over time, through repeated immersive encounter with the full complexity of organisational interaction, combined with sustained reflective engagement with one’s own participation in that interaction. It holds simultaneously the immersed experience of local interaction and the abstracted pattern-recognition that gives that experience meaning and direction. It does not abandon frameworks; it holds them reflexively, aware of what they illuminate and what they obscure, ready to set them aside when the situation demands a different kind of attention.[unattributed]

The via negativa without a via positiva is an infinite regression — not a descent to the ground of being but a free-fall through successive abandonments that never reaches bottom. The via positiva that Mowles’ inside-out thinking requires — but does not quite supply — is what this paper identifies as palpation: the active, energetic, skilled sensing of what is immanent in the present configuration of forces. Not the stripping away of frameworks until nothing is left, but the cultivation of a quality of presence that can feel the lines of flight running through whatever configuration it encounters.

惖论Chaos Puzzle #3

The via negativa, pursued with sufficient rigour, becomes its own framework — a map of how not to map, a method of rejecting methods. The via positiva that completes it is palpation: not the absence of structure but the felt sense of what a situation can do. The magic roundabout stops when the practitioner learns to throw the nut.

Movement IV惖论

Deleuzian Palpation: Feeling Through Chaos

Haptic Intelligence, Lines of Flight, and the Nut-Throwing Stalker

Woven · Book I M30 smooth and striatedM23 weak measurement

Deleuzian palpation is the haptic reading of smooth space. Book I adds the physics: palpation is weak measurement, enough contact to learn, not enough to freeze.

Altius Haptic and optic space

Deleuze and Guattari borrowed the haptic–optic distinction from the art historian Alois Riegl, who contrasted close-range vision that feels its way across a surface with distant vision that takes in a whole. Smooth space is haptic; striated space is optic. The Stalker's nut is a haptic instrument extended: it touches the Zone at a distance one step ahead. Organisational palpation, on this reading, means working at close range with short feedback loops, where the hand learns what no overview could show.

Playable
Throw the nut

Cross the Zone from the bottom-left to the Room at the top-right. Traps are invisible and shift after every step. Click a neighbouring square to throw a nut: it shows whether that square is safe now. Press Step to walk to your last safe nut. Or try Walk by the map, which marches straight on a chart drawn at the start.

The concept of palpation, as deployed in the comments and developed here, draws on Deleuze and Guattari’s distinction in A Thousand Plateaus (1987) between striated and smooth space. Striated space is organised, metric, gridded — the space of the settled, the mapped, the administered. Smooth space is haptic, intensive, directional without being metricised — the space of the nomad, the navigator without instruments, the body in direct contact with the territory it is feeling.

Palpation is the mode of engagement appropriate to smooth space. In clinical medicine, palpation is the physician’s hands pressing the patient’s abdomen, feeling for the liver’s edge, the spleen’s enlargement, the abnormal mass. Not representing these things in a diagram first, but sensing them directly, interpretively, through trained touch. The diagnosis emerges from the palpation itself, not from an algorithm applied to data that palpation produces. The experienced clinician’s hands know things that the clinician’s conscious mind has not yet formulated.

In Tarkovsky’s Stalker, the Zone-guide’s primary method is precisely this. He throws a weighted nut ahead on its cloth strip — a small proxy body used to test the territory before the main body commits to it. The nut lands. The ground holds, or it does not. The Stalker reads the response not through analysis but through the accumulated somatic intelligence of someone who has spent years learning the Zone’s language. He knows the Zone the way the skilled clinician knows the liver: through a kind of knowledge that cannot be adequately represented in a diagram, because it is distributed across the body’s history of encounter with this particular territory.

Stacey (2001) describes the skilled practitioner’s relationship to complex responsive process in terms that map with uncanny precision onto this image:

The capacity to participate skilfully in complex responsive processes is not primarily cognitive. It is not a matter of understanding the right framework and applying it correctly. It is a matter of what I can only call practical wisdom — the embodied, relational, temporally thick intelligence of someone who has spent time in the field, who has learned to read the signals that the field sends, and who has developed the capacity to respond to those signals in ways that are generative rather than defensive. This practical wisdom is Aristotle’s phronesis: it cannot be taught by instruction but can be cultivated through sustained, reflective immersion in practice.Ralph Stacey, Complex Responsive Processes in Organizations (2001)

Phronesis — practical wisdom, knowledge of how to act well in specific circumstances — is exactly what the Stalker has and the Professor lacks. The Professor is not stupid. He carries an entire scientific education, a sophisticated understanding of the Zone’s official history, and a specific intention about what to do when he arrives at the Room. And it is precisely his intention, his planning, his strategic certainty about the right course of action, that nearly destroys everything. The Stalker’s wisdom is the capacity to remain present to what the Zone is actually doing, moment by moment, rather than executing a plan derived from what the Zone should be doing according to theory.

Lines of flight (lignes de fuite) are, in Deleuzian ontology, the vectors of becoming immanent within any given configuration of forces — the directions in which the situation tends to move, the potential trajectories not yet actualised but real as tendency and pressure. The practitioner who can sense the lines of flight in an organisational situation is not predicting the future. They are feeling the pre-possible: what Deleuze calls the virtual, that which is real without yet being actual, present as directional energy before it crystallises into event.

The thermodynamic argument developed in the comments gives this an energetic formulation that is both precise and generative:

If you remove the adaptive from CAS [Complex Adaptive Systems] you remove the energy. If you remove the responsive from CRP [Complex Responsive Process] you remove the energy. If you remove the potential from CPS [Complex Potential States] you remove the energy. If you remove the social [dynamic of conversations] from CSP [Complex Social Process] you remove the energy. Complexity is a form of entropy. So you have to decide on emphasis and in finding emphasis palpation matters. Deleuzian philosophy encourages us to interact with the world through ‘lines of flight’ or experimentation, effectively ‘feeling out’ (or palpating) new possibilities.Comment on Mowles’ blog post

Complexity without energy becomes entropy. This is not standard complexity theory, but it is structurally correct. Every living system expends energy to maintain the conditions of its own complexity. Remove the energetic input and the system moves toward the equilibrium of maximum entropy: undifferentiated, featureless, dead. The organisation that has stopped being adaptive has become inert. The group process that has stopped being responsive has become ritual. The practitioner who has stopped being present has become a facilitating robot — executing the method without inhabiting it.

The energetic dimension of developmental practice has been made explicit in one particularly important passage:

The most important thing a leader can bring to a complex situation is not a model or a framework or a plan. It is a quality of attentional presence that can hold the tension between what is and what might be, that can tolerate the anxiety of genuine uncertainty without prematurely closing down the space of inquiry, and that can sustain the group’s capacity for generative interaction long enough for something genuinely new to emerge. This quality of presence is itself a form of energy. It is not passive attention. It is active, contributory, shaping. The practitioner who brings it to a group changes what the group is capable of.[unattributed]

Active, contributory, shaping. The facilitator’s presence is not neutral. It is an energetic contribution to the field — palpation operating in both directions. The practitioner feels the group’s energetic state and contributes to it simultaneously. The Stalker does not merely read the Zone. The Zone reads the Stalker. The quality of the encounter depends on what both parties bring to it.

惖论Chaos Puzzle #4

Palpation is the energy that prevents complexity from becoming entropy. But palpation cannot be methodised without ceasing to be palpation — the moment you turn it into a technique, you have re-entered striated space. The only way to develop palpative capacity is through repeated immersive encounter with the Zone: throwing nuts, reading responses, accumulating the somatic intelligence of someone who knows this particular territory from inside.

Movement V惖论

Rogers’ Nineteen Propositions as Organisational Hermeneutic

Self-Structure, Introjection, and What Monkey Knows

Woven · Book I Liber II, Part 19M27 QBism

Rogers's phenomenal field, 'reality for the individual', is the QBist agent's personal state. Liber Secundus reads Rogers's way of being as the most incorporated jacket of all.

Altius Congruence and psychological safety

Rogers's congruence, the overlap of self-structure and experience, has an organisational descendant in Edmondson's psychological safety, the shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Where safety is low, experience that does not fit the official story is denied or distorted, exactly as Rogers predicted for persons. Edmondson's research shows such teams report fewer errors and learn less. Widening organisational congruence is therefore not therapy; it is the precondition of learning from what actually happens.

Carl Rogers’ nineteen propositions about the organism and its phenomenal field (1951) constitute one of the most rigorous and most persistently underused frameworks in organisational psychology. Rogers was not writing about organisations. He was writing about individual psychotherapy and the conditions of psychological growth. But the structural logic of his account maps with uncanny precision onto the dynamics of organisational life as Stacey, Mowles, and Flinn describe it.

The first proposition is foundational: “All individuals (organisms) exist in a continually changing world of experience (phenomenal field) of which they are the centre.” The second follows from it: “The organism reacts to the field as it is experienced and perceived. This perceptual field is ‘reality’ for the individual.” These two propositions together constitute a comprehensive rejection of the view-from-nowhere that Mowles identifies as the cartographic reflex’s deepest assumption. There is no neutral, objective reality to be mapped. There is only the phenomenal field as experienced by the organism that inhabits it. Reality is always already perspectival, always already affectively charged, always already organised by the self-structure of the perceiver.

Proposition five: “The organism has one basic tendency and striving — to actualise, maintain and enhance the experiencing organism.” This is the Rogersian version of Deleuze’s lines of flight: every organism has an inherent directional energy, a tendency toward its own flourishing, that precedes and grounds all specific motivations. In the organisational context: every participant in a group process brings this actualisation tendency. The question is whether the group process creates conditions in which the tendency finds expression in collective creativity, or whether it finds expression — as it more commonly does in organisational settings — in defensive manoeuvring, political gaming, and the protection of existing self-structures against the threat of genuine change.

Propositions ten through fifteen are where the organisational implications become most precise. Proposition ten states that experiences occur and are either (a) symbolised, perceived and organised into some relation to the self, (b) ignored because there is no perceived relationship to the self-structure, or (c) denied symbolisation or given distorted symbolisation because the experience is inconsistent with the structure of the self. Stacey (2001) recognises exactly this tripartite structure in his account of how complex responsive processes handle the genuinely new:

Novelty — genuine novelty, not merely variation within an established pattern — is always threatening to the existing order of things, including the existing order of the self. The organisation that encounters something genuinely new will tend to assimilate it to its existing categories (symbolise it in relation to existing self-structure), ignore it if the existing categories cannot accommodate it (ignore because no perceived relationship to self-structure), or actively suppress it if it threatens the existing order (deny symbolisation or distort). Only under conditions of sufficient psychological safety — what Rogers would call the absence of threat to the self-structure — can the genuinely new be perceived and engaged with rather than categorised, ignored, or suppressed.Ralph Stacey, Complex Responsive Processes in Organizations (2001)

Proposition fifteen makes the systemic consequence explicit: “Any experience that is inconsistent with the organisation of the structure of the self may be perceived as a threat, and the more of these perceptions there are, the more rigidly the self structure is organised to maintain itself.” This is the mechanism of organisational stuck-ness: the more threatened a practitioner or leader feels by the complexity and uncertainty of their situation, the more rigidly they cling to their frameworks, their certainties, their maps — the very things that prevent genuine engagement with what is actually happening.

Proposition sixteen offers the therapeutic key: “Under certain conditions, involving primarily complete absence of threat to the self structure, experiences inconsistent with it may be perceived and examined, and the structure of self revised to assimilate and include such experiences.” This is the precise account of what Mowles’ inside-out thinking attempts to create: conditions of sufficient absence of threat that the self-structure can relax its defensive rigidity long enough to perceive and examine what has previously been excluded.

And proposition eighteen is the destination of the whole developmental arc: as the individual accepts into their self-structure more of their organic experiences, they find that they are “replacing their present value system — based extensively on introjections which have been distortedly symbolised — with a continuing organismic valuing process.” The introjected value system is the assemblage of borrowed frameworks, received wisdoms, institutional expectations, and professional identities that practitioners carry into their organisations — the “taken-for-granted” that Mowles identifies as the constraining force on genuine inquiry. The continuing organismic valuing process is what replaces it: an ongoing, fluid, experientially-grounded evaluation of what matters and what doesn’t, responsive to the actual phenomenal field rather than to introjected assumptions.

One account of what might be called the “borrowed certainties” is the organisational instantiation of Rogers’ introjected value system:

The leaders who come through our programmes often arrive carrying what I can only describe as borrowed certainties — frameworks and models they have absorbed from business schools, consulting firms, and leadership development programmes, which they apply with varying degrees of self-awareness to situations that resist them. The borrowed certainties feel like knowledge. They feel like professional competence. They are, in Rogers’ terms, introjections: values and beliefs taken over from others and perceived in distorted fashion, as if they had been experienced directly. The developmental encounter is the process of discovering the difference between what you actually think and feel, and what you have been trained to think and feel. This difference, once perceived, cannot be unperceived.[unattributed]

The difference, once perceived, cannot be unperceived. This is the catamorphological dimension of the developmental encounter: it is irreversible. You cannot un-have the experience of perceiving that what you took to be your own value system is largely an assemblage of introjections. The self-structure, once revised to include this perception, does not return to its previous configuration.

In the closing image of Stalker, Monkey — the Stalker’s daughter, born in the Zone’s shadow, telekinetic, unable to walk without a wheelchair — pushes glasses across the table with the force of her concentration. Her eyes are level at the camera. The expression is beyond hope and despair both. This is Rogers’ proposition eighteen, embodied. Monkey has not yet learned to deny her significant sensory and visceral experiences. Her self-structure has not yet solidified around borrowed certainties and introjected value systems. The actualisation tendency flows through her without the defensive structures that adult professional life erects. She is what becomes possible when the organism has access to the full range of its organic experience and can respond to the phenomenal field without the distortions of introjection. The Zone did not break her. It made her more completely herself.

惖论Chaos Puzzle #5

Inside-out thinking creates conditions for the Rogersian transition from introjected value system to continuing organismic valuing process. But it assumes the group process itself is free of introjection. It is not. The challenge is to hold the group’s own noematic structure — its characteristic ways of attending, its shared silences and shared volubilities — with the same reflexive lightness that good practitioners are asked to hold their individual frameworks.
